1.overview:
At Sinai, a month after the tabernacle is set up, the LORD tells Moses and Aaron to count Israel. With one leader from each tribe beside them, they register every male twenty years old and upward who can go to war, family by family. The tribal totals come in one after another, from Reuben's 46,500 to Judah's 74,600, and the sum is 603,550. The tribe of Levi is left off the list. Its men are to carry, set up and guard the tabernacle and to camp around it, so that no wrath falls on the congregation.

This is a muster for war, not a count of the whole people. Every tribe's entry repeats that the men counted were those “able to go forth to war,” and women, children and Levites stay off the roll. Israel will leave Sinai as an army, with the tabernacle in its keeping.

1.hermeneutics:
At Mari on the Euphrates, letters from the 18th century BC speak of a registration of men for royal service called *tebibtum*, a word built on a root meaning “to be clean.” E. A. Speiser argued in 1958 that a census there carried a rite of purification, and he set it beside Exodus 30:12, where every man counted pays a half-shekel ransom “that there be no plague among them.” Israel's memory of David's census, which ended in a pestilence (2 Samuel 24:1–15), shows the same unease about counting people. A first hearer would feel that risk here. The count goes ahead because the LORD orders it, and the Levites camp around the tabernacle “that there be no wrath upon the congregation” (v. 53).

The totals are very large. Six hundred thousand fighting men implies a people of two million or more, where the armies Egypt and the Hittites brought to Kadesh around 1274 BC are reckoned in the tens of thousands. The Hebrew word for “thousand,” *elef*, also names a clan or a company of men. Gideon calls his *elef* “my family” (Judges 6:15), Samuel assembles Israel “by your thousands” (1 Samuel 10:19), and the tribal leaders here are “heads of thousands” (v. 16). George Mendenhall proposed in 1958 that the lists once counted such units rather than thousands; others read the totals as they stand. Either way, an ancient hearer knew *elef* as both a number and a body of men under a captain.

notes: **The formula:** each tribal entry runs the same way: generations, families, fathers' houses, number of names, twenty years and upward, able to go to war, then the figure. Only Reuben's and Simeon's entries add “by their polls” (vv. 20, 22).
**Repetition to watch:** “all that were able to go forth to war” comes 14 times (v. 3, each of the twelve entries, and v. 45). The verb *paqad*, “number,” comes 22 times.

**A turn on one verb:** Levi is “not numbered” with *paqad* (vv. 47, 49), and in v. 50 Moses is told to “appoint” the Levites over the tabernacle with the same verb. The tribes are mustered for war; Levi is mustered for the tabernacle.

Numbers opens with a date and a place, and its first subsection runs to 2:34, where Israel “pitched by their standards, and so they set forward.” Chapter 1 counts the army; chapter 2 places it around the tabernacle. Together they turn the people who left Egypt into a camp ready to march from Sinai (10:11).

**Forward:** this census defines a generation. After the spies, the LORD sentences “all that were numbered of you” from twenty years old and upward to die in the wilderness (14:29), and the second census finds none of them left but Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65).

traditions.text: The midrash asks why the book opens “in the wilderness of Sinai” and answers that the Torah was given with fire, with water, and in the wilderness. All three are free to everyone, and so is the Torah. A second reading adds that only a person who makes himself like the wilderness, ownerless and open to all comers, can acquire wisdom and Torah. The book's Hebrew name, *Bemidbar*, comes from this same opening phrase.

Rashi explains why God counts Israel so often: they are dear to him. He counted them when they left Egypt, again after the golden calf to learn how many were left, and now as he comes to dwell among them, a month after the tabernacle was raised. On this reading the census is an act of affection, a different tone from the military muster on the surface of the text.

Nahmanides admits he cannot see why God wanted the numbers at all. He suggests the count displayed God's mercy, since seventy souls went down to Egypt and now the men alone were as the sand, and that each man who passed before Moses and Aaron and was known to them by name gained merit by it. He also discusses a line he quotes from Rashi: the Hebrew for “take the sum” is literally “lift the head,” which can describe honor or what an executioner does.

Josephus tells the census as Moses' review of the host, taken “to settle the affairs of war.” He counts men from twenty to fifty, an upper age the text does not give, and his total is 603,650, a hundred more than Numbers. The Levites are left out, he says, because they were holy and free from such burdens, and Ephraim and Manasseh fill the places of Levi and Joseph among the heads of tribes.

This retelling of biblical history, preserved in Latin, has God order the count, and the written record of it, so that his promise to the fathers of seed like the stars of heaven can be seen fulfilled. It adds that only a fiftieth part of the people came up out of Egypt and the rest died there. Its census reaches 604,550, and Moses also counts the men over fifty and the boys under twenty, groups Numbers leaves out.

The rabbis taught that Israel may not be counted directly, even for a commandment, and pointed to Saul, who they said counted his army by lambs, reading the place name Telaim in 1 Samuel 15:4 as “lambs.” Hosea's promise that Israel will be as the sand “which cannot be measured nor numbered” (Hosea 1:10) became the proof text. One answer to the verse's tension fits this chapter: Israel has a number when God counts them, and is beyond counting by human hands.

Origen notices who is left off the list: women, slaves, the mixed company from Egypt, and boys under twenty. He asks what good it does a reader to know which part of the people was counted in the desert, and answers that the law is spiritual and the list maps the soul's growth. Whoever puts away childish ways and becomes strong enough to fight the evil one is counted in God's numbers, as God numbers the stars (Psalm 147:4) and as the very hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered (Matthew 10:30).

Paul reminds the Corinthians that the fathers who passed through the sea and ate spiritual meat “were overthrown in the wilderness.” Hebrews asks with whom God was grieved forty years and answers that it was those who sinned and whose bodies fell in the desert, shut out of his rest by unbelief. Both look back to the men registered here, the generation Numbers later sentences to die before reaching the land (14:29).

John hears the number of the sealed and gives it as a tribal roll, twelve thousand from each tribe. The list differs from this one in telling ways. Judah stands first, as in the camp of Numbers 2, Levi is counted with the rest, Dan is missing, and Joseph appears beside Manasseh instead of Ephraim. Numbers does the reverse: it keeps Levi off the roll and makes up the twelve by counting Ephraim and Manasseh as two tribes (vv. 32–35).

2.overview:
The LORD tells Moses and Aaron how the counted tribes are to camp: each man by his own standard, facing the tabernacle from a distance. Three tribes take each side. Judah, Issachar and Zebulun camp on the east, Reuben, Simeon and Gad on the south, Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin on the west, and Dan, Asher and Naphtali on the north. Every tribe has a captain and a total, and every group of three has its place in the line of march. The tabernacle and the Levites travel in the middle, and Israel does as commanded.

The east side, toward the sunrise and the tabernacle's door, goes to Judah, not to Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. Judah is also the largest tribe, and its camp sets out first (v. 9), with Reuben's camp second. The precedence that will mark Israel's later history, Judah at the head, is already drawn into the shape of the camp.

2.hermeneutics:
Reliefs of Ramesses II's campaign against the Hittites at Kadesh, about 1274 BC, were carved on several Egyptian temples. They show his war camp from above: a rectangle walled with soldiers' shields, entered from the east, with the king's tent in the middle, an outer room leading to an inner one. Kenneth Kitchen and Michael Homan have pointed to this camp as the closest ancient parallel to the tabernacle and its court. Numbers 2 takes the comparison further than the tent. The whole people becomes the camp, laid out square to the compass and facing inward, and the tent in its center belongs to Israel's divine king.

Ramesses marched to Kadesh with four divisions named for gods, Amun, Re, Ptah and Seth, each with its own place in the column; Amun's division led the way. An army of the period was a set of named units under standards, and the order of march was part of the plan of battle. Numbers gives Israel the same shape: four camps of three tribes, each with a standard, a captain for every tribe, and a fixed place in the column, “first,” “second rank,” “third rank,” “hindmost” (vv. 9, 16, 24, 31). The unusual feature is the middle of the column, where the tabernacle and the Levites move between the second and third camps (v. 17). The marching order is built around the presence of God.

Chapter 2 closes the opening subsection (1:1–2:34). Chapter 1 asked how many; chapter 2 asks where. The next subsection turns to the tribe left out of both, the Levites (3:1–4:49), who fill the ring between the tribes and the tabernacle.

**Forward:** the order is carried out when the cloud lifts, Judah's standard going “in the first place” and Dan's as “the rearward of all the camps” (10:14, 25). Ezekiel's restored city (48:30–34) and John's New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12–13) also set three tribal names on each of four sides.

traditions.text: This Aramaic paraphrase makes the camp twelve miles square and turns each standard into a banner of silk in three colors, matching the stones of the high priest's breastplate, with the three tribal names and a verse in the middle. Judah's carries Moses' words when the ark set out (10:35) and “the figure of a young lion.” Reuben's bears the words “Hear, Israel” and a stag; an ox was expected, the Targum says, but Moses changed it so the sin of the calf would not be remembered. Ephraim's shows a young man and Dan's a serpent.

The midrash hears love in the standards. God arranged Israel by banners like the ministering angels so that each tribe could be told apart, and the proof is Song of Solomon 2:4, “his banner over me was love,” where the Hebrew for “banner” is *degel*, the word used for the standards here. Rabbi Abahu compares God to a man who finds his whole cellar turned to vinegar except one cask of good wine, which is as dear to him as the rest: of seventy nations, Israel is that cask.

The midrash matches the camp to the order of creation. God made four directions and surrounded his throne with four living creatures, and he arranged the standards to correspond. Judah, holder of the kingship, takes the east, where light comes into the world, flanked by Issachar, the tribe of Torah, and Zebulun, the tribe of wealth. Judah is first, the midrash notes, in camping, in marching, and in bringing offerings (Numbers 7:12).

Traces the layout to Jacob's funeral. Jacob told his sons to carry his bier three to a side in exactly this arrangement, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun on the east and so on, with Joseph excused because he was a king and Levi because he would one day carry the ark. When God told Moses to make standards, Moses feared quarrels over who camped where. God answered that the tribes already knew their places from their father's bier (Genesis 50:12).

Rashi gives two readings of the “ensign” of each house: a colored cloth matching the tribe's stone in the breastplate, as the Targum also says, or the places Jacob assigned at his bier, as in the Tanhuma. He takes “far off” to mean two thousand cubits, the distance kept from the ark when Israel crossed the Jordan (Joshua 3:4). That was a Sabbath day's walk, so every tribe could come to the tabernacle on the Sabbath.

A Spanish commentator who reports older tradition for the images on the standards: a man on Reuben's, a lion on Judah's, an ox on Ephraim's and an eagle on Dan's. These are the four faces of the living creatures in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 1:10), so the camp around the tabernacle mirrors the creatures around God's throne. His list differs from the Targum's stag and serpent, a sign that the images were never fixed.

Josephus pictures the camp with roads cut between the tents and the tabernacle in the midst, three tribes to each side. It looked, he says, like a well-ordered market with craftsmen in their shops, “a city that sometimes was moveable, and sometimes fixed.” He also describes the silver trumpets that set the camp moving one quarter at a time, east first, then south, then the tabernacle, then west and north.

Origen's Latin text of v. 2 told each man to march according to his order, and he sets it beside Paul's “let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40), and says one Spirit speaks in both. He applies the rule to the church: rank should follow merit and understanding. He complains that a worldly man sometimes holds a high seat while a spiritual one is left in the crowd, which breaks the order of law and gospel alike.

On the “signs” of each house he compares souls to handwriting. Everyone writes the same letters, yet Paul's hand is not Peter's, and the chastity of Paul differs from the chastity of Peter. Each soul marches under its own sign, and Origen holds out hope of moving to a brighter one, since in the resurrection “one star differeth from another star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41). Moses, he says, saw these differences between souls and wrote them into the law as a mystery.

3.overview:
The chapter opens with “the generations of Aaron and Moses” and names Aaron's four sons, recalling that Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire. The LORD then gives the tribe of Levi to Aaron as helpers and claims the Levites as his own in place of every firstborn son in Israel, a claim dating from the night he struck the firstborn of Egypt. The Levites are counted from a month old. Gershon camps west, Kohath south, Merari north, and Moses, Aaron and Aaron's sons east, each clan with its share of the tabernacle to keep. Then Israel's firstborn are counted: 22,273, which is 273 more than the Levites. The extra 273 are redeemed at five shekels each, and the silver goes to Aaron.

The chapter is a head-for-head exchange. Each Levite stands in for one firstborn son, which is why even babies a month old are counted, and the leftover lives are paid for in silver.

3.hermeneutics:
A Hittite text of the 14th–13th centuries BC, the *Instructions for Temple Officials*, sets out a temple's night watch. Priests patrol inside the temple all night without sleeping, guards keep watch outside in the precinct, and a high priest leads the rounds. A foreigner who approaches the gods must die, and so must the official responsible for any section where an offense occurs. Jacob Milgrom drew on this text in 1970 to explain the Levites' duty. Read beside it, v. 38 is a guard roster. The priests hold the entrance, the Levite clans ring the other three sides, and “the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death” (vv. 10, 38) is the standing order of the watch.

Among Israel's neighbors a god's claim on the firstborn could be taken literally. Second Kings tells of a Moabite king who offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall during a siege (2 Kings 3:27), and the burials of infants in the sacred precincts of Carthage and other Phoenician colonies have long been read as child sacrifice, though the reading is still debated. Exodus states Israel's version of the claim in its starkest form: “the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me” (Exodus 22:29). Numbers 3 shows how the claim is met. A whole tribe given to holy service stands in for the firstborn, and the balance is paid at five shekels, the value Leviticus 27:6 sets on a boy under five years old.

notes: **One formula per clan:** each Levite clan gets the same items: its families, its number, its side of the tabernacle, its chief, and its charge (vv. 21–26, 27–32, 33–37).

**Numbers that do not add up:** the clan figures (7,500 + 8,600 + 6,200) make 22,300, but v. 39 gives 22,000, and the exchange runs on 22,000. The text does not explain the gap. The redemption itself balances: 273 × 5 = 1,365 shekels (v. 50).

**Repetition to watch:** *bekhor*, “firstborn,” comes 13 times. *Zar*, “stranger” or outsider, links the frame: the “strange fire” of v. 4 and “the stranger that cometh nigh” of vv. 10 and 38 use the same word.

Chapters 3–4 form the Levite subsection (3:1–4:49). It opens with the only “these are the generations” heading in Numbers (3:1), the formula that divides Genesis. Chapter 3 counts every Levite male for the exchange with the firstborn; chapter 4 counts the working Levites, thirty to fifty, for carrying the tabernacle.

**Backward and forward:** the claim on the firstborn goes back to the Passover night (Exodus 13:2, 11–15). The Levites are formally purified and presented in 8:5–26, where the substitution is stated again (8:16–18).

traditions.text: A revelation on priesthood says the Lord “confirmed a priesthood also upon Aaron and his seed,” and that this lesser priesthood continued with the house of Aaron among Israel until John the Baptist. It names the offices of teacher and deacon as appendages belonging to it. Numbers 3 is where Aaron's sons are listed as the anointed priests and the Levites are given to them as helpers (vv. 3, 9).

These revelations call the second priesthood the Priesthood of Aaron because it was conferred on Aaron and his seed throughout their generations. A literal descendant of Aaron has a legal right to the bishopric, the presidency of that priesthood, and D&C 68 gives that right to the firstborn among the sons of Aaron. The chapter's two threads, Aaron's line and the claim of the firstborn, meet again in Restoration church order.

The same revelation speaks of “the sons of Moses and of Aaron” offering an acceptable offering in the house of the Lord, and says that those faithful to both priesthoods become the sons of Moses and of Aaron and the seed of Abraham. Numbers 3:1 also joins the two names in its heading, the generations of Aaron and Moses, though the list that follows names only Aaron's sons. Rashi's explanation of that gap appears below, and it too makes Aaron's sons into sons of Moses.

Rashi notices that v. 1 promises the generations of Aaron and Moses but names only Aaron's sons. They are counted as Moses' children too, he says, because Moses taught them Torah, and Scripture treats anyone who teaches his neighbor's son as though he had fathered him. They became his on the day the LORD spoke with Moses at Sinai, when he first taught them what he heard.

A Roman officer named Kontrokos puts the missing three hundred to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai: the clans total 22,300, so where did the other three hundred Levites go? Yohanan answers that the three hundred were themselves firstborn. A firstborn Levite could not stand in for an Israelite firstborn, Abaye explains, since it was enough for him to cancel his own status. In the same exchange Kontrokos asks why Moses' silver for the tabernacle seems to come up short, and Yohanan defends Moses' accounting.

In the Hebrew text of v. 39, the name Aaron carries dots above it, one of a handful of words marked this way in the Torah. Rashi, following the Talmud and Sifre, says the dots show that Aaron himself was not among the Levites counted. He then gives the Kontrokos answer for the missing three hundred.

Josephus places the priests first around the tabernacle and the Levites next. Counted from thirty days old, he says, the Levites numbered 23,880 males, a figure that matches neither the 22,000 of v. 39 nor the 22,300 of the clan lists. Numbers 26:62 later gives the Levites as 23,000.

Origen points out that Levi was not a firstborn; he was Leah's third son, after Reuben and Simeon. Yet the Levites are taken in place of the firstborn. He reads this as a lesson that God reckons as firstborn those he judges by their hearts, as he made the younger Jacob firstborn over Esau, so that being taken for the firstborn is something greater than being born first.

On the 22,000 Levites and firstborn he looks for meaning in the number twenty-two. There are twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet, twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob, and, by tradition, twenty-two kinds of created things. The Book of Jubilees had already paired twenty-two works of creation with the twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob. For the extra 273 firstborn, he admits, he sees no easy explanation.

When Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the temple, Luke explains the visit by the law of the firstborn: every male “that openeth the womb” is to be called holy to the Lord. His Greek translates the Hebrew phrase the KJV renders “openeth the matrix” in v. 12, the verse where the Levites are taken in place of such sons. Luke mentions the offering for Mary's purification but no redemption money, and the scene presents the firstborn son to the Lord.

4.overview:
The LORD orders a second count of the Levites, this time of the men from thirty to fifty years old who will do the work of moving the tabernacle. When the camp is ready to travel, Aaron and his sons go in first and wrap each holy object: the ark in the veil, a covering of skins, and a cloth of blue; then the table, lampstand, altars and vessels, each in its own coverings. Only then do the Kohathites come in to carry them. The Gershonites carry the curtains and hangings and the Merarites the boards, bars, pillars and sockets, both under Ithamar. The working Levites number 8,580.

The Kohathites carry the holiest things in Israel, yet they may not touch them or even look at them uncovered, “lest they die” (vv. 15, 20). The chapter's concern is to keep them alive: the priests wrap everything first and assign every man his load (v. 19).

4.hermeneutics:
In Egypt the image of a god left its temple inside a small closed shrine of gilded wood, set on a model boat that priests carried on poles on their shoulders. Reliefs on Hatshepsut's Red Chapel at Karnak (15th century BC) show such processions, and at the Opet festival the barque of Amun was carried this way between Karnak and Luxor. Onlookers saw the shrine and its bearers, never the god inside. Numbers 4 uses the same picture and sharpens it. The ark goes out under three layers of covering, on the shoulders of Levites who are forbidden even to see what they carry (vv. 6, 15, 20; 7:9).

Portable furniture built to come apart was old in Egypt before Israel's time. In 1925 George Reisner's expedition found at Giza the burial goods of Queen Hetepheres, mother of the pyramid-builder Khufu (about 2600 BC). Among them were the gold-cased poles and beams of a canopy frame with fitted joints, made to be taken down and set up again quickly, and a box for its curtains. The Merarites' load in vv. 31–32 is that kind of object: boards, bars, pillars and sockets, every piece counted by name. A tent-shrine of jointed parts needed a crew who knew each piece and where it went.

notes: **Same order twice:** Kohath, Gershon, Merari in the duties and again in the census. Each count closes with a refrain that Moses and Aaron numbered them at the LORD's word (vv. 37, 41, 45), and the total repeats it (v. 49).
**Weighted toward Kohath:** Kohath's duties take 17 verses, Gershon's 8, Merari's 5, and only Kohath's carry warnings of death (vv. 15, 19, 20).

**Repetition to watch:** *avodah*, “service,” 20 times; *massa*, “burden,” 9 times. Entering “the host” (*tsava*, vv. 3, 23, 30, 35, 39, 43) is the military word of 1:3. The Levites are mustered too, for the sanctuary.

Chapter 4 closes the Levite subsection (3:1–4:49). Chapter 3 counted the Levites from a month old to balance the firstborn; chapter 4 counts only men of working age, because its concern is the march. The wagons of 7:6–9 complete the arrangement: Gershon and Merari receive wagons and oxen, Kohath none.

**Forward:** the rule that the holy things ride on shoulders returns when David moves the ark. Uzzah dies touching it on an oxcart (2 Samuel 6:6–7), and the second attempt succeeds with Levites bearing it on staves, “as Moses commanded” (1 Chronicles 15:2, 13–15).

traditions.text: A thematic link. When John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron in May 1829, he said it would not be taken from the earth until “the sons of Levi do offer again an offering” to the Lord in righteousness. D&C 84 extends the promise to the sons of Moses and of Aaron offering in a house of the Lord yet to be built. The Levites of this chapter, mustered for the service of the sanctuary, are the line those words name.

The Greek translation made for the Jews of Egypt starts the Levites' service at twenty-five years old in v. 3, the age the Hebrew gives only in 8:24. In v. 14 it adds a line the Hebrew lacks: the priests are to cover the laver and its base with a purple cloth and a covering of skin and set it on bars. The laver is the one piece of the court's furniture the Hebrew list leaves without a wrapping, and Origen's list of seven covered items (below) comes from this Greek text.

traditions.date: date debated; final form after AD 600
traditions.text: The Aramaic paraphrase of v. 20 says the Kohathites must not go in to gaze while the priests cover the vessels of the sanctuary, “that they die not by the flaming fire.” It names the danger the text leaves unnamed: fire from the holy things, like the fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1–2). Onkelos, the more literal Targum, renders the verb simply as covering. Numbers Rabbah builds on the fire (next entry).

The midrash notices a pattern in the numbers. Gershon's working men are a little over a third of the clan and Merari's a little over half, but Kohath's fall short of a third. Its explanation: sparks went out from between the ark's staves to burn Israel's enemies and sometimes struck the bearers, so Kohathites either avoided the ark or, in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahman's version, crowded and quarreled to carry it for the reward. Either way the LORD's answer is v. 19: the priests assign each man his task, so no one is cut off.

Nahmanides collects three readings of the Hebrew phrase in v. 20, literally “as the holy is swallowed.” Rashi and Onkelos take “swallowed” as wrapped, so the Kohathites may not watch the covering. The Talmud reads it as stealing a sacred vessel, a sin God punishes with death. Ibn Ezra takes it as the moment the screening veil is taken down and the ark stands exposed, before it is covered.

The rabbis tie Uzzah's death to this chapter. David, they say, was made to stumble over something schoolchildren know, that the sons of Kohath carry the holy things on their shoulders (7:9), and he put the ark on a cart. When Uzzah reached out to steady it, God's rebuke was that the ark had carried its own bearers across the Jordan; surely it could carry itself. The same page discusses the men of Beth-shemesh, struck because they looked into the ark (1 Samuel 6:19), a case close to the warning of v. 20.

The rabbis set this chapter's age of thirty beside the twenty-five of 8:24 and reconcile them: from twenty-five a Levite trained, and from thirty he served. From the five years of training they drew a rule for students in general. They add that the age limits applied to the tabernacle in the wilderness; in Shiloh and the Temple a Levite was disqualified only when his voice failed for singing.

Origen points out that the Levites, like the fighting men of chapter 1, are counted as men who go forth, here to the service of the tent. He lists seven things the priests must cover before the Kohathites touch them, from the ark to the laver (his Greek Bible included the laver), so that nothing is left bare. Only the sons of Aaron may see these things unveiled; the others carry them covered. His Greek Bible gave twenty-five, not thirty, as the starting age in v. 3, matching 8:24.

He applies the rule to teachers in the church. Whoever has been entrusted with the holy vessels, the hidden things of wisdom, should keep them veiled and not hand them bare to people not ready for them, or he becomes a cause of death to the hearers. He also contrasts the Kohathites, who carry on their shoulders, with Gershon and Merari, whose heavier loads go on wagons (7:7–8): the holiest things are carried by persons, not by beasts.

5.overview:
Three laws keep the camp fit for the LORD who dwells in it. The first sends out anyone with leprosy, a discharge, or uncleanness from a corpse, male and female alike. The second covers wrongs against another person: the offender confesses and repays in full with a fifth added. The third and longest is for a husband who suspects his wife of adultery when there is no witness. He brings her to the priest with a barley offering. She swears an oath, the curses are written and washed into holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor, and she drinks it. If she is guilty, her body shows it; if not, she goes free and will conceive.

The trial takes the verdict out of the husband's hands. Without a witness he may not punish her himself. The case goes before the LORD at the sanctuary, and an innocent wife leaves cleared (v. 28).

5.hermeneutics:
The Laws of Hammurabi (Babylon, about 1750 BC) treat two cases close to this one. If a man accuses his wife but she was not caught with another man, she swears an oath and returns to her house (§131). If others point the finger at her and she was not caught, she must leap into the river for her husband's sake (§132), and the river decides. Numbers joins the two: the husband's suspicion begins the case, the wife swears an oath, and a divine test settles it. The test is different. The river could drown a woman outright, while the drink of Numbers 5 is holy water and a little dust, and what it does rests on the oath and on the LORD (v. 21).

Egyptians knew the idea of drinking a text. Healing stelae of the child Horus were carved with spells against snakes and scorpions, and water poured over the inscriptions was drunk so that the words passed into the body. The Metternich Stela in New York, from the 4th century BC, is the best-known example of a type common in the first millennium BC. In v. 23 the priest writes the curses in a scroll and washes the ink into the water, so the oath the woman has just accepted with “Amen, amen” (v. 22) goes into her body, to clear her or to convict her.

notes: **One word across two laws:** *ma'al*, “trespass,” names a wrong against the LORD in v. 6 and a wife's unfaithfulness in vv. 12 and 27, each time as verb and noun together. Cheating a neighbor and breaking faith in marriage are counted as the same kind of breach.
**Defile:** the verb *tame* comes 8 times, from the camp in v. 3 to the wife in vv. 13–29, with the adjective “defiled” in v. 2.
**Repetition to watch:** “jealousy” (noun and verb) 10 times in vv. 14–30; “water” 11 times in vv. 17–27; the roots for “bitter” and “curse” 6 times each.

Chapters 5–6 form a subsection of laws (5:1–6:27) between the arrangement of the camp (chs. 1–4) and the leaders' offerings (ch. 7). It moves from the edge of the camp inward: the unclean sent out, wrongs between neighbors, a marriage under suspicion, the Nazarite's vow, and the priestly blessing that puts the LORD's name on Israel (6:27).

**Backward and forward:** v. 3 echoes the purpose of the tabernacle, “that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). Deuteronomy 23:14 applies the rule to the war camp: the LORD walks in its midst, so it must be holy.

traditions.text: A thematic link. Verses 6–7 require a wrongdoer to confess and to make good the harm. The Book of Mormon tells of Alma the Younger and the sons of Mosiah traveling through the land “zealously striving to repair all the injuries” they had done to the church and confessing their sins. D&C 58 gives confessing and forsaking sins as the sign that a person has repented, pairing confession with a changed course as this law pairs it with repayment.

Philo explains that proven adultery carried death under the law, but where guilt was only suspected the law would not let men judge; it brought the case before “the tribunal of nature,” since God alone sees the soul. He reads the barley as food fit for beasts and for the needy, a sign that adultery is bestial, and the earthen vessel as easily broken, like the adulterer's life. A wife falsely accused, he adds, may hope for children.

Josephus sets the rite at the temple. The priest stands the woman at the gates, removes her veil, writes the name of God on parchment, and after the oath wipes the name into the water and adds dust from the temple. If she is innocent, Josephus says, she will bear a son in the tenth month; if guilty, she dies in disgrace. His detail that the divine name itself is written and washed away is the point the rabbis develop (Sifre, below).

On the first law Josephus says Moses barred lepers and those with discharges from the city, and kept menstruating women out until the seventh day. He then turns the law into an argument. Some writers, he says, claimed that Moses was himself a leper who led lepers out of Egypt; a leper, Josephus replies, would never have made laws that shut lepers out.

The Mishnah describes the ritual as performed in the Second Temple. A woman who maintained her innocence was taken to the Eastern Gate by the Nicanor Gate, where women after childbirth and healed lepers were also purified. The priest tore her garment and loosened her hair, replaced white clothing with black, and tied an Egyptian rope above her breasts, and other women were allowed to watch as a warning (Ezekiel 23:48).

The same tractate records the end of the rite. When adulterers multiplied, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai stopped the bitter water, citing Hosea 4:14, where God declines to punish the daughters because the men themselves go astray. The same mishnah sets this beside another rite that lapsed, the heifer whose neck was broken for an unsolved murder (Deuteronomy 21:1–9), stopped when murderers became too many.

This early rabbinic commentary dwells on v. 23. The curses must be written in ink that can be washed off, on a proper scroll, by the priest. And if God allows a scroll written in holiness, with his own name in it, to be erased in water to make peace between a man and his wife, how much more should the books of heretics, which sow hatred and strife, be erased from the world.

Rashi asks why this law follows the law of priestly gifts (vv. 9–10). His answer, from the Talmud: whoever withholds the priest's due will end up coming to the priest anyway, bringing his wife for the ordeal. He also reads the doubled “any man” of v. 12 as two betrayals, of God above and of her husband below.

traditions.text: The Aramaic paraphrase calls the barley “the food of beasts,” as Philo does, and explains the double “Amen” of v. 22. The woman says amen once for the time of betrothal and once for the time since the marriage, so the oath covers both. It also adds that a husband who has not given the priest his dues is still bound to bring his wife, the link Rashi draws as well.

This early Christian account of Mary's life applies the rite to her pregnancy. When the priest learns that Mary is with child, the high priest makes both Joseph and Mary drink “the water of the ordeal of the Lord” and sends each into the hill country. Both return unharmed, and the priest declines to condemn them. In this telling the husband drinks too, which Numbers does not require.

6.overview:
Any man or woman may take a vow of separation to the LORD, the vow of a Nazarite. For its length the Nazarite drinks no wine and eats nothing from the vine, lets the hair grow uncut, and goes near no dead body, not even a parent's. If someone dies suddenly beside him, he shaves, brings offerings, and starts the vow over. When it is complete, he shaves at the tabernacle door and puts the hair in the altar fire. The chapter ends with the blessing Aaron and his sons are to speak over Israel: “The LORD bless thee, and keep thee.”

The Nazarite is an ordinary Israelite living by rules close to the high priest's. Like the high priest, he may not defile himself even for father or mother (Leviticus 21:11). Verse 7 says the *nezer*, the “consecration,” of his God is upon his head, the same word Leviticus 21:12 uses for the high priest's crown.

6.hermeneutics:
In 1979 the archaeologist Gabriel Barkay found two tiny rolled-up silver sheets in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem. Unrolled, they carry a form of vv. 24–26 in the old Hebrew script. Most scholars date them to about 600 BC, though some argue for a later date, and they are usually described as the oldest surviving copies of any biblical text. They were made to be worn, rolled up like amulets. People carried the blessing on their bodies as protection, so “keep thee” was heard as a prayer for guarding, and v. 27's putting of the LORD's name on Israel was done in silver.

Dedicating grown hair to a god was a known practice around the eastern Mediterranean. In the *Iliad*, Achilles had let a lock grow because his father vowed it to the river Spercheius for his safe return home; at Patroclus' funeral he cuts it off instead (book 23). Lucian, a Syrian-born writer of the 2nd century AD, describes young people at Hierapolis in Syria cutting hair that had been kept sacred since birth and leaving it in silver and gold vessels in the temple, each with a name written on it. Against that background, long hair marked an Israelite as visibly under a vow. Numbers keeps the custom and places it inside the tabernacle's own sacrifices: the cut hair goes into the altar fire (v. 18), and the vow is open to any man or woman.

notes: **Separation:** words built on the Hebrew root *nazar*, “separate,” including the title *nazir* and the noun *nezer*, occur 24 times in vv. 2–21. “Head” comes 8 times, since the hair is where the vow shows.
**The blessing:** each line names the LORD, three times in all, and the lines grow from 3 to 5 to 7 Hebrew words. Verse 27 says what the three lines do: they put his name on Israel.
**A repeated heading:** “this is the law of the Nazarite” opens the closing rite (v. 13) and is repeated at its end (v. 21).

Chapters 5–6 gather laws for a camp where the LORD dwells: the unclean sent outside (5:1–4), wrongs repaid, the jealousy ordeal, and the Nazarite vow. The blessing closes this run of laws; 7:1 then steps back to the day the tabernacle was set up, a month before the census of 1:1.

**Backward and forward:** Aaron had already blessed the people with lifted hands on the day the priests began their service (Leviticus 9:22). Psalm 67:1 echoes v. 25: “cause his face to shine upon us.”

traditions.text: A thematic link to v. 25. When Jesus blesses his Nephite disciples as they pray, “the light of his countenance did shine upon them,” and they become as white as his own garments. The language of Aaron's blessing becomes a scene, with the Lord's face shining on those he blesses.

When the Seleucid king had defiled the temple, Judas Maccabeus gathered Israel at Mizpah. Among the things brought out before God were the priests' garments, the firstfruits, and Nazarites “who had accomplished their days.” Their vows were complete, but with the altar profaned they could not offer the closing sacrifices of vv. 13–20, and the people cried to heaven asking what to do with them.

Philo calls this “the great vow.” People offer the firstfruits of their goods, he says, and when nothing is left to give they offer themselves, since “every man is his own greatest and most valuable possession.” He reads the rules as signs: no wine, because the vower's reason is dedicated to God, as priests on duty drink only water; no approach to the dead, even parents, because the body is kept pure.

Josephus lists the Nazarites among the dues owed to the priests. Those who let their hair grow and drink no wine consecrate their hair when the vow ends, and it is allotted to the priests for the fire. He describes the vow as a custom still practiced in his own day.

A whole tractate, Nazir, works out the vow's details. A vow with no stated length lasts thirty days, even if the vower says it is “until the end of the world.” A lifelong Nazarite may thin his hair when it grows too heavy and bring offerings, but one who vows to be “like Samson” may never cut it and brings no offering when defiled.

The rabbis disagreed about whether the vow was a good thing. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar read v. 11, where the priest makes atonement because the Nazarite “sinned by the dead” (literally “by the soul”), as a sin against himself for denying himself wine; how much more, then, is someone who fasts from everything a sinner? Another teacher, Rabbi Elazar, drew the opposite lesson from v. 5, which calls the Nazarite holy.

Simeon the Righteous, an early high priest, said he ate the guilt offering of a defiled Nazarite only once. A handsome shepherd from the south had seen his own curls reflected in a spring, felt pride take hold, and vowed to shave his hair for the sake of heaven. Simeon kissed him on the head and applied v. 2 to him, because this vow was made for the right reason.

The oldest rabbinic commentary on Numbers reads each line of the blessing many ways. “Keep thee” means keeping your possessions, your body, keeping you from the evil impulse or from harmful spirits, or keeping your soul at death. “Lift up his countenance” raised a problem, since Deuteronomy 10:17 says God “regardeth not persons,” literally does not lift faces; Sifre answers that he lifts his face toward Israel when they do his will.

In the temple the priests spoke the blessing as one unbroken unit and pronounced the divine name as written. Elsewhere they used a substitute title, and the people answered amen after each line. In the temple the priests raised their hands above their heads, except the high priest, who kept his below the gold plate on his forehead because it bore the name.

The angel says John the Baptist “shall drink neither wine nor strong drink,” the rule of a Nazarite set apart before birth. Paul shaves his head at Cenchrea because of a vow. Later, in Jerusalem, James and the elders ask him to pay the costs of four men completing their vows and to purify himself with them, so that all may see he keeps the law.

Hegesippus, an early Christian historian quoted by Eusebius, says James the brother of the Lord was holy from his mother's womb. He drank no wine or strong drink, and “no razor came upon his head.” The word Nazarite is not used, but the description follows vv. 3–5, so early Christians remembered the leader of the Jerusalem church as living by the vow for life.

7.overview:
On the day Moses finishes setting up and anointing the tabernacle, the twelve princes of the tribes bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen. Moses gives them to the Levite clans who haul the tabernacle's frames and curtains. The sons of Kohath get none, because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. Then for twelve days, one prince a day, the princes bring gifts for the dedication of the altar: a silver dish and bowl full of flour and oil, a gold spoon of incense, and twenty-one animals. When the gifts are done, Moses goes into the tent and hears the voice speaking from above the mercy seat.

The twelve gifts are identical, and the text writes out every one in full, six verses per prince. One entry and a line saying the others did the same would have covered it. Instead each tribe gets its own day, its own name, and exactly the same words.

7.hermeneutics:
Temples across the ancient Near East kept written accounts of what came in. Cuneiform archive tablets list offerings item by item with their quantities and close with a total line, introduced in Sumerian and Akkadian by a word meaning “all together.” In 1965 Baruch Levine compared vv. 12–88 with these archival records, and Jacob Milgrom pointed to the matching totals here, each introduced by “all” (vv. 85–88). Read that way, the chapter's sameness is the style of a temple ledger. Each donor is entered by name and day, each item by kind and weight, and the sums are checked at the end: 2,400 shekels of silver, 120 of gold, 252 animals.

There were no coins in this world. Coinage began in Lydia, in western Anatolia, around 600 BC, and before that silver and gold were money by weight. The shekel was a weight, and inscribed stone weights from Judah put it at roughly 11.4 grams. By that standard each silver dish weighed about 1.5 kilograms and each bowl about 800 grams. Every weight is given “after the shekel of the sanctuary” (v. 13), a fixed standard kept by the tabernacle. So the gifts were equal in a way anyone could check on the scale, and the ledger records that they were.

notes: **Twelve identical entries:** each prince gets six verses in the same order: name and day, silver dish and bowl, gold spoon, burnt offering, sin offering, peace offerings, and a closing “this was the offering of” the prince. These 72 verses hold about three quarters of the chapter's Hebrew words (803 of 1,072).
**Small differences:** only Nahshon, who goes first, is not called “prince” (v. 12). The order follows the camp of ch. 2, Judah's three tribes first, not the birth order of Jacob's sons.
**Length:** at 89 verses this is the longest chapter in the Torah. In the whole Bible only Psalm 119 is longer.

Verse 1 goes back to the day the tabernacle was set up (Exodus 40:17), a month before the census that opens the book, so the chapter stands apart from what surrounds it. It closes the work of building and furnishing, and v. 89 shows the finished tabernacle in use: the voice promised in Exodus 25:22 now speaks from between the cherubim.
**Forward:** the shoulder rule of v. 9 is remembered when the Levites bring the ark to Jerusalem “upon their shoulders,” as Moses commanded (1 Chronicles 15:15).

traditions.text: Josephus retells the gifts briefly: the princes paired up to bring a wagon and a yoke of oxen each, six in all, to carry the tabernacle on the march, and each brought a silver dish and bowl weighing two hundred shekels together. He then says Moses no longer went up Mount Sinai but went into the tabernacle and learned there from God what the people should do. That is his reading of v. 89.

Sifre identifies the princes of v. 2 with the Israelite officers whom Pharaoh's taskmasters beat when the brick quota was not met (Exodus 5:14). The men who took blows for their tribes in Egypt are the ones honored at the altar. Rabbi Nathan explains why they gave first here: at the tabernacle collection they had waited to supply whatever was lacking, found only the onyx and setting stones left to give (Exodus 35:27), and would not be last again.

Moses would not take the gifts until God told him to, and then he did not know the order. Should the princes give by the birth order of Jacob's sons, which puts Reuben first, or by the order of the march, which puts Judah first? God answered by the march, and each prince on his own day, so that Nahshon, who went first like a king, would not offer again alongside the others.

Sifre notices that each entry ends with the offering of the prince himself, and takes it to mean he paid from his own goods, not his tribe's. It also lists what made these gifts unusual: an individual brought incense, brought a sin offering when no sin had been committed, and offered on a Sabbath, none of which an individual could otherwise do.

The midrash insists the identical gifts were not identical in meaning. Each prince offered with his own tribe's future in mind, drawing on traditions handed down from Jacob, so Nahshon's dish and bowl stood for the kings of David's line who would rule land and sea. Rashi passes on a numerical play from the same work: the Hebrew letters of “silver charger” add up to 930, the years of Adam's life.

Only Issachar's entry doubles the verb “offered” (vv. 18–19). Rashi explains that Reuben had protested at following Judah, and the doubled verb marks Issachar's turn as commanded. It also hints at Issachar's two merits: its learning (1 Chronicles 12:32) and its advice that the princes bring these gifts at all.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 7:18, from Sifre Numbers 53

traditions.text: Ramban asks the question every reader of this chapter asks, and answers with honor. The princes agreed on the gift together, but someone had to go first, and a single entry for Nahshon followed by a note that the rest did likewise would have slighted the other eleven. So each is named with every item and his own day, and the totals of vv. 84–88 gather them back into one to show they were equal before God.

The word for “had fully” finished in v. 1, *kallot*, is spelled without a vowel letter, so it looks like *kallah*, “bride.” On the day the tabernacle stood, Rashi says, Israel was like a bride going under the wedding canopy, a reading he takes from the Midrash Tanhuma.

Two verses seemed to clash. Leviticus 1:1 says God spoke to Moses out of the tent of meeting, outside the veil, while Exodus 25:22 promises to speak from above the mercy seat, inside it. Verse 89 settles it, the rabbis said: the voice came from heaven to the space between the cherubim and went out from there into the tent, where Moses heard it.

The Hebrew for “dedicating” in vv. 10, 84 and 88 is *hanukkah*. When Judas Maccabeus rebuilt the defiled altar, Israel “kept the dedication of the altar eight days,” and the feast was made yearly. The Mishnah then assigns this chapter as the Torah reading for each day of Hanukkah, so the princes' twelve days are read across the festival's eight.

Why did Uzzah die when David moved the ark on a new cart (2 Samuel 6:3–7)? The Talmud blames David, who had called the Torah's laws “songs,” so God let him stumble over a rule that even schoolchildren know. That rule is v. 9: the sons of Kohath received no wagons, because the holy things are carried on the shoulders.

8.overview:
Aaron lights the seven lamps so they shine forward from the lampstand of beaten gold. Then the Levites are cleansed and presented. They are sprinkled with water, shave their whole bodies, and wash their clothes; the people lay their hands on them, and Aaron presents them before the LORD as an offering from Israel. Two bulls are offered for them, and they begin work under Aaron and his sons. The LORD explains that he takes the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn, whom he claimed on the night Egypt's firstborn died. Levites serve from twenty-five to fifty, then assist their brothers.

The Levites are handled the way an offering is handled. Israel lays hands on them as on a sacrifice (v. 10), and Aaron presents them with the motion used for wave offerings (v. 11). Israel gives some of its own people to God, and God gives them to Aaron (v. 19).

8.hermeneutics:
Egyptian priests kept a strict bodily purity. Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, reports that their priests shaved the whole body every other day so that no lice or other foulness would be on them as they served the gods, wore only linen, and washed twice a day and twice a night (Histories 2.37). The common Egyptian word for an ordinary priest, *wab*, means “pure one.” Against that background the Levites' shaving of “all their flesh” (v. 7) marks them as temple servants in a way any neighbor would recognize. The difference is that Israel's rite happens once, at installation, and the whole people take part by laying hands on them (v. 10).

A Hittite text from the later 2nd millennium BC, the *Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel*, sets out the duties of temple staff, including guard duty at the temple, with penalties for those who neglect it. Jacob Milgrom compared its arrangements with the shared custody of the tabernacle by priests and Levites. In Numbers to “keep the charge” is often guard duty around the sanctuary (1:53; 3:7–8, 38). That is the work a Levite over fifty still does when he stops carrying loads (v. 26). Verse 19 gives the reason for the guard: the Levites stand between Israel and the holy things, so that no plague breaks out when the people come near.

notes: **Done as commanded:** the lamps end with “Aaron did so” (v. 3), and the Levite section ends by saying twice that Israel did to the Levites as the LORD commanded (vv. 20, 22).

**Presented:** the Hebrew verb for presenting the Levites, the one used for a wave offering, comes four times (vv. 11, 13, 15, 21). “Cleanse” comes five times (vv. 6, 7 twice, 15, 21), and “Levites” 20 times in 26 verses.
**Five times:** v. 19 names “the children of Israel” five times in a single verse.

Numbers 8:1–10:10 finishes the preparations at Sinai: the lamps lit, the Levites installed, the Passover kept, and the cloud and trumpets set to move the camp. Chapter 8 completes what chs. 3–4 began. There the Levites were counted and assigned their loads; here they are purified and put to work.
**Forward:** Numbers 18:6 calls the Levites a gift to the priests, and David later counts them for temple service from twenty years old (1 Chronicles 23:24, 27).

traditions.text: A thematic link to the Levites' cleansing. Malachi foresaw a day when the Lord would purify the sons of Levi like silver so they could offer in righteousness, and the risen Jesus gave the prophecy to the Nephites. When John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, he said it would remain until the sons of Levi “do offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.”

Revelations to Joseph Smith speak of a lesser priesthood that continued with the house of Aaron in Israel until John the Baptist. Section 84 says it “was confirmed upon Aaron and his sons” and names teacher and deacon as its appendages. Section 107 calls it the Priesthood of Aaron, an appendage to the Melchizedek Priesthood with power in administering outward ordinances.

Josephus says the lampstand's seven branches and lamps were made in imitation of the seven planets, with the sun among them. Its seventy ornaments stood for the seventy divisions of the planets. He reads the tabernacle as a whole as a model of the universe, so the lamps of v. 2 become the lights of heaven.

Philo quotes the exchange of Levites for firstborn and calls the Levites the ransom of all the rest of Israel. He reads it as a general rule that the good man is the ransom of the worthless, citing God's willingness to spare Sodom for ten righteous men. In a city, he says, good men are what keep it standing; in a single soul, the reasoning part plays the Levite's role.
traditions.cite: On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain 118–126

traditions.text: Sifre explains “over against the candlestick” (v. 2): three lamps on each side were turned toward the central lamp, so that, as Rabbi Nathan put it, the middle one is honored. It reads the verb for lighting, literally “make go up,” as a hint that a step stood before the lampstand for the priest. On v. 3 it adds that “Aaron did so” is said in his praise: he changed nothing.

Why do the lamps come right after the princes' gifts? Rashi, drawing on the Midrash Tanhuma, says that when Aaron saw the twelve princes dedicate the altar, he was distressed that neither he nor his tribe had a share in it. God told him his part was greater than theirs, because he would light and tend the lamps. The two chapters are read as one story about who serves at the sanctuary.

Rashi cites a teaching of Rabbi Moses the Preacher on why the Levites had to shave their whole bodies (v. 7). They stood in for the firstborn, who had worshiped the golden calf; idol worship is called sacrifice to the dead (Psalm 106:28), and a leper too is likened to the dead (Numbers 12:12). So the Levites shave as lepers do at their cleansing.

Rashi notices what v. 19 does with Israel's name: five times in one verse, where pronouns would have done after the first. He takes it as a sign of God's affection for Israel, the five mentions matching the five books of the Torah, and credits the idea to a midrash.

Numbers 4:3 counts Levites from thirty years old, but v. 24 says twenty-five. The rabbis reconciled them: from twenty-five a Levite learns the work, and from thirty he does it. They also noted that age disqualifies a Levite but bodily blemishes do not, the reverse of the rule for priests.

What does a Levite over fifty still do? Sifre, as Rashi summarizes it, says he stops carrying loads on his shoulders but may still close the temple gates, sing, and load the wagons. Verse 26 is read to mean he serves alongside his brothers, not that he waits on them.

John sees the risen Lord standing among seven golden candlesticks, holding seven stars. The Lord explains that the candlesticks are the seven churches of Asia, so the lights Aaron kept burning in the holy place become congregations that must keep their light. The church at Ephesus is warned that its candlestick can be removed.

Clement repeats the planetary reading also found in Josephus: the lampstand's three branches on each side of the center showed the seven planets, with the sun in the midst. He then adds a Christian meaning. The golden lamp is “a symbol of Christ,” who casts light at various times and in various ways (Hebrews 1:1) on those who believe in him.

9.overview:
In the first month of the second year, at Sinai, Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day at evening. Some men, unclean from a dead body, ask Moses why they must be kept back. Moses waits for the LORD's answer, and it comes as a new law: anyone unclean or far away on a journey keeps the Passover a month later, on the fourteenth of the second month. Whoever is clean and at home yet skips it is cut off, and a resident foreigner keeps the same rule. The chapter closes with the cloud over the tabernacle: when it lifts, Israel moves; when it stays, for two days or a month or a year, Israel stays.

The second Passover begins with a question from ordinary people. Moses does not know the answer and says so: “Stand still, and I will hear” (v. 8). A new law grows out of their case.

9.hermeneutics:
Assyrian kings did not move an army on their own judgment. Hundreds of their questions to the sun god Shamash survive from the 7th century BC, edited by Ivan Starr in *Queries to the Sungod* (1990). A diviner put a yes-or-no question, such as whether the king should send troops on a campaign, and read the answer in the organs of a sacrificed sheep. The queries even list ways the rite could be spoiled, among them an unclean person taking part. Numbers 9 deals with the same kind of decision, when to march and when to stay, in another way. No one consults an oracle, and no specialist reads the sign. The answer hangs over the tent where the whole camp can see it every morning.

Mesopotamian texts describe gods and kings wrapped in a fearsome radiance, the *melammu*. In Sennacherib's annals it is a weapon: Luli, king of Sidon, fled overseas because “the terror-inspiring glamor” of the Assyrian king's lordship overwhelmed him (Luckenbill's 1924 translation). Israel's God also shows himself in light, as cloud by day and fire by night (vv. 15–16). Here the light is not aimed at enemies. It rests over the tent in the middle of the camp and tells Israel when to pack and when to stay put.

notes: **A refrain:** the Hebrew phrase *al pi YHWH*, literally “at the mouth of the LORD” (KJV “at the commandment of the LORD”), comes seven times in vv. 18–23, three of them in the last verse. The verb “journey” comes nine times in vv. 17–23.
**Growing spans of time:** the cloud may stay “a few days” (v. 20), only overnight (v. 21), or “two days, or a month, or a year” (v. 22). However long the wait, the answer is the same.
**Passover** is named nine times in vv. 1–14.

The Passover marks one year since Egypt. The cloud passage looks ahead: it explains how the camp will move before the cloud first lifts at 10:11. Verse 15 picks up Exodus 40:34–38, where the cloud first covers the finished tabernacle.
**Forward:** Hezekiah relies on this law when Judah cannot keep the Passover on time, holding it on the fourteenth day of the second month (2 Chronicles 30:2–3, 15).

traditions.text: Nephi, mocked by his brothers as he builds a ship, reminds them that Israel was led by the Lord their God, “leading them by day and giving light unto them by night.” Even so, he says, they hardened their hearts and reviled Moses. The cloud and fire of vv. 15–23 become his argument that God can lead Lehi's family through its own wilderness.

This Greek work by a Jew of Alexandria gives the guiding to Wisdom herself, who was to Israel “a cover by day, and a light of stars” at night. Later it calls the pillar of fire a guide on an unknown journey and a harmless sun. Psalm 105:39 had already called the cloud a covering.

Jubilees retells the Passover law as an ordinance written on the heavenly tablets and tells Israel not to put it off “from day to day, or from month to month.” It keeps the rule of v. 13 almost word for word: the man who is clean and close at hand and does not come is cut off, because he did not bring the LORD's offering in its season. It never mentions the second Passover, so its insistence on the fixed day stands without the exception this chapter makes.

Philo stresses that at Passover the whole nation acts as priests, each man offering his own victim. That is why the men in mourning grieved twice, for their dead and for losing that honor. He explains the law for travelers by the Jewish dispersion: one country cannot hold the whole nation, which has sent out colonies everywhere, and those abroad have done no wrong.

Josephus says the people stayed in place while the cloud stood over the tabernacle, “supposing that God there inhabited among them,” and moved when it moved. He then records that Moses offered the Passover in the wilderness, the first since leaving Egypt, and only after that did the camp set out from Sinai.

Verse 1 is dated a month earlier than 1:1, and Sifre draws a rule from it: the Torah does not always keep chronological order. Rashi adds why the book does not open with this chapter. It would have begun with something to Israel's discredit, since in forty years in the wilderness this was the only Passover they offered.

Who were the unclean men? Rabbi Yose the Galilean said they carried Joseph's coffin out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19), and Rabbi Akiva said they were Mishael and Elzaphan, who carried out the bodies of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:4). Rabbi Isaac thought both too early to explain their state and made them men who had buried an unclaimed corpse. From their case the rabbis drew the rule that one busy with a commandment is exempt from another.

The men did not ask to eat while unclean; Rashi says they proposed that clean priests sprinkle the blood for them. Moses' “stand still” showed the confidence of a pupil sure his teacher would answer. This law should have come through Moses like the rest, but it came through these men because merit is brought about through the worthy.

The Mishnah extends the second Passover to anyone who forgot or was prevented, and asks how far is “afar off” (v. 10). Rabbi Akiva set the line at Modiin, about a day's walk from Jerusalem; Rabbi Eliezer said anyone outside the temple court. Rabbi Yose pointed to the dot that scribes place over the last letter of the Hebrew word, as if to say the journey need not really be far.

When the soldiers do not break Jesus' legs on the cross, John sees the Passover rule fulfilled: “A bone of him shall not be broken.” The rule is given for the first Passover (Exodus 12:46) and repeated for the second in v. 12, so John reads Jesus' death as the Passover sacrifice.

Paul tells the Corinthians that all their fathers were under the cloud and were baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea. The cloud that led the camp becomes a figure of baptism. Paul's point is a warning: being under the cloud did not keep many of that generation from falling in the wilderness, and Christians should not assume their own baptism protects them either.

10.overview:
Moses makes two silver trumpets. They call the assembly or the princes, set the camps marching, and sound in war and over feast-day sacrifices. Then, on the twentieth day of the second month, the cloud lifts and Israel leaves Sinai, tribe by tribe in the order of the camp, with the Levites carrying the tabernacle and its holy things between the divisions. Moses urges Hobab, his Midianite in-law, to come along, and the ark goes ahead a three days' journey. When it sets out Moses cries, “Rise up, LORD”; when it rests, “Return, O LORD.”

The camp has a cloud to tell it when to move and an ark that goes ahead to find a resting place (v. 33). Moses still asks Hobab, who knows the desert, to be to them “instead of eyes” (v. 31). The text never says whether Hobab came, though Judges 1:16 and 4:11 later find his Kenite descendants living in Israel.

10.hermeneutics:
Metal trumpets were signal instruments in Egypt's army. Two survive from the tomb of Tutankhamun (died c. 1323 BC), one of silver and one of bronze or copper, found by Howard Carter in 1922; the bronze one lay in a chest with military equipment. Each is a straight tube ending in a flared bell, and when they were sounded for a BBC radio broadcast in 1939 they gave out loud, blaring blasts. Israel's trumpets are of the same kind: hammered silver (v. 2), blown in set patterns to assemble, to march, and to raise the alarm in war (vv. 3–9). Numbers puts them in the priests' hands and gives them one more purpose, unknown to any army: the blast brings Israel to remembrance before the LORD (vv. 9–10).

In Egyptian temples a god's image traveled in a portable shrine shaped like a boat, the sacred barque, carried on poles on the shoulders of priests. Reliefs from Hatshepsut's Red Chapel at Karnak and from later temples show such barques carried in festival processions like the Opet festival at Thebes. The ark is also a portable chest with carrying poles (Exodus 25:14), borne by the Kohathites (v. 21) and moving at the head of a procession. What it carries is different. The barque held the god's statue, while the ark holds the tablets of the covenant and no image at all, and Moses speaks to an unseen LORD who rises up and returns with it (vv. 35–36).

notes: **Journeying:** the Hebrew verb for setting out or journeying occurs 14 times in vv. 11–36. The camp counted and arranged in chs. 1–4 is finally moving.
**Timed arrival:** the tabernacle frame goes ahead with Gershon and Merari, so it is already standing when Kohath arrives with the holy things (v. 21).
**Trumpet calls:** the verb “blow” comes 8 times in vv. 1–10. The sounded “alarm” (*teruah*) comes 3 times, all for setting the camps in motion (vv. 5–6).

Verses 1–10 close the first section of Numbers, the preparations at Sinai (1:1–10:10). Verse 11 opens the second, the journey through the wilderness, as the cloud lifts for the first time and the rule laid down in 9:15–23 takes effect.

**Forward:** the very next verse after the ark's words is “when the people complained” (11:1). The march that begins in perfect order turns within days into the complaints and rebellions of chs. 11–14.

traditions.text: A thematic link to the ordered march. At Winter Quarters in January 1847, before the trek west, Brigham Young received the word and will of the Lord for “the Camp of Israel in their journeyings to the West.” The Saints were to be organized into companies with captains of hundreds, fifties, and tens, under a covenant to keep all the Lord's commandments and statutes. Like Israel leaving Sinai in its divisions, the camp was to move as an organized people.

Josephus credits Moses with inventing the trumpet's form and describes it: a little less than a cubit long, a narrow tube slightly thicker than a flute, ending in a bell like ordinary trumpets, and called in Hebrew *asosra*. He gives the signals as in vv. 3–6, adding a third and fourth blast for the western and northern camps. He also notes the trumpets' use at the altar on Sabbaths and festivals, as v. 10 commands.

Sifre records a dispute over whether a priest with a blemish could blow the temple trumpets. Rabbi Tarfon swore he had seen his own uncle, lame in one leg, standing and blowing them, a rare eyewitness memory of the temple service. Sifre also reads “make thee” (v. 2) as a sign that Moses' own trumpets were for his generation, not to be handed down to later ones.

Rashi reads “make thee” in two ways. The trumpets were to be paid for from Moses' own funds, not the public treasury. They were also to be blown before him as before a king, since Deuteronomy 33:5 says he “was king in Jeshurun,” so the summons of v. 3 gathers the assembly to Moses as to a ruler.

Rashi identifies Hobab with Jethro and takes Reuel as his father; Jethro's daughters called their grandfather “father” in Exodus 2:18. Jethro had several names in Rashi's tradition, among them Hobab, “lover,” because he loved the Torah. Moses pleaded with him to stay, Rashi says, so that no one could claim Jethro had converted only for a share of the land and left once he learned converts would not receive one.

Sifre says the camp covered the three days' journey of v. 33 in a single day, because God wanted to bring them into the land at once. It compares Israel to people who ask a king to escort them to a governor, then grumble at the long road as he follows the governor from city to city. It is the king who has the right to complain, and Israel complained anyway (11:1).

In Hebrew scrolls vv. 35–36 are set off by two inverted letters *nun*. Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel said the verses stand here to separate one punishment from the next, and that in the future they would be moved to their proper place. Rabbi Judah the Prince said they form a book of their own, which splits Numbers in three and gives the Torah seven books, the “seven pillars” of wisdom's house (Proverbs 9:1).

The Mishnah shows v. 10 in practice in the second temple. At the daily offering two priests stood with silver trumpets in their hands and sounded a long blast, a broken blast, and a long blast again, signaling the Levites to sing the psalm of the day. Each ordinary day had at least twenty-one trumpet blasts and a festival day up to forty-eight. On the New Year two trumpets flanked the ram's-horn shofar, which carried the main sound of the day.

The Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll plans the final battle of the sons of light with trumpets modeled on this chapter, separate ones for summoning the congregation, the leaders, and the troops. Each set of trumpets carries its own written inscription, and the priests blow them to direct the battle. The silver trumpets of vv. 2–9 become the instruments of the end-time war.

Psalm 68 opens with Moses' words from v. 35: “Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered.” Preaching on the psalm, Augustine says this has already come to pass, because Christ has risen up, so the cry raised over the ark becomes a prophecy of the resurrection. He takes the scattering of the enemies as the dispersion that followed Jerusalem's defeat in the war with Rome.

11.overview:
Three days out from Sinai the people complain, and fire burns the edge of the camp until Moses prays; the place is named Taberah. Then the mixed multitude craves meat, and Israel weeps for the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt. The LORD answers with seventy elders who share Moses' spirit and prophesy, two more of them, Eldad and Medad, prophesying in the camp. Then a wind brings quail in heaps around the camp, and a plague strikes while the meat is still between the people's teeth. They bury the dead at Kibroth-hattaavah.

Moses complains too. He asks why the LORD has laid the whole people on him, says he is not their mother, and asks to be killed rather than go on (vv. 11–15). His complaint is not punished. It is answered with seventy helpers, while the people's craving is answered with more meat than they can eat.

11.hermeneutics:
Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, was told that an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded how much the builders' radishes, onions and garlic had cost: sixteen hundred talents of silver (2.125). These were the staple rations of Egypt's laborers. The menu Israel remembers in v. 5 is the food of a work gang. The people call it “free,” and Egypt starts to sound like a full table rather than a brickyard.

Across the region, prophecy was known as a seizure by a god. At Mari on the Euphrates in the 18th century BC one kind of prophet was called *muhhûm*, “the ecstatic.” The Egyptian envoy Wenamun, about 1100 BC, reports that at Byblos a god seized one of the king's young attendants and put him in a trance, and the youth spoke for the god. A hearer who knew such things would take the elders' prophesying in v. 25 as a public sign that the spirit, and the authority that went with it, had come on them.

Quail fly north from Africa in spring and come down worn out after crossing the sea. Diodorus Siculus describes settlers on the north Sinai coast stretching nets along the shore to catch them (1.60.10). Israel leaves Sinai in the second month (10:11), which is spring. The wind “from the sea” in v. 31 is the season's flight path, and the text's wonder lies in the numbers and the timing, a month's meat on the day Moses said it would come.
