notes: **The pattern in small:** vv. 1–3 run the whole cycle in four verses: complaint, anger, Moses' prayer, a place named for what happened. The quail story repeats it at length and ends with another place name (v. 34).
**Bear and burden:** the verb *nasa*, “bear” or “carry,” comes 5 times (vv. 12 ×2, 14, 17 ×2) and the noun “burden” twice (vv. 11, 17).

**One word, two answers:** *ruach* is “spirit” five times (vv. 17, 25 ×2, 26, 29) and “wind” once (v. 31). The strand about Moses ends with spirit, the strand about the people with wind. “Weep” comes 5 times and “flesh” 8.

The unit runs from the departure at 10:11 to the camp in the wilderness of Paran at 12:16, and this chapter begins the run of complaint stories that carries on through the spies and Korah. Before Sinai, manna and quail came with no punishment (Exodus 16); after the covenant, the same complaint brings fire and plague.

**Backward and forward:** Jethro had already told Moses he could not carry the people alone (Exodus 18:18–22), and Moses recalls this burden in Deuteronomy 1:9–12. His wish in v. 29 is taken up in Joel 2:28–29, which Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18).

traditions.text: Philo uses v. 17 to show that a divine spirit is not cut up or shared out when others receive it. Moses' spirit passes to the seventy the way fire “can light ten thousand torches” and stay as it was. Knowledge, he adds, works the same way, since a teacher loses nothing by teaching. It answers a question the verse leaves open, whether Moses had less after the gift.

The rabbis modeled Israel's high court on this chapter. The Great Sanhedrin had seventy-one judges: the seventy of v. 16 with Moses at their head, since they were to stand “with thee.” Rabbi Yehuda answered that Moses presided but was not counted, so the court should have seventy. Lesser courts of twenty-three were derived from another passage (35:24–25), but the highest court took its size from the elders who stood with Moses at the tent.

Seventy elders from twelve tribes does not divide evenly, so the Talmud has Moses choose six from each tribe and draw lots: seventy slips marked “elder” and two left blank. Rabbi Shimon gives another reason Eldad and Medad stayed in the camp: they thought themselves unworthy, and as a reward their prophecy did not stop when the others' did. The Talmud then offers three answers to what they prophesied: Moses' death and Joshua's leadership, the coming quail, or the war of Gog and Magog.

This Aramaic paraphrase gives Eldad and Medad words to say, and it uses all three of the Talmud's answers. Eldad says, “Behold, Mosheh shall be gathered from the world,” and Joshua will lead Israel into Canaan. Medad foretells the quail, and together they foresee a king from Magog defeated in the last days and the dead of Israel raised.

The early commentary refuses to take “freely” (v. 5) at face value: a people denied straw for their bricks were not given free fish. The word must mean free of commandments, so what Israel misses is life without Sinai's demands. Rabbi Shimon adds that the manna could taste like anything a person wished except the five vegetables of v. 5, which is why the people still craved them.

Rashi notes two ways to read the end of v. 25. Following the Sifre, the elders prophesied that one day only and not again; Targum Onkelos renders it “they did not cease,” meaning the gift stayed with them. On v. 31 he passes on the Sifre's picture of quail flying two cubits off the ground, chest high, so no one had to stretch or stoop to gather them.

The rabbis noticed a tension between v. 20, a whole month of meat, and v. 33, death while the meat was still between the people's teeth. Their answer: ordinary people died at once, while the wicked ate for a month in misery and then died. They also played on the spelling of the word for quail: the righteous ate it in peace, and to the wicked it tasted like thorns.

Josephus sets the complaint at Hazeroth and widens it: the people are short of water and afraid the manna will fail. One man urges them “not to be unmindful of Moses,” which only makes the crowd angrier. When doubters ask how so much meat could be found, Moses answers that the proof will soon appear, and the quail come at once. Many die afterward, and Josephus leaves out the seventy elders altogether.

Listing the wilderness failures as warnings for the church at Corinth, Paul begins with craving: “we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.” The verb matches the place name of v. 34, the graves of those who lusted, and Paul says such things happened as examples for later believers. Psalm 78:29–31 had already retold the quail story as a warning in the same way.

This Roman visionary work quotes a book now lost, written in the names of the two men who prophesied in the camp: “The Lord is nigh unto them that turn unto him,” and gives as its source a book of Eldad and Modat. It shows that early Christians read a prophecy credited to Eldad and Medad. It also shows that v. 26, which records that they prophesied but not what they said, invited later writers to supply the words, as the Targum and Talmud did.

12.overview:
At Hazeroth, Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of the Cushite woman he has married (KJV “Ethiopian”), then ask the real question: has the LORD spoken only by Moses? The LORD calls all three to the tent, comes down in the cloud, and tells Aaron and Miriam that he speaks to prophets in visions and dreams but to Moses “mouth to mouth.” When the cloud lifts, Miriam is white with skin disease. Aaron pleads with Moses, Moses cries out for her healing, and she is shut out of the camp for seven days while the people wait.

The complaint names the wife, but the LORD's answer never mentions her. It is entirely about how God speaks to Moses. Moses says nothing in his own defense. The narrator calls him the meekest man on earth (v. 3), and his only words in the chapter are a five-word prayer in Hebrew for his sister (v. 13).

12.hermeneutics:
In the Bible and in Egyptian texts, Cush usually means Nubia, the Nile country south of Egypt, and Jeremiah 13:23 knows its people for their dark skin. But Habakkuk 3:7 sets “Cushan” beside Midian, and Moses' known wife Zipporah was a Midianite (Exodus 2:21). A first hearer could have understood either a second, foreign wife from the far south or Zipporah under an old name for her people. The text does not settle it, and it drops the wife after one verse.

In the ancient Near East a god's word usually reached a king secondhand. Letters to Zimri-Lim, king of Mari in the 18th century BC, pass on dreams and visions reported by prophets and ordinary people, and the king often had such messages checked by divination before acting on them. Verses 6–8 accept dreams and visions as the normal channel for prophets, then place Moses outside it: God speaks with him directly, “not in dark speeches.”

Skin disease was a stock divine punishment for those who wronged authority. Esarhaddon of Assyria's succession treaty (672 BC) calls on the moon god Sin to clothe any oath-breaker in leprosy, bar him from the presence of gods and king, and send him to roam the desert like the wild ass. Miriam's punishment follows the same pattern, disease and exclusion, but it is limited: seven days outside the camp, and the whole people waits for her.

notes: **Speak:** the verb *dabar* comes 6 times (vv. 1, 2 ×2, 6, 8 ×2). Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses and ask whether the LORD has spoken only by him; the LORD answers that he speaks with Moses, and asks why they were not afraid to speak against him.
**Miriam first:** she is named before Aaron, the opening verb is feminine singular, and only she is struck. Aaron confesses for both of them (v. 11).
**Seven days** comes 3 times (vv. 14 ×2, 15), and the march waits on Miriam's return.

The chapter closes the unit that began when the camp left Sinai (10:11). Verse 16 brings Israel into the wilderness of Paran, where the cloud had been heading (10:12) and from which the spies will be sent (13:3). After the people's complaints in ch. 11, the challenge now comes from Moses' own family.

**Backward and forward:** Miriam was called a prophetess at the sea (Exodus 15:20), which gives her claim in v. 2 its weight. Deuteronomy 24:9 tells Israel to remember what the LORD did to Miriam, and Deuteronomy 34:10 ends the Torah with no prophet like Moses, “whom the LORD knew face to face.”

traditions.text: The vision that opens the Book of Moses shows what v. 8 describes. Moses “saw God face to face, and he talked with him,” and God calls him “my son.” Moses adds that he saw with spiritual eyes rather than natural ones, since he would otherwise have withered in God's presence, and that he was transfigured.

When Hiram Page was writing revelations for the church from a stone, this revelation to Oliver Cowdery settled the question in the terms of Numbers 12. No one but Joseph Smith was to receive commandments and revelations for the church, “for he receiveth them even as Moses,” and Oliver was to declare them as Aaron did. D&C 107 later describes the presiding high priest as one who is to be like Moses: a seer, revelator, translator and prophet.

The early commentary reads the complaint as concern for Moses' wife. Miriam noticed that Zipporah no longer adorned herself and learned that Moses had stopped living with her in order to be ready for God's word at any time. Rashi tells it from another rabbi: Zipporah heard that Eldad and Medad were prophesying and said, “Woe to their wives.” The Sifre adds that if Miriam was punished though she meant no harm and spoke privately, one who slanders on purpose and in public deserves worse.

The standard Aramaic translation does not say “Cushite” but “the beautiful woman,” and says Moses had put her away. Rashi explains that as everyone agrees about a Cushite's dark skin, everyone agreed about her beauty, and that the letters of *Kushit* add up to the same number as “beautiful of appearance.” Both readings keep her as Moses' one known wife and make her a cause for praise.

The Mishnah's chapter on reward measure for measure uses v. 15. Miriam waited by the Nile for one hour to see what would happen to her baby brother (Exodus 2:4). So all Israel waited seven days for her before marching on. The same passage sets Miriam beside Joseph, who buried his father and whose bones Moses carried out of Egypt, as examples of good done and repaid in kind.

When students complained that a prayer leader was too brief, Rabbi Eliezer asked whether he was any briefer than Moses, whose whole prayer for Miriam was “Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee.” Rav Hisda drew a second rule from the same verse: one who prays for another need not say the person's name, since Moses never named Miriam.

Rabbi Akiva noticed that the LORD's anger was kindled “against them” (v. 9) and concluded that Aaron was struck with leprosy too, and that “Aaron looked upon Miriam” means he turned back, healed. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira objected that either Akiva was revealing what the Torah had chosen to cover, or he was slandering a righteous man. The same two rabbis argue the same way over the Sabbath-breaker of 15:32.

Josephus tells a story that Exodus lacks. As a general for Egypt, Moses besieged a city of the Ethiopians, and the king's daughter Tharbis, watching him fight, fell in love with him. She arranged the surrender on condition that he marry her, and he did. It gives the “Ethiopian woman” of v. 1 a history from Moses' years in Egypt.

Hebrews quotes v. 7, “Moses was faithful in all his house,” and builds on its word for him, servant. Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant, Christ is faithful over it as a son, and the readers are that house if they hold fast. The verse that sets Moses above other prophets here sets Christ above Moses.

Writing to a church that had pushed out its leaders, Clement of Rome twice calls Moses “faithful in all his house.” The second time he uses it to introduce the budding of Aaron's rod (Numbers 17), told as Moses' way of ending a dispute over who should hold the priesthood. The quarrel of Numbers 12 and the rivalry of ch. 17 become precedents for keeping order in church office.

Irenaeus reads Moses' marriage to an Ethiopian woman as a sign of the church. By marrying her Moses made a foreigner an Israelite, showing in advance that the wild olive is grafted into the cultivated one (Romans 11:17). The Ethiopian bride stands for the church taken from among the Gentiles.

13.overview:
At the LORD's command Moses sends twelve men, a leader from each tribe, from the wilderness of Paran to search out Canaan, and he renames one of them, Oshea son of Nun, Jehoshua. They travel from the wilderness of Zin to the far north, see the sons of Anak at Hebron, and cut a cluster of grapes at Eshcol so heavy that two men carry it on a staff. After forty days they come back to Kadesh: the land flows with milk and honey, they say, but its people are strong and its cities walled. Caleb urges the people to go up at once. The others spread an evil report and say they looked like grasshoppers.

The report changes as it goes. It starts with what the men saw and carried home, and it ends with what they felt. In the last line they claim to know how they looked in the giants' eyes (v. 33).

13.hermeneutics:
Egypt's own literature knew Canaan as a rich country. In the Story of Sinuhe, a Middle Kingdom tale from about 1900 BC, an Egyptian exile settles in a district of Canaan called Yaa and describes it: figs and grapes, more wine than water, plenty of honey and oil, every kind of fruit on its trees, barley and wheat. The spies' first sentence (v. 27) matches that picture. No one in the chapter disputes that the land is good. The question is what the spies do with the fact.

Papyrus Anastasi I, a satirical letter used to train Egyptian scribes in the 13th century BC, mocks a scribe who has never led troops through Canaan. It warns of a narrow pass where Shasu nomads lurk in the bushes, some of them four or five cubits tall and fierce of face. Soldiers in Egypt told tales of giants in the Canaanite hills too, and the letter exaggerates on purpose. The spies' sons of Anak (vv. 22, 28, 33) belong to the same kind of traveler's fear.

Verse 22 dates Hebron by an Egyptian city: it was built seven years before Zoan, the city the Greeks called Tanis, in the eastern Delta. Zoan stood for Pharaoh's court in later Israel's memory (Isaiah 19:11; Psalm 78:12). The note assumes hearers who knew Egypt's old cities and could measure Canaan's age against them.

notes: **Search:** the verb *tur*, “search” or “spy out,” comes 7 times here (vv. 2, 16, 17, 21, 25, 32 ×2) and 5 more in ch. 14.

**The turn at “Nevertheless”** (v. 28): each of Moses' questions gets a fair answer. After Caleb speaks, the others answer a question Moses never asked, whether Israel can win (v. 31), and the good land becomes one that “eateth up the inhabitants” (v. 32).
**Anak** runs through the report (vv. 22, 28, 33). In v. 33 the sons of Anak are joined to the *nephilim*, the “giants” of Genesis 6:4, the only other place the word appears in the Torah.

The spies unit (13:1–14:45) begins in the wilderness of Paran, where 12:16 left the camp, and ends with defeat at Hormah. Its key verb looks back to 10:33, where the ark went ahead of Israel “to search out” a resting place; now men are sent to search instead.

**Backward and forward:** In Deuteronomy 1:22 the people ask for the spies before the LORD commands it here. Caleb's report is repaid in Joshua 14:6–14, where at eighty-five he claims Hebron, and he drives out the three sons of Anak named in v. 22 (Joshua 15:14).

traditions.text: Rebuking his brothers, Nephi retells the conquest the spies feared from its other side. After the Jordan crossing the Lord made Israel mighty to drive out the people of the land, and Nephi asks whether those people were righteous; he answers that they were not. “The Lord esteemeth all flesh in one,” he says, and the land was taken from its inhabitants because they had rejected God's word, not because Israel was stronger.

Rashi reads “Send thou” (v. 2) as “send for yourself”: God was not commanding the mission but allowing it, since in Deuteronomy 1:22 the people had asked for spies. He also asks why the story follows Miriam's punishment. The spies had just seen what happens to someone who slanders, he says, and slandered the land anyway.

The Talmud notices that v. 22 says the spies went up but “he came” to Hebron, in the singular. Caleb went alone to the graves of the patriarchs to pray that he would be saved from the spies' plan. Joshua did not need to, since Moses had already prayed for him by adding God's name to his: *Jehoshua*, “may the LORD save you.”

Rabbi Yitzhak taught that the spies' names fit their deeds, though only some could be explained. Sethur “hid” the works of God, and Nahbi “concealed” God's word that the land was good. On the grasshoppers of v. 33, Rav Mesharshiyya asked how the spies could know what the giants thought, and called them liars; another answer has them overhearing the Canaanites say there were grasshoppers in the trees.

The rabbis worked out how big the Eshcol cluster was. Carried on a staff “between two,” it needed two staffs and four bearers, and Rabbi Yitzhak made it eight men under a frame of poles, with one spy carrying a pomegranate and another a fig. Joshua and Caleb carried nothing, either because it was beneath their rank or because the fruit was brought to frighten the people and they would have no part in it.

Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa read the spies' words in v. 31, “they are stronger than we,” with a darker sense. The Hebrew can also mean “stronger than he,” and he took it to mean the spies were saying the Canaanites were too strong even for God. Their sin then lay not only in slandering the land but in doubting its owner.

On the *nephilim* of v. 33 Rashi draws on older tradition: the sons of Anak descended from Shemhazai and Azael, angels who fell from heaven in the generation of Enosh. This links the spies' giants to Genesis 6:4 and to the fallen Watchers of 1 Enoch, where Semjaza and Azazel lead the angels who came down. Rashi also explains the name Anak from the word for a necklace, as if the sun hung around their necks because they were so tall.

In a treatise on why Scripture changes names, Philo takes up v. 16. The name Hosea, he says, asks a question, what sort of person this is, while Joshua means “the salvation of the Lord,” the name of the best possible character. The new name marks what the man has become, and it sets him apart from the other spies, whose names the chapter lists without comment.

Josephus has the twelve range from the border of Egypt to Hamath and Lebanon and come back praising the excellence of the fruit. Then they pile up obstacles: deep rivers, high mountains, strong cities, and at Hebron “the posterity of the giants.” In his telling the spies are frightened first and pass their fear to the people, who weep all night and decide to stone Moses and Aaron and go back to Egypt.

Barnabas notes that Moses gave the son of Nun the name Jesus, the Greek form of Joshua, when he sent him to spy out the land. He reads the renaming as prophecy: the Father was revealing everything about his Son, so that the people would listen to this one man alone. The name of the spy becomes the name of the Savior.

Justin presses the same point on his Jewish partner in debate: Oshea, sent to spy out Canaan, was named Jesus by Moses, and no one asks why. As Joshua led the people into the land and divided it by lot, Justin argues, Jesus the Christ will gather the scattered people and give the good land to each, as an eternal possession rather than a temporary one.

14.overview:
The congregation weeps all night, wishes it had died in Egypt or in the wilderness, and talks of choosing a captain to lead it back. Joshua and Caleb plead that the land is good and the LORD is with them, and the people are about to stone them when the glory of the LORD appears. The LORD threatens to destroy Israel and make a nation of Moses. Moses pleads, and the LORD pardons, but he swears that no one of this generation except Caleb and Joshua will see the land. They will wander forty years, a year for each day of the search, and the ten spies die by plague. The next morning the people go up to fight anyway and are beaten back to Hormah.

Moses' prayer works by quoting. In vv. 17–18 he repeats the words the LORD proclaimed about himself at Sinai (Exodus 34:6–7) and asks him to act on them.

14.hermeneutics:
Moses' argument in vv. 13–16 assumes that the nations read a people's fortunes as the record of its god. About 840 BC the Moabite king Mesha explained on his victory stele why Omri of Israel had oppressed Moab for many days: Chemosh, Moab's god, was angry with his land. When Mesha won the land back, that too was Chemosh's doing. In that world a people's death in the desert would be read as its god's anger or as its god's weakness. Moses fears that Egypt and Canaan will choose weakness, and he asks the LORD to guard his name.

The same stele says Israel held the district of Medeba through Omri's days and half the days of his son, “forty years.” The figure does not match the biblical reigns closely, and it works as a round number for a generation. The sentence of vv. 33–34 uses that span with a precise rule, a year for each day of the search, so that the generation that refused the land lives out its life outside it.

Mesha also goes to war only when his god sends him. Chemosh says to him, “Go, take Nebo from Israel,” and he goes by night and takes it. In such a world an army that marched without its god's word was asking for defeat. Verses 40–45 show Israel doing exactly that: the people go up after the LORD has said not to, while the ark of the covenant and Moses stay in the camp.

notes: **The hinge is v. 28:** “as ye have spoken in mine ears, so will I do” to you. The sentence grants the people's own wish.

**Fall:** the verb comes 5 times. The people fear they will fall by the sword (v. 3), Moses and Aaron fall on their faces (v. 5), carcases will fall in the wilderness (vv. 29, 32), and Moses warns the attackers that they will fall by the sword (v. 43).
**Murmur** comes 6 times (vv. 2, 27 ×3, 29, 36), and “forty” 3 times in vv. 33–34, matching the forty days of 13:25.

The chapter closes the spies unit begun at 13:1 and turns the book. The generation counted in chs. 1–4 is now sentenced to die in the wilderness. The second census in ch. 26 counts their children, and 26:64–65 confirms that only Caleb and Joshua were left.

**Backward and forward:** Moses' plea follows the pattern of his plea after the golden calf, where he also asks what the Egyptians would say (Exodus 32:11–14). Psalm 95:10–11 turns the oath of this chapter into a warning for every later generation.

traditions.text: This revelation on priesthood reads the wilderness oath as the loss of more than a land. Moses sought to sanctify the people so that they might behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts, and the Lord swore that they would not enter his rest while in the wilderness, “which rest is the fulness of his glory.” So he took Moses and the Holy Priesthood from their midst, and the lesser priesthood continued.

traditions.date: c. 544 BC and c. 82 BC (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: Two Book of Mormon preachers use the wilderness oath, in the language of Psalm 95, as a warning to their own people. Jacob labored to bring his people into God's rest, “lest by any means he should swear in his wrath” that they should not enter, as in the provocation in the wilderness. Alma calls Israel's rebellion the first provocation and urges his hearers not to harden their hearts but to enter the rest of God.

In his praise of Israel's famous men, Ben Sira honors Joshua and Caleb for standing against the congregation in Moses' days. They turned away wrath and stopped the evil report, and so of six hundred thousand men on foot only these two were kept alive to bring the people into the land flowing with milk and honey. He adds that Caleb kept his strength into old age, as Joshua 14:11 says.

Pirkei Avot sets the “ten times” of v. 22 in a list of tens: ten miracles in Egypt and ten at the sea, ten plagues in Egypt and ten at the sea, and ten trials by which the fathers tried God in the wilderness. The Talmud adds that the sentence was sealed by the spies' words in particular. If those who slandered wood and stones were punished so, it reasons, how much more one who slanders a person.

The Mishnah counts the decree that the fathers would die in the wilderness as the first of five disasters on the Ninth of Av, the day the Temple later fell twice. The Talmud explains the date from v. 1: the people wept that night for nothing, so God said he would give them a reason to weep on it for generations.

Did the wilderness generation lose the world to come as well as the land? Rabbi Akiva said yes, reading v. 35 in two parts: “consumed” in this world, “there they shall die” in the next. Rabbi Eliezer disagreed and applied Psalm 50:5 to them: they were the ones who made a covenant with God by sacrifice.

Jewish law requires ten men for public prayer, and the Talmud finds the number here. The LORD calls the ten spies an “evil congregation” (v. 27), since Joshua and Caleb are not counted, so a congregation is ten. The quorum for sanctifying God's name was learned from the men who brought the evil report. The same chain of reasoning links the spies to Korah's company in ch. 16, also called a congregation.

Josephus explains the attack of vv. 40–45 as pride. The people decided they could win without Moses, claiming that God's help came from their ancestors' merit and their own virtue, and went out “not waiting for any assistance from their legislator.” Beaten and chased back to the camp, they took the defeat as God's anger and accepted Moses' leadership again. Moses then led them further into the wilderness, away from the Canaanites, to wait for a better time.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and asks who the rebels were: all who came out of Egypt with Moses, “whose carcases fell in the wilderness,” which echoes v. 29. They could not enter because of unbelief. Even Joshua (KJV “Jesus”), who did lead the next generation in, did not give them the final rest, so that rest is still offered “to day,” and the writer warns his readers not to fall short of it the same way.

Paul counts the wilderness deaths among the warnings for the church: God was not pleased with many of them, and they were overthrown in the wilderness, and Christians should not murmur as some of them did. Jude uses the same history against false teachers: the Lord saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed those who did not believe.

15.overview:
Laws resume. When Israel comes into the land, every burnt offering or sacrifice is to come with flour, oil and wine in set amounts, more for a ram than for a lamb and more for a bullock than for a ram, and the stranger offers by the same rule. A cake from the first of the dough goes to the LORD. Sins of ignorance, whether by the whole congregation or by one person, are forgiven through offerings, but the one who sins presumptuously is cut off. A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is held until the LORD gives judgment and is stoned outside the camp. Last, Israel is to put fringes with a cord of blue on the borders of their garments.

The timing matters. The day after a generation is told it will die in the wilderness, the LORD speaks of “when ye be come into the land” (vv. 2, 18). The promise stands, for their children.

15.hermeneutics:
In Mesopotamian temples the statues of the gods were served regular meals: bread, meat, beer and wine set before them and later taken away. Verses 4–10 also make each animal offering a full meal, meat with flour, oil and wine, and they scale the portions to the animal. But nothing is set before an image. The offering is made by fire as a “sweet savour,” and the wine is poured out as a drink offering.

The “ribband of blue” (v. 38) was wool dyed *tekhelet*, a blue-violet made from murex sea snails. The dye was a specialty of the Phoenician coast, and it took a great many snails to color a little wool, so blue and purple cloth was a luxury of kings and temples across the region. In Israel the color marked the holiest things: the tabernacle curtains, the high priest's robe, the cord that tied on his gold plate (Exodus 26:1; 28:31, 37). Verse 38 puts one cord of it on every Israelite's clothes, and v. 40 gives the reason: to “be holy unto your God.”

The hem of a garment stood for the person who wore it. At Mari, officials who reported a prophet's message sometimes sent along a lock of the prophet's hair and a piece of the hem of his garment, so the message could be checked. When David cut off the skirt of Saul's robe, his heart struck him for it (1 Samuel 24:4–5). The fringe turns the edge of every Israelite's clothing, the part that said who he was, into a reminder of whose he was.

rows.text: Sins of ignorance and of presumption

notes: **The stranger** (*ger*) comes 7 times (vv. 14, 15 ×2, 16, 26, 29, 30), with “one ordinance,” “one law” and “one manner” for native and stranger alike (vv. 15–16, 29).

**Ignorance and the high hand:** the noun for unintentional sin comes 7 times in vv. 24–29. One verse then names the opposite, sin done “presumptuously,” literally “with a high hand” (v. 30), and the Sabbath case follows at once.
**Remember** comes twice (vv. 39, 40), and the chapter closes with the words that open the Ten Commandments: the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt (v. 41; Exodus 20:2).
The chapter is a unit of its own, a block of law set between the refusal at Kadesh (chs. 13–14) and Korah's rebellion (chs. 16–17), with one wilderness story inside it.

**Backward:** the fringes are given so that Israel will “seek not after” its own heart and eyes (v. 39). The Hebrew verb is the one used for the spies who searched the land in chs. 13–14; what they did with their eyes, every Israelite is now warned against. **Forward:** Deuteronomy 22:12 repeats the command for fringes on the four corners.

traditions.text: A thematic link, not a reading of this chapter: King Benjamin's sermon draws the same line between sins of ignorance and open rebellion. Christ's blood atones for those who have “ignorantly sinned,” but “wo, wo unto him who knoweth that he rebelleth against God.” For such a person, Benjamin says, salvation comes only through repentance and faith in Christ.

Verses 37–41 became the third paragraph of the Shema, recited morning and evening. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha explained why it comes last: the paragraph before it applies by day and by night, while the fringes were worn only by day. Because v. 41 recalls the Exodus, the paragraph is still said at night, and the Mishnah records how Ben Zoma proved that the Exodus must be remembered at night as well.

Rabbi Meir asked why blue was chosen for the fringes. His answer is a chain of likenesses: the blue is like the sea, the sea is like the sky, and the sky is like the throne of God's glory, which Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:26 describe in the color of sapphire. Looking at the cord, the wearer looks toward the throne. The Mishnah adds that the blue and the white threads each count without the other.

Rashi explains how a fringe can remind one of “all” the commandments (v. 39). The letters of *tsitsit* add up to 600, and with eight threads and five knots the total is 613, the traditional number of the Torah's commandments. He also notes that “seek not after” uses the spies' verb: the heart and the eyes are the body's spies, since the eye sees, the heart desires, and the body sins.

Why does a law about fringes end by recalling the Exodus (v. 41)? Rashi, following the Talmud, answers that the God who told a firstborn from one who was not in Egypt can also tell true blue dye from a cheap imitation. Whoever passes off indigo-dyed wool as the real blue on his fringes will answer to him. From the Sifre he adds that Israel was brought out of Egypt on condition that it take on God's decrees.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 15:41; b. Bava Metzia 61b

traditions.text: The tractate on the dough offering of vv. 17–21 sets its size: one twenty-fourth of the dough for a household, one forty-eighth for a baker who sells in the market. If the dough was made unclean on purpose, the larger share is still owed, so that a sinner should not profit. The Bible names no amount, and the rabbis supplied one.

The Sifre reads v. 32 as a reproach: Israel kept only the first Sabbath and broke the second. Rabbi Akiva named the gatherer as Zelophehad, whose daughters later say he “died in his own sin” (27:3). Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira objected that Akiva was exposing what Scripture had covered, and said the man was one of those who presumed to go up the hill in 14:44.

Philo retells the case at length. The man crossed the quiet camp to pick up sticks while others had gone out to pray, and they nearly killed him on the spot but held back because they were private persons and left the penalty to the magistrates. He was held while Moses asked God, and Philo stresses that gathering wood is preparing fuel, and fire is the first thing forbidden on the Sabbath.

The woman with the issue of blood came behind Jesus and touched the hem, or border, of his garment, and the sick at Gennesaret begged to touch it too. The Greek word is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for the fringes of v. 38. Read that way, they reached for the cord that marked him as a keeper of the commandments.

Jesus faults some scribes and Pharisees who “enlarge the borders of their garments” so that others will see. The complaint assumes the command of v. 38 and turns its own purpose against the display. The fringe was meant to keep the wearer's eyes on the commandments, not to draw other people's eyes to the wearer.

Hebrews warns that for those who “sin wilfully” after receiving the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. It is the same line this chapter draws between sins of ignorance, for which offerings atone, and sin with a high hand, for which none is given. Hebrews adds that whoever despised Moses' law died without mercy, and asks how much worse it is to despise the Son of God.

16.overview:
Korah, a Levite, joins with the Reubenites Dathan and Abiram and 250 leaders of the congregation to challenge Moses and Aaron: “all the congregation are holy,” so why should these two stand above it? Moses sets a test for the next day. Each man brings a censer of incense before the LORD. The ground opens under the tents of Dathan and Abiram, and fire from the LORD burns the 250 who offered incense. Their bronze censers are beaten into a covering for the altar. The next day the whole congregation blames Moses and Aaron for the deaths, and a plague breaks out until Aaron runs into the camp with incense.

Watch the incense. It kills the 250 who offer it without being called, and it saves the people when Aaron carries it. The same act that condemned the rebels becomes the sign of the priest God chose, standing “between the dead and the living” (v. 48).

16.hermeneutics:
In the Baal myth from Ugarit (13th century BC), Death is a god, Mot, who swallows his victims. He is pictured with one lip to the earth and one to the heavens, and Baal must go down into his mouth (KTU 1.5 ii 2–6). Israel's neighbors could hear “the earth opened her mouth” (v. 32) as the jaws of the underworld. Numbers keeps the image and drops the god. The ground opens only when Moses has finished speaking, at the LORD's “new thing” (v. 30), and closes again. The rebels “go down quick into the pit” (Hebrew *sheol*) alive, which is what the old poems feared from Mot.

Ancient peoples read plague as the anger of a god over a wrong left unpaid. The Hittite king Mursili II (14th century BC) prayed over a plague that had killed people in his land for twenty years. He asked the gods to reveal the cause by oracle, dream, or prophet, and found it in a broken treaty oath and a neglected river offering. Then he confessed his father's sin and offered restitution. In Numbers no oracle is needed, since the people's murmuring is in plain view (v. 41). The remedy is no payment. It is a priest with incense taken from the altar, and the priest is Aaron, the man whose right to burn incense had just been challenged (vv. 46–48).

notes: **Two grievances:** Korah wants the priesthood (v. 10); Dathan and Abiram attack Moses as a would-be prince who has brought them nowhere (vv. 13–14). Each group meets its own end, earth for one and fire for the other.
**“Holy”:** Korah claims the whole congregation is holy (*qadosh*, v. 3); Moses answers that the LORD will show “who is holy” (vv. 5, 7). The adjective appears only in these three verses.
**Choosing:** “The man whom the LORD doth choose” (v. 7) sets up the rods of 17:5, where the same verb returns.

Chapters 16–17 form one story: a challenge to Aaron's priesthood, answered three times (fire, plague stopped by his incense, the budding rod). In Hebrew, ch. 17 begins at KJV 16:36, so the censer plates and the plague open the next chapter there. The unit follows the fringes law (15:37–41) and leads into the priests' charge in ch. 18.

**Backward and forward:** Nadab and Abihu died offering incense the LORD had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1–2). King Uzziah later takes a censer into the temple and is struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:18–19).

traditions.text: A thematic link. The fifth article states that a man “must be called of God,” by prophecy and by the laying on of hands from those in authority. Korah's claim rested on the holiness of the whole congregation; Latter-day Saints read the chapter as a case of authority taken without a call.

A thematic link. Writing from Liberty Jail, Joseph Smith explained why many are called but few chosen: their hearts aspire to the honors of men. When men use the priesthood to gratify pride or “vain ambition,” the heavens withdraw and the authority is lost. Moses' charge against Korah, “ye take too much upon you” (v. 7), names the same fault.

A dispute for the sake of heaven will last; one not for heaven's sake will not. The Mishnah's example of the first is Hillel and Shammai, and of the second, Korah and all his company. Another saying in the tractate lists “the mouth of the earth” among ten things made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, ready for v. 32.

Ties the revolt to the fringes law just before it (15:38). Korah asks Moses whether a garment made entirely of blue wool still needs a blue thread on its tassels, and whether a house full of Torah scrolls still needs a mezuzah. When Moses says yes to both, Korah mocks the commandments as Moses' own invention. The midrash adds that Korah dressed the 250 in all-blue garments.

The rabbis debated whether Korah's company had any hope. Rabbi Akiva reads the earth closing upon them as this world and their perishing as the world to come. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira answers that they are like a lost thing that is sought and found, citing Psalm 119:176. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer applies Hannah's song to them: “he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up.”

On the son of Peleth is named in v. 1 and then disappears from the story. The Talmud explains why: his wife asked him what he stood to gain, since whichever man led, he would remain a follower, and she kept him home. The same page says Moses going to Dathan and Abiram himself (v. 25) teaches that one must not let a quarrel continue.

Asks why a clever man like Korah would risk this. Following the Tanhuma, he says Korah foresaw the prophet Samuel and the temple singers among his descendants and assumed he would be spared. He was half right. His sons repented and did not die (26:11), and Samuel and the singers came from them (1 Chronicles 6:33–38).

Makes Korah a rich and eloquent man who envied Moses and argued that if the priesthood belonged to the eldest tribe, Reuben should have it. That explains why Reubenites joined a Levite's revolt. In his telling Korah dies by fire with the 250 men, not in the earth with Dathan and Abiram.

Gives Korah seven sons who refuse to join him, saying that God, not their father, formed them, and that they will walk in his law. God declares that the swallowed men will pine away in darkness until the world is renewed, and then die and not live. The sons echo the note in 26:11 that “the children of Korah died not.”

Second Timothy 2:19 quotes the Greek of v. 5, “The Lord knoweth them that are his,” and adds a call to depart from iniquity, which recalls Moses telling Israel to depart from the rebels' tents (v. 26). Jude lists the rebellion (“gainsaying”) of Core alongside Cain and Balaam as patterns for false teachers.

Hebrews states the principle at stake in the chapter: no one takes the honor of high priesthood on himself, “but he that is called of God, as was Aaron.” It then applies the rule to Christ, who did not glorify himself but was named priest by God.

Writing to Corinth, where younger members had pushed out their elders, Clement twice uses this chapter. Jealousy brought Dathan and Abiram “down alive to hades,” and their hardened hearts are a warning to anyone stirring up sedition. Chapter 43 goes on to the rods of ch. 17.

In his treatise on church unity, Cyprian makes Korah, Dathan, and Abiram the model of schism. They claimed the power of sacrifice against Moses and Aaron, and the earth and the fire answered them. He pairs them with Uzziah and the censer and with Nadab and Abihu, the same links the unit notes draw.

17.overview:
To end the murmuring against Aaron, the LORD has the leader of each of the twelve tribes bring a rod with his name written on it, with Aaron's name on the rod of Levi. Moses lays the rods in the tabernacle before the testimony. By the next morning Aaron's rod has budded, blossomed, and borne ripe almonds, while the others are unchanged. Each leader takes back his own rod, and Aaron's is returned to the sanctuary as a lasting sign. The people cry out that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die.

Notice how the chapter ends. The proof was meant to stop the complaints, and it does, but it leaves Israel terrified: “we die, we perish, we all perish” (v. 12). The question of who may come near the LORD and live is left open for the next chapter to answer.

17.hermeneutics:
In Egypt a staff was a sign of who a man was. Officials were shown holding long staffs, and surviving New Kingdom staffs carry their owners' names and titles, such as one inscribed for a chief craftsman of the god Amun (Brooklyn Museum 37.277E). A leader's rod with his name cut into it was his signature and his office together. The Hebrew word here, *matteh*, means both “rod” and “tribe,” and Numbers uses it for the tribes from its first chapter (1:16). Twelve rods with twelve names are twelve tribes in miniature, and the test asks which tribe the LORD claims, not just which man.

Ancient kings kept their treaties in temples. A Hittite treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza (14th century BC) says a duplicate was laid up before the storm god Teshub and was to be read aloud at set times, so the god himself held the record. Israel's covenant tablets, “the testimony,” lie in the ark in the same way (Exodus 25:16). Aaron's rod is put back “before the testimony” to be kept “for a token against the rebels” (v. 10). It joins the jar of manna (Exodus 16:33–34) as evidence filed with the covenant, a standing witness that the matter was settled in God's own presence.

notes: **Rod:** *matteh* occurs 17 times in thirteen verses. The word that names the tribes names the test.
**Growth in four steps:** v. 8 piles up the stages, budded, brought forth buds, bloomed blossoms, yielded almonds, all in one night. A dead stick passes through a whole season.
**Murmurings:** the chapter opens with the aim of stopping Israel's murmurings (v. 5) and repeats it when the rod is kept (v. 10). The goal is met, but in v. 12 the murmuring turns into fear.

In the Hebrew Bible this chapter begins at KJV 16:36, so the censer plates, the plague, and the rods form one chapter there. The rods are the third proof of Aaron's call after the fire and the stopped plague. The people's cry in vv. 12–13 is answered at once in 18:1–7, where priests and Levites guard the sanctuary so Israel need not die.

**Echoes:** the almond blossom recalls the almond-shaped cups of the lampstand (Exodus 25:33). Jeremiah later sees “a rod of an almond tree” as a sign that the LORD will perform his word (Jeremiah 1:11–12).

traditions.text: The revelation on priesthood traces how the Lord's authority passed down through Israel. It says the Lord “confirmed a priesthood also upon Aaron and his seed,” one that continues and abides with the higher priesthood. This chapter shows that grant being settled in public: twelve tribes put forward their rods, and God alone makes Aaron's flower, closing the dispute that Korah began.

Explains that the second priesthood is called the Priesthood of Aaron “because it was conferred upon Aaron and his seed.” It is called lesser because it is an appendage to the Melchizedek Priesthood and administers outward ordinances. The name Latter-day Saints use for this priesthood today goes back to the choice of Aaron's house that the budding rod confirms.

Retells the test with each tribal head inscribing the name of his tribe and Aaron writing “the tribe of Levi” on his own. The owners could still recognize their rods the next morning, and the almonds on Aaron's were ripe because the rod had been cut from an almond tree. Josephus counts the rods as the third time God ordained Aaron, after the fire and the plague, and says the long sedition ended there.

Has Moses refuse to defend his brother's appointment with words, since it is hard to change minds already made up, and pray instead for a visible sign. Philo then reads the almond as a figure of virtue. In the almond, seed and fruit are one, so its beginning and end are the same, and each virtue, he says, is both the start and the goal of a life lived by nature.

Compares the flowering rod to the peeled rods Jacob set at the watering troughs in Laban's country (Genesis 30:37–39), which it calls almond rods (KJV “hazel”; the Hebrew *luz* is usually taken as almond). As the flocks bred according to those rods, it says, so the priesthood was established by these. The congregation is pictured as a flock and the almond wood ties the two stories together.

Records a teaching that when King Josiah hid the ark to spare it from exile, the jar of manna, the anointing oil, and “Aaron's staff with its almonds and blossoms” were hidden with it. The rod's later history thus follows the ark's, the same grouping Hebrews 9:4 assumes.

Says Moses cut all twelve rods from a single beam so no one could claim Aaron's had been fresh wood. It plays on the Hebrew of v. 8: the rod “bore almonds” (*vayigmol shekedim*) because it repaid (*gamal*) those who strove against Levi. The midrash adds that kings held this staff until the temple fell, and that it will be in the hand of the Messiah (Psalm 110:2).

Explains the stages of v. 8 one by one: the blossom, the bud that forms once the flower falls, and the ripened nut. Then he asks why the rod bore almonds of all fruits. The almond blossoms earlier than any other tree, and so, he says, punishment comes quickly on whoever challenges the priesthood, as leprosy broke out at once on Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:19).

In describing the first tabernacle, Hebrews puts Aaron's rod inside the ark of the covenant with the golden pot of manna and the tablets. Numbers says only that the rod was laid “before the testimony,” as the manna was (Exodus 16:34), so Hebrews reflects a reading in which the tokens were kept together. The Talmud's list of things hidden with the ark has the same grouping.

Retells the test to settle a church quarrel over who should hold office. Clement adds that Moses tied and sealed the rods with the chiefs' signet rings, sealed the tabernacle doors, and showed the seals unbroken in the morning. Moses knew the result beforehand, Clement says, but acted this way so that no disorder would arise in Israel.

In a long list of rods and trees that point to Christ and the cross, Justin includes Aaron's rod, which “declared him to be the high priest,” right before Isaiah's rod from the root of Jesse. The chain was built for debate with a Jewish teacher, and it shows how early this chapter entered Christian reading of the Old Testament.

18.overview:
The LORD speaks to Aaron and sets out who may approach the sanctuary and how its servants will live. Aaron and his sons alone serve at the altar and within the veil, and they bear the guilt if the holy things are mishandled. The Levites are given to them as helpers and guards, but must not touch the altar or the holy vessels. The priests receive the most holy portions of the offerings, the best of the oil, wine, and grain, the firstfruits, and the firstborn. They get no land, because the LORD is their inheritance. The Levites receive Israel's tithe and give a tenth of it to the priests.

Read it as an answer to the people's cry at the end of ch. 17, “shall we be consumed with dying?” A guarded order of priests and Levites stands between the people and the holy place, “that there be no wrath any more upon the children of Israel” (v. 5).

historicalContext.text: Leviticus 6–7 (priests' portions); Deuteronomy 18:1–5 (the LORD as the Levites' inheritance); Nehemiah 10:37–38 (the tithe of the tithe in practice).

18.hermeneutics:
Temples in the ancient world had guards, and guarding was a matter of life and death. The Hittite *Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel* (CTH 264, 14th–13th century BC) order temple staff to spend the night in the temple and post watchmen who patrol all night. Whoever commits an offense against the sacred precinct is to be killed, with no pardon. Numbers 18 sets up the same kind of guard. The Levites “keep the charge” of the tent around the priests, and “the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death” (v. 7). The difference is the reason for the guard. It is there to protect Israel from the holy place, “that there be no wrath any more” (v. 5), as well as to protect the holy place from intruders.

In Egypt, the food set before a god each day did not go to waste. After the god had received it, the offerings were passed on to the temple staff, a practice Egyptologists call the reversion of offerings, and the shares were graded by rank. Temple personnel ate from the god's table. Numbers 18 works on a similar principle, since what Israel gives “unto the LORD” is then “given” to Aaron and his house (vv. 8, 12, 19). The Egyptian temples also owned vast estates. Here the priests and Levites own no land at all; “I am thy part and thine inheritance” (v. 20).

breakdown.label: Priests and Levites guard the sanctuary; outsiders must not approach
The priests' share of the holy offerings
Firstfruits, devoted things, and firstborn; a covenant of salt
No land for priests and Levites; the tithe to Levi
The Levites give a tenth of the tithe to Aaron

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through four speeches, three to Aaron and one to Moses.

rows.text: To Aaron: the charge of the sanctuary
To Aaron: no inheritance; tithes for Levi
To Moses: the Levites' tithe of the tithe

notes: **Aaron addressed alone:** “the LORD spake unto Aaron” (vv. 1, 8, 20). Nowhere else in Numbers does the LORD speak to Aaron without Moses.
**Given:** the verb *natan*, “give,” occurs 12 times. The Levites are a gift to the priests (v. 6), the priesthood itself a gift (v. 7), and the offerings are given to Aaron's house.
**Keeping the charge:** *mishmeret*, “charge” or “guard duty,” occurs six times in vv. 3–8; “inheritance” (*nachalah*) six times in vv. 20–26; “tithe” six times in vv. 21–28.

Chapters 18–19 turn from narrative to law, but they grow out of the Korah story. Chapter 18 answers the people's fear of approaching the tabernacle (17:12–13) by fixing who may come near and who bears the risk. Chapter 19 then deals with the other danger in the camp, the uncleanness of death, after so many had died (16:49).

**Echoes:** salt and covenant are joined in Leviticus 2:13 and in the “covenant of salt” given to David (2 Chronicles 13:5). The Levites' landlessness returns when Joshua divides Canaan (Joshua 13:14, 33).

traditions.text: When John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, he said it would remain on the earth until the sons of Levi “do offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.” D&C 84 speaks of the sons of Moses and of Aaron offering an acceptable offering in the Lord's house. Both look to a restored form of the service this chapter assigns to Aaron's house and the Levites.

Names the bishopric as the presidency of the Aaronic Priesthood and says that only a literal descendant of Aaron has a legal right to that office and its keys. A high priest may serve as bishop when no such descendant can be found. The revelation keeps the lineal claim this chapter gives to “thou and thy sons with thee,” and also provides for the office when no heir of Aaron is known.

A thematic link. The revelation sets the law of tithing for the Church in this dispensation: after an initial consecration of surplus property, members pay one-tenth of their interest annually. Like Numbers 18, it ties the tenth to the support of the work and “for my holy priesthood,” though its tithe goes to the Church rather than to a tribe.

traditions.source: Tosefta, cited in the Babylonian Talmud
traditions.text: Counts twenty-four gifts given to Aaron and his sons, all of them found in Numbers 18. They are framed by a general statement (v. 8) and another general statement (v. 19), with the details in between, and sealed by the “covenant of salt.” Whoever gives them, the passage says, is as one who keeps the whole Torah and brings every offering.

Reads “covenant of salt” (v. 19) as a covenant made with something that is sound, lasting, and keeps other things from spoiling. He adds from the Sifre that Scripture states the priests' gifts in general terms at the start and the end, with the details in between, out of affection for them. On v. 20 he notes that Aaron's house would not share even in the spoils of war.

Numbers says only “the best” of oil, wine, and grain (v. 12). The Mishnah sets a measure for this heave offering: a generous person gives one fortieth, an average one a fiftieth, and a stingy one a sixtieth. A whole tractate grew from these few verses.

Explains why the law gave the priests no land: so that God himself would be their inheritance, sharing with them what grateful people offer him, and so that they would have no business to manage except worship. He then lists the firstfruits, firstborn, and portions as their honors and rewards.

Places this law right after the budding rod and lists the priests' revenues as the practice of his own day. The Levites give the priests a tenth of their tithe and thirteen of their forty-eight cities. The firstborn of man is redeemed for five shekels, and whatever the priests receive may be eaten by their wives and children, except the sin offerings, which the males alone eat in the temple.

Paul defends the right of gospel preachers to be supported by pointing to this chapter: “they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar.” In the same way, he says, the Lord ordained that those who preach the gospel should live of the gospel, though Paul himself declined the right.

Hebrews cites the law that the sons of Levi take tithes from their brethren, who are also descendants of Abraham. It then argues that Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes to Melchizedek, making Melchizedek's priesthood the greater one.

This early church manual tells believers to give the firstfruits of the winepress and threshing floor, of cattle and sheep, to the prophets, “for they are your chief-priests.” If there is no prophet, the firstfruits go to the poor. The winepress and threshing floor are the same two sources named in vv. 27 and 30.

Forbids clergy to serve as executors of wills on the model of the Levites. When the other tribes divided the land, he writes, Levi received nothing but the tithes, so that those who served at the altar would not be pulled into worldly business. Clergy, supported by the gifts of the brethren, are to live the same way.

19.overview:
The LORD commands a red heifer without blemish, never yoked, to be slaughtered outside the camp before Eleazar the priest. Her blood is sprinkled seven times toward the tabernacle, and she is burned whole with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet. The ashes are stored outside the camp. Anyone who touches a corpse, a bone, or a grave, or enters a tent where someone has died, is unclean seven days. On the third and seventh days a clean person mixes the ashes with running water and sprinkles him with hyssop. Whoever refuses this purification is cut off, because he defiles the sanctuary.

Notice the reversal. The water cleanses the unclean, yet every clean person who handles it becomes unclean: the priest, the one who burns the heifer, the one who gathers the ashes, the one who sprinkles (vv. 7–10, 21). Purity flows one way and impurity the other.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Numbers as compiled later from older and priestly sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Not dated; given in the wilderness, with Eleazar already acting for Aaron (v. 3). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Outside the camp, where the heifer is killed and her ashes kept “in a clean place” (v. 9); the law also looks ahead to tents and graves, and to fields where men are slain (v. 16).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 31:19–24 applies the water of separation after the war with Midian; Leviticus 14:4–7 uses cedar, scarlet, and hyssop for a cleansed leper.

19.hermeneutics:
Israel's neighbors fed their dead. In Mesopotamia the *kispu* rite brought food and drink to dead ancestors at regular times, and palace records from Mari (18th century BC) list supplies for funerary offerings on fixed days of each month. In Egypt priests served in endowed tomb chapels, where offerings to the dead were a temple duty. Numbers 19 draws a hard line between the dead and the worship of God. Touching a corpse makes a person unclean for seven days, and coming to the sanctuary in that state “defileth the tabernacle” (v. 13). The worshiper at the tithe later swears he has given nothing “for the dead” (Deuteronomy 26:14). The realm of death is real here, but it has no claim on the holy place.

Purifying with water and plants was common practice. Mesopotamian priests prepared a holy-water vessel (*agubbû*) and dropped tamarisk and other plants into it, and Assyrian palace reliefs show winged figures carrying a bucket and a cone, ready to sprinkle the king. Numbers 19 shares the vessel, the “running water” (literally “living water,” v. 17), and the sprinkling with a plant, hyssop. What it adds is ash from a slaughtered animal whose blood has been sprinkled toward the tabernacle, so that the water carries the force of an offering. The text calls the burned heifer a sin offering (“a purification for sin,” v. 9). And it uses no incantation and names no demon. The uncleanness comes from contact with death, and it is removed by obeying the statute.

breakdown.label: The red heifer killed, sprinkled, and burned outside the camp
The handlers made unclean; the ashes stored
Touching a corpse: seven days, third and seventh day purification
Death in a tent, open vessels, the field, bones, graves
Ashes, running water, and hyssop: how to sprinkle
Refusing purification; the sprinkler and the toucher unclean

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence: first the ashes are made (vv. 1–10), then the law for their use (vv. 11–22).
notes: **Unclean:** the root *tame'*, “unclean,” occurs 19 times in 22 verses (verb, adjective, and noun). Every paragraph ends with someone unclean.
**Sevens:** “seven” or “seventh” occurs eight times: seven sprinklings of blood (v. 4), seven days of uncleanness (vv. 11, 14, 16), and the seventh day of cleansing (vv. 12, 19, twice each).
**Water of separation:** the phrase (*mê niddah*) occurs five times (vv. 9, 13, 20, 21 twice), and “water” eleven times.

Chapters 18–19 are law set between the Korah story and the arrival at Kadesh. After the deaths of 16:31–49, the camp needed a way to deal with corpse impurity without endangering the sanctuary that ch. 18 had just put under guard. Chapter 20 opens with a death, Miriam's, so the law comes just before it is needed.

**Echoes:** the ashes are used after the war with Midian (31:19–24). Ezekiel promises that God will “sprinkle clean water” on Israel (Ezekiel 36:25), and Hebrews names “the ashes of an heifer” as a type (Hebrews 9:13).

traditions.text: A whole tractate is devoted to the red heifer. It asks how many were ever prepared: Moses made the first and Ezra the second, and after Ezra came five (Rabbi Meir) or seven (the sages), made by high priests such as Simeon the Just. Maimonides later counted these nine and added that the tenth would be made by the king Messiah.

traditions.source: Mishnah, Parah, on the heifer's color
traditions.text: “Red” and “without spot” were taken strictly. Two black or white hairs growing from one follicle disqualify the animal, and Rabbi Joshua ben Batera says even one hair on its head and one on its tail does. Hence the later reputation of a fully red heifer as one of the rarest things in Israel.

To have water drawn by someone who had never touched the dead, courtyards were built over bedrock in Jerusalem, with a hollow beneath to block impurity from any hidden grave. Women gave birth there and raised their children in them. The children rode oxen to the Siloam spring sitting on doors, filled stone cups, and brought the water up to mix with the ashes.

traditions.source: Mishnah, Parah, and the Dead Sea Scrolls
traditions.text: Verse 9 asks for a “clean” man, and Jews argued over what that meant. The Mishnah says the priest who burned the heifer was deliberately made unclean and then immersed, so he served before sunset, to refute Sadducees who held that only those whose sun had set were clean enough. The Qumran letter known as 4QMMT takes the strict side: all who slaughter, burn, gather, and sprinkle must be pure “at sunset.”

A gentile tells Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, the sage who rebuilt Jewish learning after AD 70, that the rite looks like sorcery. He answers by comparing it to fumigating a man possessed by a spirit. When the man leaves, the disciples ask for the real answer, and he says that the dead do not defile and the water does not purify. God has decreed a statute, and it may not be broken.

Opens its discussion of the chapter with Ecclesiastes 7:23, where Solomon says he sought wisdom but it was far from him. The rabbis took this law as the one that baffled even the wisest of kings, a statute (*chukkah*) to be kept without a reason being given (v. 2).

Adds a reading that ties the heifer to the golden calf. As a servant girl's child soiled the king's palace and the mother was called to clean it up, so the cow comes to atone for the calf. The red color recalls sins “red like crimson” (Isaiah 1:18), and the heifer that never bore a yoke recalls a people who threw off the yoke of heaven.

Places the first use of the ashes at Miriam's death. After thirty days of mourning, Moses purified the people with a heifer slain by the high priest, burned with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet wool, its ashes mixed into spring water and sprinkled on the third and seventh days. Numbers gives the law without a date, so Josephus ties it to the moment the next chapter needs it. In his version the high priest himself slays the heifer, where Numbers has someone else slay it before Eleazar (v. 3).

Asks why the law uses ashes and water when others purify with sea or spring water alone. His answer is that a person approaching God must first know himself, and the body is made of earth and water. Sprinkled with ash and water, the worshiper is reminded that he came from these and will return to them, and so lays aside pride.

Hebrews names this chapter directly: if “the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean” purify the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ purge the conscience “from dead works.” The phrase turns the chapter's corpse impurity into a figure for sin, the same move the rabbis made by tying the heifer to the calf.

Reads the rite as a figure of Christ. The heifer is Jesus, the men who offer it are the sinners who brought him to slaughter, and the scarlet wool on the wood is the cross. In its version children do the sprinkling, which it reads as the apostles preaching forgiveness. Numbers says only “a clean person” (v. 18), but the Mishnah also has children, raised apart from all contact with the dead, carry the water.

20.overview:
Israel comes to Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, and Miriam dies and is buried there. With no water, the people turn on Moses and Aaron. The LORD tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock before the congregation. Instead Moses calls the people rebels, asks whether he and Aaron must bring water out of the rock, and strikes it twice. Water pours out, but the LORD tells Moses and Aaron that because they did not believe him and sanctify him, they will not bring Israel into the land. Edom refuses Israel passage, so Israel turns toward Mount Hor. There Aaron's garments are put on his son Eleazar, Aaron dies, and Israel mourns him thirty days.

Watch the word “rebels.” Moses hurls it at the people (v. 10), and the LORD turns it back on Moses and Aaron: “ye rebelled against my word” (v. 24).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Numbers as compiled later from older and priestly sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: “The first month” (v. 1), most likely of the fortieth year, since Aaron dies in the fortieth year, fifth month (33:38). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 gives about 1407 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, “in the uttermost” of Edom's border (v. 16); the king's highway through Edom; Mount Hor “by the coast of the land of Edom” (v. 23).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 17:1–7 (an earlier Meribah); Numbers 27:12–14 and Deuteronomy 32:51 (why Moses may not enter); Deuteronomy 2:4–8 (passing Edom); Numbers 33:37–39 and Deuteronomy 10:6 (Aaron's death).

20.hermeneutics:
Moses' message to Edom is written like a diplomatic letter. It opens “Thus saith thy brother Israel” (v. 14), reviews past history, and makes a formal request with terms: no fields, no vineyards, no well water, only the king's highway, and payment for anything drunk (vv. 17, 19). In the Amarna letters (14th century BC) great kings who saw each other as equals wrote to one another as “brother,” and a letter of request often began by recalling past dealings. Israel claims that standing with Edom on the strength of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 36:1). Edom's flat refusal and armed march out (v. 20) answer the request with a show of force.

Pasture and water at a border were things a stronger power granted. An Egyptian frontier report in Papyrus Anastasi VI (late 13th century BC) records that Shasu herdsmen of Edom were allowed past a fortress in the eastern Delta to reach the pools of Pithom, to keep themselves and their flocks alive. In that report, Edomite herders ask Egypt for water. In Numbers 20, Israel, newly out of Egypt, asks Edom for passage and offers to pay for the water. The refusal sends Israel the long way around Edom (21:4), and the chapter's water comes from the rock at Kadesh, not from any neighbor's wells.

No water; the people contend with Moses and Aaron

Moses and Aaron barred from the land; the waters of Meribah
Edom refuses Israel passage on the king's highway
Mount Hor: Aaron's garments to Eleazar; Aaron dies

structure.summary: Inclusio: the chapter opens with Miriam's death (v. 1) and closes with Aaron's (vv. 22–29).

open.text: Miriam died there, and was buried there

close.text: Aaron dies on Mount Hor; thirty days of mourning

rows.text: Water from the rock; Moses and Aaron's sentence

notes: **Rebels:** the root *marah* appears twice, in Moses' “ye rebels” (v. 10) and God's “ye rebelled” (v. 24), and “Meribah” (strife) twice (vv. 13, 24).
**Rock:** Numbers uses *sela'* five times (vv. 8, 10, 11). Exodus 17:6 used *tsur* for the rock Moses was told to strike.
**Perish:** the verb *gava'* (“die, perish”) occurs only five times in Numbers: the people's cry in 17:12–13, their wish to have died with their brethren (v. 3, twice), and Aaron's death (v. 29).

The subsection runs from the return to Kadesh to the victories east of the Jordan (20:1–21:35). The leaders of the Exodus generation pass here: Miriam and Aaron die, and Moses learns that he too will not enter. The priesthood passes to Eleazar in the garments that marked Aaron's office.

**Backward and forward:** Exodus 17:1–7 told of an earlier Meribah, where striking the rock was commanded. Moses' exclusion is recalled at 27:12–14 and Deuteronomy 32:51, and Psalm 106:32–33 says he “spake unadvisedly with his lips.”

traditions.text: Nephi twice recalls that Moses smote the rock and water came forth. Urging his brothers to help build the ship, he reminds them that Moses did it “by his word according to the power of God.” Later he sets the miracle beside the brass serpent as proof that God gave Moses power, and as a pledge that salvation comes only through Christ. Nephi does not say which of the two water miracles (Exodus 17 or Numbers 20) he means, and he does not mention the sin.

Explains why the water fails right after Miriam's death. Three good providers led Israel out of Egypt, and three gifts came through them: the well by Miriam's merit, the cloud by Aaron's, the manna by Moses'. When Miriam died the well disappeared, which is why v. 2 follows v. 1, and it came back only through the merit of Moses and Aaron.

Asks why Miriam's death comes right after the law of the red heifer. His answer: as offerings bring atonement, so does the death of the righteous. He adds that Miriam, like Moses and Aaron, died by the “kiss” of God, though the text does not say so of her out of reverence.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 20:1; b. Moed Katan 28a

traditions.text: Rashi has a story to explain the second blow. Moses and Aaron first spoke to the wrong rock and nothing came. Remembering that at the first Meribah they had been told to strike (Exodus 17:6), they struck the right rock, which only dripped at first because God had said to speak to it, and so they struck again.

On v. 12, Rashi says that had Moses spoken to the rock, Israel would have reasoned that if a rock that neither hears nor speaks obeys God, how much more should they. That is what “to sanctify me” means. He notes that Moses had doubted God's power before, in private (11:22), and was spared then, while this failure happened before all Israel, and Scripture records it so no one would think Moses shared the sin of the generation that died.

Expands the embassy to Edom. Moses offers hostages as security and asks leave to buy provisions, paying even for water. When the king refuses and comes out armed, Moses consults God by the oracle and is told not to begin a war, so he goes around through the wilderness. Deuteronomy 2:4–6 gives the same instruction to buy food and water from Esau's descendants.

Places Mount Hor among the high mountains around Petra, the city the Arabs regarded as their capital. Aaron puts off his high priest's garments and hands them to Eleazar, then dies in sight of the people, aged 123, on the first day of the month the Hebrews call Abba. Josephus' account of these years has no Meribah story and no sin of Moses at the rock. Earlier in the same section he gives Miriam a costly public funeral on a mountain called Sin and thirty days of mourning, details Numbers does not record.

Explains why all the house of Israel mourned Aaron (v. 29), while for Moses the text says only “the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 34:8). Aaron never told anyone they had done wrong and spent his life making peace between quarreling neighbors and between husbands and wives, so men and women alike wept for him. Many children were named Aaron, it adds, by couples he had reconciled.
traditions.cite: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12; Rashi on Numbers 20:29

traditions.text: Paul says Israel in the wilderness all drank the same spiritual drink, from the spiritual Rock that followed them, “and that Rock was Christ.” He uses the wilderness stories as warnings to believers in Corinth: those who lusted, those who tempted God and were bitten by serpents, those who murmured and were destroyed. The complaint at Kadesh fits that pattern, and the Rock that follows them recalls the rabbis' wandering well.

Building on Paul, Augustine reads the double blow of v. 11 as a sign of the cross. The rock was Christ in sign, and it was struck twice with a rod because the cross has two beams. He makes the point in two separate sermons on John, tying the water from the rock to Christ as the bread and drink that come down from heaven, which the soul receives by faith.

21.overview:
King Arad attacks from the south, and Israel answers with a vow; the Canaanite towns are destroyed and the place is named Hormah. Then, going around Edom, the people complain again about the road, the lack of water, and the “light bread.” Fiery serpents bite and many die, and Moses at God’s command sets a serpent of brass on a pole: whoever is bitten and looks at it lives. The march goes north through a string of camps, with snatches of old song, until Israel defeats Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan and holds the land east of the Jordan.

The chapter turns the wilderness story around. At Hormah Israel had been beaten (14:45); here it wins at the same place and goes on winning. Even the serpent scene ends differently from earlier plagues: the people confess “We have sinned,” and the cure asks only for a look.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Numbers as compiled later from older and priestly sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The fortieth year after the Exodus, between Aaron’s death in the fifth month (33:38) and Moses’ speeches in the eleventh (Deuteronomy 1:3–4): about 1406 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or about 1210 BC on the later date many scholars prefer.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From mount Hor “by the way of the Red sea” around Edom, across the Arnon into Amorite country around Heshbon, then north to Bashan (vv. 4, 13, 25, 33).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 33:40–49 (the camps); Deuteronomy 2:24–3:11 and Judges 11:19–22 (Sihon and Og). The Book of Mormon recalls the serpent in 1 Nephi 17:41, 2 Nephi 25:20, Alma 33:19–22 and Helaman 8:14–15.

21.hermeneutics:
Copper was mined and smelted in the Arabah, the rift valley south of the Dead Sea that Israel follows “to compass the land of Edom” (v. 4). Numbers 33:42 puts a camp at Punon, usually identified with the copper district of Feinan. At Timna, in the same valley, Beno Rothenberg excavated an Egyptian mining shrine that was later refitted as a tent sanctuary, probably by Midianites, in the 13th or 12th century BC. Among its finds was a copper snake about five inches long with a partly gilded head. A metal serpent was a known object in this country. Against that background the command of v. 8 is startling: Israel, forbidden images, is told to make the kind of thing its neighbors set up in shrines, and the text ties the healing to the look and to God’s word, with no rite attached.

In the 9th century BC Mesha, king of Moab, set up a victory stone at Dibon. He names Chemosh as Moab’s god, says Omri of Israel had oppressed Moab “because Chemosh was angry with his country,” and mentions towns from this chapter: Dibon, Medeba, Jahaz, Aroer, and “the road in the Arnon.” He also says he killed the people of Nebo and devoted them to Ashtar-Chemosh, the same practice of devoting a town to destruction that Israel vows at Hormah (vv. 2–3). Beside Mesha, the taunt song of vv. 27–30 sounds like the region’s own war poetry. It calls Moab “people of Chemosh” (v. 29) and treats defeat as something a god allows, just as Mesha does.
