Fiery serpents and the serpent of brass
Camps to the Arnon; the Book of the Wars of the LORD
The well at Beer and its song; on to Pisgah
Sihon refuses passage; Heshbon taken; the taunt song
Jaazer taken; Og of Bashan defeated

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from a victory to the serpents and on to two more victories.

rows.text: Arad: a vow, and Hormah destroyed
The march north, with two fragments of song
Sihon: victory, and a quoted taunt song
Og: done to him “as thou didst unto Sihon”

notes: **Three poems:** the chapter quotes the Book of the Wars of the LORD (vv. 14–15), the song of the well (vv. 17–18), and a taunt song from “they that speak in proverbs” (vv. 27–30). Numbers seldom stops to cite older sources.

**Serpent words:** the Hebrew for “serpent” comes 5 times in vv. 6–9 and the word for “fiery” twice (vv. 6, 8). “Bite” comes 3 times (vv. 6, 8, 9) and “live” twice (vv. 8, 9), so the fulfillment in v. 9 repeats the command of v. 8 almost word for word.
**Sihon:** his name comes 8 times in vv. 21–34, and Og’s defeat is told by pointing back to him (v. 34).

Chapters 20–21 move Israel from Kadesh to the edge of Moab: Miriam and Aaron die, Edom refuses passage (20:14–21), and the long series of complaints by the generation that left Egypt ends with the serpents. With 22:1 the camp settles in the plains of Moab, where the rest of the book takes place.

**Forward:** Hezekiah breaks the brass serpent in pieces because Israel had been burning incense to it, and calls it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). Sihon and Og become a fixed memory in Israel’s praise (Psalm 135:10–12).

traditions.text: Rebuking brothers who mock his shipbuilding, Nephi retells the wilderness story and includes the “fiery flying serpents.” He stresses how little was asked: “the labor which they had to perform was to look,” and yet many perished because the way was so simple. Numbers says nothing about anyone refusing to look; Nephi supplies that detail and makes the scene a story about unbelief.

Teaching the poor among the Zoramites, Alma calls the serpent “a type” raised up in the wilderness so that whoever looked might live. Few understood its meaning, he says, and some would not look because they did not believe it would heal them. He applies it directly to his hearers: cast about your eyes and believe in the Son of God, who will suffer and rise again.

Nephi son of Helaman says Moses bore record of the Son of God: as Moses “lifted up the brazen serpent in the wilderness,” so the coming one would be lifted up, and those who look to him with faith and a contrite spirit might live eternally. Centuries earlier the first Nephi had listed the healing of the bitten among Moses’ God-given powers, in testifying that there is no other name than Jesus Christ whereby man can be saved. These are close to John 3:14–15 (below).

This Alexandrian Jewish book remembers the serpents as a short correction that left Israel holding a sign of salvation to remind them of the law. It then guards against reading the bronze image as a charm: whoever turned toward it “was not saved by the thing that he saw, but by thee.” The Mishnah makes the same point (next entry).

In a discussion of the shofar, the Mishnah asks whether Moses’ raised hands won the battle with Amalek, and then whether the serpent killed or gave life. Its answer is the same for both: when Israel looked upward and submitted their hearts to their Father in heaven they were healed, and when they did not they wasted away.

Rashi notices that God told Moses only to make a “fiery” one (v. 8) and named no metal. Following Genesis Rabbah, he says Moses chose copper because God had called the creature *nachash*, so he made it of *nechoshet*, one word answering the other.

The Aramaic Targum turns the place names after the well into a story: from the wilderness the well was a gift (Mattanah), and it went with them into the valley (Nahaliel) and up to the heights (Bamoth). Rashi follows the Targum and adds, from Midrash Tanchuma, that the well finally ceased in the plains of Moab, where Moses died. Paul knows a similar tradition when he speaks of the Rock “that followed them” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
traditions.cite: Onkelos on Numbers 21:18–20; Rashi on Numbers 21:19–20

traditions.text: This rule of a sectarian community, found in the Cairo Genizah and at Qumran, quotes v. 18 and decodes it: “The well is the Law,” and those who dug it are the captivity of Israel. The lawgiver who directed the digging is the one who interprets the Law. The same document reads Balaam’s star in 24:17 as a leader of its own community.

Josephus passes over Arad and the serpents and goes straight from Aaron’s death to the Arnon. He says Moses welcomed the fight with Sihon as a way to wean the Hebrews from the idleness that had bred their earlier revolts. He describes Og as a man of rare size and strength, and adds the iron bed of Deuteronomy 3:11, kept at Rabbah of the Ammonites.

Speaking with Nicodemus at night, Jesus takes this chapter as a figure of his death: as Moses lifted up the serpent, “even so must the Son of man be lifted up,” so that whoever believes may have eternal life. The healing look of v. 8 becomes believing, and the pole becomes the cross.

Paul lists the serpents among the wilderness warnings to the Corinthians: some Israelites “tempted Christ” and were destroyed of serpents. In his reading the one Israel tried in v. 5 was Christ himself.

This early Christian letter says Moses, who had forbidden images, made a brazen serpent anyway to show a type of Jesus. Barnabas has Moses tell the bitten to come to “the serpent which is placed on the tree” and to hope that the dead serpent could make them alive. Numbers speaks of a pole; Barnabas’ “tree” points to the cross.

Justin raises the problem himself: why would God, who forbade every likeness, command a bronze serpent? He answers that it was a sign and a mystery, by which God declared he would break the power of the serpent “which occasioned the transgression of Adam.” The sign, he insists, did not teach anyone to believe in a serpent.

22.overview:
Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Balak, Moab’s king, is terrified. He sends elders of Moab and Midian with fees to hire Balaam son of Beor, a famous seer from Pethor on the Euphrates, to curse them. God forbids Balaam to go. A grander embassy comes, and God lets him go on condition that he speak only God’s word. On the road the angel of the LORD blocks the way three times; the donkey sees the angel, turns aside, is beaten, and at last speaks. Balaam’s eyes are opened, and he arrives at Balak’s high places promising to say only what God gives him.

Watch who sees. The famous seer is blind to the angel his donkey sees three times, and the God who opens the donkey’s mouth (v. 28) is the same God who will put words in Balaam’s (v. 38).

22.hermeneutics:
In 1967 a Dutch expedition at Tell Deir Alla, in the Jordan Valley east of the river, found fragments of an inscription painted in ink on plaster, dated about 800 BC. Its heading names Balaam son of Beor and calls him a divine seer. The gods come to him at night and he sees a vision; in the morning he fasts and weeps and tells his people what the council of the gods has decided. So Balaam was a remembered figure in Transjordan, outside Israel and its scriptures. The night visits of vv. 8–9 and 19–20 fit the way such a seer was known to work, and the question Numbers raises is whose word that kind of man will carry.

Kings in the ancient Near East used specialists to work against enemies with words and rites. Egyptian execration texts of the early second millennium BC write the names of hostile rulers and peoples, Asiatic towns among them, on pottery bowls and figurines that were then smashed or buried. Balak’s plan is of this kind: weaken the enemy with a curse first, then fight (v. 6). The “rewards of divination” the elders carry (v. 7) are a professional’s fee, and the whole story assumes that a skilled curse could change a war.

Pethor is usually identified with Pitru, a town on the Sajur river near the Euphrates south of Carchemish, which Shalmaneser III of Assyria says he took in the 9th century BC. That puts Balaam hundreds of miles from Moab, so each embassy is a long journey (vv. 5, 15).

notes: **Three times:** the donkey (v. 28) and the angel (vv. 32, 33) both say “these three times,” and Balak will say it once more when Balaam has “altogether blessed them” (24:10). Three turns on the road preview three failed curses.
**Seeing:** the donkey “saw” the angel three times (vv. 23, 25, 27), as the angel later says (v. 33), before Balaam sees anything (v. 31). “Angel of the LORD” comes 10 times in vv. 22–35.
**Mouth:** the LORD opens the donkey’s mouth (v. 28), and Balaam tells Balak he can speak only what God puts in his mouth (v. 38). The same word returns at each oracle (23:5, 12, 16).

Chapters 22–24 are one story with its own frame. It opens with Israel camped in the plains of Moab (22:1) and closes when Balaam and Balak go home (24:25). Israel never acts in it; the people are only seen from the hills.

**Backward and forward:** Moab is “distressed because of” Israel (v. 3) with the same Hebrew verb Exodus 1:12 uses of Egypt, which also feared Israel’s numbers. Numbers 31:8 later reports that Balaam was killed among the Midianites.

traditions.text: This expansive Aramaic paraphrase identifies Balaam with Laban the Aramean, Jacob’s father-in-law, and explains Pethor as “a name signifying an interpreter of dreams.” In v. 22 it names his two servants Jannes and Jambres, the names later tradition gave Pharaoh’s magicians and that 2 Timothy 3:8 uses for those who withstood Moses. Making Balaam into Laban turns his hiring into the latest round of a family feud as old as Genesis 31.

Philo describes Balaam as the most celebrated diviner of his day, who had foretold rain in summer and drought in winter. He makes the second embassy’s money decisive: Balaam, allured by the gifts, still pleaded God’s orders but “no longer with sincerity.” On the road he draws the lesson of the donkey, that a man who boasted he could see the Creator of the world could not see what his beast saw.

In Josephus the Midianites, Balaam’s friends, take the lead in hiring the greatest prophet of the age, who lived by the Euphrates. He tells the road scene briefly: the donkey, sensing a divine spirit, crushes Balaam against the wall, falls down, and by God’s will speaks “with the voice of a man.” The angel then tells Balaam the beast is not at fault.

This Latin retelling adds a backstory: Balak reminds Balaam that he once cursed the Amorites for Balak’s father, Zippor, and they fell. God answers Balaam by recalling Abraham and the binding of Isaac, and warns, “if thou curse them, who is he that shall bless thee?” The donkey scene shrinks to a single sentence.

Pirkei Avot counts the mouth of the donkey among ten things created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, with the manna, the well, and Moses’ staff. On this view the speaking donkey was provided for at creation and held in reserve for this road. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan inserts the same list, with the speaking donkey, into its rendering of v. 28.

Another saying sets the disciples of Abraham against the disciples of Balaam the wicked. Abraham’s have a good eye, a humble spirit, and a modest appetite; Balaam’s have an evil eye, a haughty spirit, and an appetite without limit. The portrait draws on this chapter, where Balaam is bargained up by a second, richer embassy.

The Talmud enjoys v. 30. Balak’s princes ask why Balaam rides a donkey and not a horse; he makes excuses, and the donkey answers each one, so that Balaam cannot win an argument with his own animal. The rabbis then ask how a man who did not know his donkey’s mind could claim, as he does in 24:16, to know the knowledge of the Most High. Elsewhere Rabbi Yohanan explains why Joshua 13:22 calls Balaam a soothsayer: he began as a prophet and ended as a mere diviner.

Rashi asks why God let his presence rest on a wicked foreigner at all, and answers from Midrash Tanchuma: so the nations could not say they would have changed if only they had had prophets. On v. 28 he notes that the donkey’s “three times” uses an unusual word, *regalim*, which also names the three pilgrimage feasts. He hears a rebuke in it: would you uproot a nation that keeps three festivals a year?

Peter warns against false teachers who have followed Balaam’s way and, like him, loved the wages of unrighteousness. He adds the road scene as the rebuke: a dumb beast speaking with a man’s voice “forbad the madness of the prophet.” The reading picks up the money of vv. 7, 17, and 37.

Jude sets Balaam between Cain and Korah as patterns for intruders in the church, who “ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward.” Like 2 Peter and the Mishnah’s disciples of Balaam, Jude makes greed the key to his character, a trait Numbers itself only hints at through the fees of vv. 7 and 17.

Writing to Bishop Chromatius, Ambrose asks how a diviner, unlawful in Israel, could receive true oracles. He says Balaam spoke one thing and intended another, and that God let him go as a trial of a covetous man, not as approval. The angel, he notes, “shewed himself to the ass, but not to the diviner.”

23.overview:
Balak and Balaam stand on a height where part of Israel’s camp can be seen. Seven altars are built and a bull and a ram offered on each, and Balaam goes off alone to meet God, who puts a word in his mouth. Instead of a curse he speaks a blessing on a people that dwells alone and cannot be counted. Balak takes him to the top of Pisgah and repeats the sacrifices, and the second oracle goes further: God does not change his mind, and no enchantment works against Jacob. Balak tells him to neither curse nor bless, then tries a third place, the top of Peor.

The two rounds are told almost step for step alike, and the sameness is the point. A new view and a fresh set of altars change nothing, because Balaam can only report what God has already decided (vv. 19–20).

23.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian diviners, the *bārû*, sought omens by sacrificing a sheep and reading its liver, and clay models of livers inscribed with omens have been found at Mari and in Babylonia. Balaam’s routine looks like that profession at work: altars and victims first, then a withdrawal to see what will come (vv. 3, 15), and 24:1 says outright that he had gone “to seek for enchantments.” The chapter keeps the stage set of a diviner and changes what happens on it. No omen is read. God meets Balaam and puts a word in his mouth (vv. 4–5, 16), and the second oracle declares that there is no enchantment or divination against Jacob (v. 23).

In the 9th century BC Mesha of Moab recorded on his victory stone that he made a “high-place for Chemosh” at Qarhoh. Balak’s heights belong to that world. The high places of Baal, the top of Pisgah, and the top of Peor were holy sites as well as lookouts, and each move gives a new angle on the camp (v. 13), as if a different place might bring a different answer.

The animal of v. 22 that the KJV calls a “unicorn” is the *re’em*, the wild ox or aurochs (Akkadian *rīmu*). Assyrian kings boasted of hunting wild bulls as the most dangerous game. Read as a wild bull, the line gives Israel’s God-given strength the image of the most powerful horned animal the region knew, and it leads into the lion of v. 24.

notes: **The second panel grows:** the first parable runs 4 verses (vv. 7–10), the second 7 (vv. 18–24). The second answers the first, moving from “How shall I curse?” (v. 8) to “I cannot reverse it” (v. 20).
**Bless:** the verb comes 6 times, in pairs (vv. 11, 20, 25). Balak’s two complaints use the doubled form, “blessed them altogether” and “nor bless them at all.”
**Parable:** “took up his parable” (vv. 7, 18) is the formula that introduces each of Balaam’s seven oracles in chs. 23–24.

The middle of the Balaam story. Chapter 22 brought Balaam to the heights; ch. 23 holds the first two of the three blessings Balak never wanted, and the third round, begun at Peor in vv. 27–30, runs on without a break into 24:1–9.

**Echo:** v. 19 returns almost word for word when Samuel tells Saul the kingdom is taken from him (1 Samuel 15:29). Joshua 24:10 sums up these scenes from God’s side: “I would not hearken unto Balaam.”

traditions.text: Philo says that when Balaam went apart, the prophetic spirit entered him and drove out his art of divination, since holy inspiration cannot share a house with magic. In his version of v. 9 Israel dwells alone by “the peculiar nature of their remarkable customs.” He reads v. 10 as Balaam’s wish that his soul be remembered among the souls of the righteous.

Philo explains Balak’s second move (v. 13) as a guess that the deity might change his mind, or that a change of place might alter the decision. The second oracle answers him directly: God does not change his purpose like a man, since “his word is also his deed.” In Philo’s version of v. 23, Israel needs no augury because it trusts the one Governor of the world.

Josephus rewrites the oracles as a single speech that opens “Happy is this people,” promising them the land, glory over earth and sea, and descendants more numerous than the stars. When Balak complains, Balaam answers that no one can stay silent or choose his words when the spirit of God seizes him. Philo makes the same point (above).

Pseudo-Philo’s Balaam calls Israel a fire that consumes water and a vine that no one can uproot. He admits he has lost the days of his life by letting Balak persuade him, and laments that “when I cursed I perished,” and when he blessed he was not blessed himself.

The Talmud explains Balaam’s power as knowing the one brief moment each day when God is angry, and cursing then. It reads v. 8, “How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?” as the result: through all the days of Balaam, God did not become angry. Micah 6:5, which tells Israel to remember Balak and Balaam, becomes a reminder of that restraint.

The sages once wanted to add Balaam’s blessings to the twice-daily Shema. One proposed reason, that v. 22 mentions the Exodus, is rejected because many passages do. The reason kept is 24:9, whose lying down and rising echo the Shema’s “when thou liest down, and when thou risest up,” and the plan was dropped as too long for the congregation.

Onkelos renders “the shout of a king is among them” (v. 21) as the Shekhinah, the dwelling presence, of their King among them. Where the Hebrew says God has not beheld iniquity in Jacob, Onkelos says there are no idol worshippers in Jacob. Both renderings turn a statement about God’s view of Israel into a description of Israel’s worship.

The Targum expands v. 10 into a confession. Balaam foresees that if Israel kills him with the sword he will have no portion in the world to come, and still he says, “nevertheless if I may but die the death of the true!” Numbers 31:8 reports that Israel did kill him with the sword, which gives the wish its irony.

Following Midrash Tanchuma, Rashi takes the rocks and hills of v. 9 as Israel’s founders: Balaam looks at their beginnings and sees them rooted in the patriarchs and matriarchs, firm as rock. In “the dust of Jacob” (v. 10) he hears the commandments Israel keeps with dust, such as the ashes of the red heifer (19:9) and the dust in the test of a suspected wife (5:17).

On v. 4 Rashi notes that Balaam says “the seven altars,” as if they were known. Following Midrash Tanchuma, he has Balaam boast that Israel’s fathers built seven altars between them, four by Abraham, one by Isaac, and two by Jacob, and that he alone has matched them all, with a bull and a ram on each where Abraham offered one ram. On v. 23 Rashi explains that Israel needs no enchanters because God’s decrees are told to them by their prophets or by the Urim and Thummim.

Writing to Bishop Chromatius, Ambrose starts from v. 19: God cannot lie, and that impossibility is a sign of his strength. He compares Balaam to Caiaphas, who prophesied without meaning to (John 11:51), so that the grace of the oracle belongs to God who calls. Balaam’s wish to die the death of the righteous (v. 10) he reads as a figure of baptism, dying to sin and rising to new life.

24.overview:
Seeing that God means to bless Israel, Balaam stops looking for omens, faces the camp spread out by tribes, and the spirit of God comes on him. His third oracle praises Israel’s tents like gardens by a river and ends with “Blessed is he that blesseth thee.” Balak, furious, sends him home without his fee. Balaam answers with a fourth oracle he was never asked for: a star and a sceptre will rise out of Israel and smite Moab. Three short sayings about Amalek, the Kenites, and ships from Chittim follow, and the two men go their ways.

Balak paid for a curse and got four blessings, the last one unrequested and aimed at Moab itself. The star of v. 17 is placed “not now” and “not nigh,” in a future Balaam can see but not reach, which is why later readers kept watching for it.

24.hermeneutics:
The Deir Alla plaster text, which names Balaam son of Beor (see ch. 22), also shows the religious vocabulary his oracles use. In it the gods who meet in council are called the *shaddayin*, a plural related to Shaddai, the name the KJV renders “the Almighty” in vv. 4 and 16. That Balaam sees a vision at night and reports a decree of darkness. Numbers keeps the profile of such a seer, a man “falling into a trance” with his eyes open who sees “the vision of the Almighty,” and fills the vision with blessing for Israel and its king.

Egyptian execration texts of the early second millennium BC curse a people called the Shutu, apparently living east of the Jordan. Many scholars connect them with “the children of Sheth” in v. 17, set in parallel with Moab. If the identification holds, the line names Moab’s people by an old regional name rather than by Adam’s son Seth, and the oracle stays fixed on Balak’s own country.

Chittim (Kittim) in v. 24 takes its name from Kition on the south coast of Cyprus, a Phoenician center by the 9th century BC. In the Bible the name moves west: Genesis 10:4 lists Kittim among the sons of Javan, the Greeks, and Daniel 11:30 has “ships of Chittim” turning back a Syrian king, usually taken as the Romans of the 2nd century BC. A saying about ships from the west afflicting Asshur could be read anew in each century, which is one reason the last oracles drew so much later interpretation.

notes: **Matching openings:** the two long oracles begin with the same self-introduction, Balaam son of Beor and “the man whose eyes are open hath said” (vv. 3–4, 15–16). The fourth adds that he “knew the knowledge of the most High.”
**Seven:** “took up his parable” comes 5 times here (vv. 3, 15, 20, 21, 23). With 23:7 and 23:18 that makes seven oracles.
**Three times:** Balak’s “these three times” (v. 10) closes the count that began with the donkey (22:28, 32, 33).

The end of the Balaam story: Balaam and Balak each go home (v. 25), closing the frame opened in 22:1–4. The oracles move from Israel’s camp in front of Balaam (vv. 5–6) to “the latter days” (v. 14), so the story looks beyond the book.

**Backward:** v. 9 joins Judah’s crouching lion (Genesis 49:9) to God’s word to Abraham (Genesis 12:3), and the sceptre of v. 17 recalls Genesis 49:10. **Forward:** Agag (v. 7) is the Amalekite king Saul spares (1 Samuel 15:8), and David subdues Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 14).

traditions.text: The Greek translation reads v. 7 as “There shall come a man out of his seed,” who will rule many nations, and in v. 17 a man rises out of Israel in place of the sceptre. It also makes the king of v. 7 higher than Gog, where the Hebrew has Agag. These choices point the oracles toward a coming individual ruler, the reading Philo and the Targums develop.

Philo calls Balaam the man who saw a clear vision of God with the open, sleepless eyes of the soul. Following the Greek, he has the third oracle promise a man who will come forth from Israel, rule many nations, and see his kingdom raised to heaven. His retelling moves from Balak’s anger straight to Balaam’s private advice, so the star oracle never appears.

Josephus summarizes the last oracles without quoting them: Balaam foretold calamities for kings and famous cities, some not yet founded. Many of these, he says, had already come to pass by land and sea “till my own memory,” so the rest could be expected to follow. He leaves the star and the sceptre unmentioned.

This sectarian rule reads v. 17 as two leaders of its own community: the star is the one who explained the Law, and the sceptre is “the prince of all the congregation.” It handles the well of 21:18 in the same way, finding its own institutions inside Balaam’s and Moses’ words.

The Targum makes v. 17 openly messianic: when the mighty King of Jacob’s house reigns, the Messiah, “the Power-sceptre of Israel,” will be anointed. It adds the armies of Gog to the enemies he defeats, tying Balaam’s oracle to Ezekiel 38–39. Targum Onkelos is briefer but likewise reads the star as a king and the sceptre as the Messiah.
traditions.cite: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Onkelos on Numbers 24:17

traditions.text: Rabbi Akiva read the star of v. 17 as Simon bar Koziba, leader of the revolt against Rome in AD 132–135, whose nickname Bar Kokhba, “son of the star,” comes from this verse. When Akiva hailed him as king Messiah, Rabbi Yohanan ben Torta answered that grass would grow from Akiva’s cheeks before the son of David came.

Rabbi Yohanan asked what Balaam saw in v. 2 when he saw Israel abiding by tribes. His answer: the doors of their tents did not face one another, so each family kept its privacy, and Balaam judged them worthy to have the Divine Presence rest on them. The Talmud uses this to forbid opening a door facing a neighbor’s door across a shared courtyard.

The Talmud reads v. 14 closely: Balaam offers to tell what “this people shall do to thy people,” but the rabbis say he meant the reverse and was already planning the advice that led to Peor (ch. 25). On the Kenites of v. 21 it has Balaam taunt Jethro, the Kenite, who had sat with him in Pharaoh’s council and fled rather than agree to drown Israel’s sons. Of the three counselors, it says, Balaam was killed, Job suffered, and Jethro’s descendants became scribes in the Sanhedrin.

Rashi reads Balaam’s turning toward the wilderness (v. 1) with a version of the Targum: Balaam faced the place of the golden calf, hoping that recalling Israel’s sin would make a curse fall. On “the man whose eyes are open” (v. 3) he reports the Talmud’s view that the singular “eye” means Balaam was blind in one eye.

Justin quotes Moses’ prophecy, “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a leader from Israel,” and ties it to the star that rose at Christ’s birth. The Magi from Arabia, he says, recognized the sign and came to worship him (Matthew 2:1–2). Justin attributes the words to Moses, who recorded them, and Origen (next entry) does much the same.

Answering the pagan critic Celsus, Origen argues that the star of Matthew 2 was a new body, like a comet, and that unlike comets it had a prophecy attached. The Magi, he says, knew Balaam’s prophecies, which Moses recorded, and when the star appeared they concluded that the man foretold with it had been born. He adds that the birth broke the power of the spirits the Magi relied on, which sent them to look for its cause.

25.overview:
At Shittim the men of Israel take up with Moabite women, eat at their sacrifices, and bow to their gods; Israel “joined himself unto Baal-peor,” and God’s anger breaks out. Moses orders the judges to kill the men involved. While the people weep at the tabernacle door, an Israelite brings a Midianite woman into his tent in full view. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, follows with a javelin and kills them both, and the plague stops after 24,000 deaths. God gives Phinehas a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood, the couple are named as Zimri and Cozbi, and God orders war on Midian.

Balaam is not mentioned here. Only later, in 31:16, does Numbers say this sin came “through the counsel of Balaam,” so the story that began with a curse that failed ends with a seduction that nearly succeeded.

25.hermeneutics:
In Canaan and its neighbors *Baal*, “lord,” was the name of a great storm god and also a title for gods of particular places. The Bible knows Baal-zephon (Exodus 14:2) and Baal-hermon (Judges 3:3), and Mesha of Moab says on his 9th-century BC victory stone that he built Baal-meon, a town Numbers 32:38 also names. Baal-peor is the lord of Peor, the height where Balak built his last seven altars (23:28). Israel camps below a local god’s mountain and is drawn into its cult, the first time in Numbers that the people worship the god of the land around them.

Assyrian kings boasted of impaling or hanging up the bodies of rebels, and the Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib’s palace show captives impaled before the conquered city. Public display of the dead was a punishment for breaking faith with an overlord. The order in v. 4 to hang up the heads of the people “before the LORD against the sun” treats Peor as treason against Israel’s divine king. The same rare verb returns when the Gibeonites hang Saul’s sons “before the LORD” (2 Samuel 21:6, 9), and Deuteronomy 21:22–23 later limits such display to a single day.

Midian was a confederation of tribes east and south of Moab, and Joshua 13:21 lists Cozbi’s father Zur among the princes of Midian, “dukes of Sihon.” Moses himself had married the daughter of a Midianite priest (Exodus 2:16–21). The union of a Simeonite prince and a Midianite chief’s daughter (vv. 14–15) was a public alliance as well as a private act, which is why the chapter names both families and ends with an order against Midian.

A single episode between Balaam’s departure (24:25) and the second census. The Hebrew text ends the chapter with “after the plague” (25:19), tying the new census to the plague; the KJV prints those words as the start of 26:1. The count that follows shows the old generation gone (26:64–65).

traditions.text: Philo says Balaam, his oracles finished, gave Balak private advice of his own: since the Hebrews could be beaten only by breaking their law, Moab’s most beautiful women should win the young men and then require them to sacrifice to their gods. Phinehas, the high priest’s son, killed the pair in the act, and God gave him peace, which no man can bestow, and a priesthood that could not be taken from his family. Philo reports 24,000 slain in one day.

Josephus also traces Peor to Balaam’s parting advice. He gives Zimri a defiant speech in the assembly, calling Moses’ laws tyranny and claiming a free man’s right to marry a foreign wife and sacrifice to gods of his choosing. Phinehas, “greatly troubled” at this, kills Zimri and Cozbi in Zimri’s tent, and other young men follow his example.

Pseudo-Philo has Balaam advise Balak to set the most beautiful women of Moab and Midian, adorned with gold and jewels, before Israel, “for otherwise thou canst not subdue them.” Balaam then goes home, and Balak does all that he showed him.

Ben Sira ranks Phinehas third in glory after Moses and Aaron, for his zeal, and says his covenant of peace gave him and his posterity the priesthood for ever. 1 Maccabees makes him a model for revolt: when Mattathias kills a Jew sacrificing at a pagan altar, he acts “zealously for the law of God like as Phinees did.” The zealot of Numbers becomes the patron of the Maccabean uprising of 167 BC.

The Mishnah turns the episode into a rule: zealots may strike down a man who has relations with an Aramean woman, though no court could sentence him. It also says that the worship of Baal-peor consisted of relieving oneself before the idol, so even that degrading act counted as idolatry.

The Talmud hedges the zealot rule tightly: had Zimri separated from Cozbi before Phinehas struck, Phinehas would have been liable for murder. It also gives Zimri an argument, bringing Cozbi before Moses to ask who had permitted Moses his own Midianite wife, the daughter of Jethro. Moses forgets the law, the elders weep (v. 6), and Phinehas, remembering it, acts; God then tells Moses to greet Phinehas first with peace.

This early rabbinic commentary links v. 1 to Balaam’s offer in 24:14 to advise Balak. It pictures market stalls with an old woman outside and a young one inside, selling linen, then wine, then producing an image of Peor. On v. 13 it adds that Phinehas never left his post: he “stands and atones” until the resurrection of the dead.

The Targum lists twelve miracles that protected Phinehas, among them a lintel that lifted to let him carry the pair out on his lance and their blood held back until he had borne them through the camp. It then pictures him pleading that 24,000 should not die for two sinners, and the plague stops. In v. 12 God makes him “an angel of the covenant, that he may ever live,” to announce the redemption at the end of days. A priest who never dies is the Targum’s reading of “an everlasting priesthood” (v. 13).

This late midrash compares Shittim with the golden calf: wherever Israel “sat down” in the wilderness, idolatry followed. It credits Phinehas with a lasting rule, a ban by the divine Name on drinking the wine of the nations, because that wine had been offered to idols and served immorality, as at Peor.

Rashi opens the chapter by saying the harlotry at Shittim came by Balaam’s advice. On v. 13 he asks why Phinehas needed a priesthood at all, since he was Aaron’s grandson. His answer, from the Talmud: the priesthood had gone to Aaron, his anointed sons, and children born after the anointing, so Phinehas, already born, did not become a priest until he had slain Zimri.

The risen Christ rebukes the church at Pergamos for holding “the doctrine of Balaam,” who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel: eating things sacrificed to idols and committing fornication. Those are the two sins of vv. 1–2, credited to Balaam’s teaching as Philo and Josephus also credit them.

Paul warns the Corinthians, who were eating in idol temples, not to commit fornication as some Israelites did, when there “fell in one day three and twenty thousand.” His figure is a thousand fewer than the 24,000 of v. 9.

26.overview:
After the plague at Baal-peor, the LORD tells Moses and Eleazar to count Israel's fighting men again, this time on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho. Tribe by tribe the clans are named and totaled, and the sum is 601,730 men. The land is to be shared out by size and by lot. The Levites are counted separately, since they receive no land. The chapter closes by noting that not one man from the census at Sinai is left except Caleb and Joshua.

Those last verses turn the list into a verdict. The total is almost the same as the first census (603,550 in 1:46), but every name behind it is new. What the LORD swore after the spies returned, that this generation would fall in the wilderness (14:29–30), has happened. The people on these rolls are the ones who will enter the land.

26.hermeneutics:
Counting an army was an administrative act with a religious edge. At Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC), the military census was called *tebibtum*, a word built on the root for “pure,” and the verb “to cleanse” could stand in for the ordinary verb for mustering troops. Officials drew up the lists town by town and name by name, and a census could be the basis for granting land to the men enrolled. Israel's law knew the same unease about counting: each man paid a ransom “that there be no plague among them” (Exodus 30:12). So a first hearer would notice that this census is ordered “after the plague” (v. 1). The roll is taken once the camp has been purged by the deaths of 24,000 (25:9), and like the Mari lists it decides who will hold land (vv. 53–54).

Lots were how ancient peoples let the gods decide. A small inscribed clay cube from Assyria, made for Yahalu, a high official of Shalmaneser III (9th century BC), calls itself his *puru*, “lot,” and asks that it come up before the gods Ashur and Adad. Legal texts from Nuzi distinguish land a man held by inheritance from land he received by lot from the crown. Numbers 26 joins two rules that seem to pull against each other: larger tribes get more land (v. 54), yet the land is assigned by lot (vv. 55–56). Size sets how much; the lot, read as God's choice, sets where. No tribe could say that Moses or Eleazar had picked its territory.

**Changes since ch. 1:** Simeon falls from 59,300 to 22,200 and Manasseh rises from 32,200 to 52,700, now listed ahead of Ephraim. The overall total is 1,820 lower.
**Four pauses for a story:** Korah's company (vv. 9–11), Judah's sons Er and Onan (v. 19), Zelophehad's daughters (v. 33), and Nadab and Abihu (v. 61). The daughters' note sets up ch. 27.

Chapter 26 opens the book's last movement. Numbers began with a census at Sinai (ch. 1) of the generation that would refuse the land; this second census, on the plains of Moab, lists the generation that will take it, and vv. 64–65 mark the handover. The count also sets up what follows: Zelophehad's daughters (v. 33; 27:1–11; ch. 36) and the land shared by lot (vv. 52–56; 33:54; 34:13).
**Forward:** Joshua 14:1–2 carries out the lot, with Eleazar and Joshua presiding.

traditions.text: This revelation on priesthood says Moses sought to sanctify Israel in the wilderness so they might see the face of God, but they hardened their hearts, and the Lord swore they should not enter his rest while in the wilderness. It defines that rest as “the fulness of his glory,” and adds that the Lord then took Moses and the Holy Priesthood out of their midst. Verses 64–65 of this chapter record the first part of that oath carried out: a whole generation gone from the rolls.

Rebuking his brothers, Nephi retells the wilderness story. The Lord led Israel by day and gave light by night, yet they hardened their hearts and reviled Moses. Nephi's summary is that “according to his word he did destroy them,” and by the same word led them; after the crossing of Jordan he made them mighty to drive out the people of the land (v. 32). The two censuses of Numbers record both halves of that sentence: the generation that fell and the one that went over.

Why count again? Rashi gives two answers from the Midrash. A shepherd whose flock has been attacked by wolves counts what is left. And Moses, who received the flock by number when Israel left Egypt, must hand it back by number now that his death is near.

In Hebrew each clan name here is framed by a *he* in front and a *yod* at the end (*ha-Chanochi*, “the Hanochites”). Following Song of Songs Rabbah, Rashi says the nations mocked Israel's pedigrees, claiming the Egyptians had fathered their children, so God set his own name *Yah* on every clan as a witness that they were their fathers' sons. He finds the same idea in Psalm 122:4, “the tribes of the LORD.”

traditions.text: Verse 11 says only that Korah's sons did not die. Rashi, citing the Talmud, explains that they had joined the plot but turned in their hearts at the last moment, and a raised place was set apart for them below. Their line survived to sing in the temple: Psalms 42 and 84, among others, carry the heading “for the sons of Korah.”

traditions.text: Asher's daughter Serah is named in Jacob's household going down to Egypt (Genesis 46:17) and again here, generations later. Rashi says she is mentioned because she was still alive. The Aramaic Targum goes further: she was escorted by angels into the Garden of Eden alive, because she had been the one to tell Jacob that Joseph was living.

traditions.text: The Talmud reconciles “by lot” (v. 55) with an inspired choice. Eleazar, wearing the Urim and Thummim, announced in advance which tribe and which region would come up together, and then drew the two from separate urns to match. It also reads “between many and few” (v. 56) as an adjustment in money, since a field in one region could be worth several times an equal field in another.

traditions.source: Sifre Numbers and Rashi, on the women
traditions.text: Verse 64 says there was not a man left from the Sinai count. Rashi, following Sifre, presses the word “man”: the decree after the spies did not fall on the women, because they loved the land. The men had proposed a captain to take them back to Egypt (14:4), while the women asked for a possession in it (27:4). That, says Sifre, is why the daughters of Zelophehad come next.

Josephus retells Baal-peor at length, even giving Zimri a speech of defiance against Moses, then moves straight from the plague to the war on Midian. He leaves out the second census entirely. The only head count he gives for these years is the round figure of six hundred thousand at the opening of book 4, so his readers never meet the clan lists or the turnover of generations that this chapter records.

Paul turns the wilderness generation into a warning for Christians: with many of them God was not pleased, “for they were overthrown in the wilderness.” He counts the dead of Baal-peor as 23,000 in one day, where Numbers 25:9 has 24,000, and says these things were written as examples for those on whom the ends of the world have come.

Hebrews asks with whom God was grieved forty years, and answers: those who sinned, “whose carcases fell in the wilderness,” shut out by unbelief. Jude reminds his readers that the Lord who saved the people out of Egypt afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Both read the empty places in this census as a lesson about faith, not about numbers.

27.overview:
The five daughters of Zelophehad, a man of Manasseh who died in the wilderness with no sons, stand at the tabernacle door before Moses, Eleazar, the princes, and the whole assembly and ask for their father's share of the land. Moses brings the case to the LORD, who says they speak right and sets a general rule: an inheritance passes to a son, then a daughter, then brothers, uncles, and the nearest kin. The LORD then tells Moses to climb the Abarim range, see the land, and prepare to die. Moses asks for a shepherd for the people, and Joshua is commissioned by the laying on of hands.

Both halves answer the same worry: what happens when the head of a house is gone. A family without a son keeps its name and land through its daughters, and a people about to lose Moses keeps its leadership through Joshua.

27.hermeneutics:
A daughter inheriting was unusual in the ancient Near East, but not unheard of. Gudea, ruler of Lagash about 2100 BC, lists among the good deeds of his reign that in a house with no son he let the daughter take the son's place. A Babylonian boundary stone from the 10th century BC records a father deeding land to his daughter by sealed document, a gift her brother later confirmed in the same words, and documents from Nuzi show brothers affirming property a father had willed to a sister. Read against that background, the daughters' request is not a revolution. What stands out is their reason, “why should the name of our father be done away” (v. 4), and the kind of land at stake. Canaan was to be shared out once, by tribe and by lot (26:52–56), so a share that left the tribe with a daughter's marriage would be lost for good. That is the problem ch. 36 takes up.

“Shepherd” was a royal title. Hammurabi, in the epilogue to his laws, calls himself the shepherd the great gods have called, “whose staff is straight.” Moses asks for a leader who will “go out” and “come in” before the people, an idiom for leading in war (Joshua 14:11; 1 Samuel 18:16), so that they will not be “as sheep which have no shepherd” (v. 17). The words are kingly, but Joshua is not given a king's freedom. He is to stand before Eleazar, who will ask for him by the Urim, and Israel will go out and come in “at his word” (v. 21).

**Closing refrain:** the verb *tsavah*, “command” or “give a charge,” occurs four times (vv. 11, 19, 22, 23). Each half ends with things done as the LORD commanded.
**Go out and come in:** the paired verbs appear twice in Moses' request (v. 17) and once more in v. 21, where Israel's movements depend on Eleazar's Urim.

Chapter 27 closes the subsection that opened with the second census. The daughters were already named in 26:33, and the census principle of land by tribe raises their question. Moses' view from Abarim and Joshua's commission begin the handover that Deuteronomy completes. The daughters' case also has a sequel: ch. 36 rules that heiresses marry within their father's tribe, so the book ends with this family.
**Forward:** the daughters claim their share before Eleazar and Joshua (Joshua 17:3–6), and Moses climbs Nebo in the Abarim range to die (Deuteronomy 32:49–50; 34:1–9).

traditions.text: A thematic link. The fifth article of faith says a man must be called of God “by prophecy, and by the laying on of hands” by those in authority. Joshua's call follows that order: the LORD names him, and Moses lays his hands on him before the priest and the congregation (vv. 18–23). Deuteronomy 34:9 later credits Joshua's spirit of wisdom to those hands.

traditions.source: Book of Mormon: Alma 45; Doctrine and Covenants 84
traditions.text: Verse 13 tells Moses he will be gathered to his people as Aaron was. The Book of Mormon reports a saying that Alma was taken up by the Spirit “even as Moses,” and notes that the scriptures say the Lord took Moses unto himself; D&C 84:25 says the Lord took Moses out of Israel's midst. The Church's Bible Dictionary concludes that Moses was translated, which is why he could come to the Mount of Transfiguration and later confer keys on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery.

The midrash imagines the sisters taking counsel when they hear the land will go to men. Human mercy favors males, they reason, but God's mercy is on all his works (Psalm 145:9). Rabbi Nathan reads the chapter's placement after 26:65 as a lesson: in that generation the women were stronger than the men, who wanted to go back to Egypt while the women asked for a holding in the land.

A baraita calls the daughters wise, skilled interpreters, and righteous. Their wisdom was timing: Moses was teaching the law of levirate marriage, and they argued that if they did not count as sons, their mother should be given to their uncle in levirate marriage. Since the case then went to the LORD, the Talmud also says a law of merit is written through people of merit, as the law of the Sabbath-breaker came through a man who deserved it.

Rabbi Akiva links the daughters' words “our father died in the wilderness” (v. 3) to the man found gathering sticks “in the wilderness” on the Sabbath (15:32) and concludes that he was Zelophehad, the “own sin” of v. 3. Judah ben Bathyra rebukes him: if true, he has exposed what the Torah chose to hide, and if false, he has slandered a righteous man.

Why did Moses have to ask (v. 5)? Rashi gives two answers from the Talmud. The ruling slipped from Moses as a rebuke for having told the judges to bring every hard case to him (Deuteronomy 1:17). Or the law was always meant to be given, but the daughters' merit earned it the honor of being written through them.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 27:5; Sanhedrin 8a; Bava Batra 119a

traditions.text: Philo calls the father Shalpaath and, unlike Numbers, gives him four daughters. They came, he says, not for wealth but to keep their father's name. Moses hesitated because land seemed the reward of men who fought in the wars; God then praised the maidens, and Philo stresses that the law speaks of “gifts” and “presents” to them, not of “recompense.” He reads the inheritance order as quietly including the father, through the uncles.

Josephus puts Joshua's appointment after the war on Midian: Moses, now old, appointed Joshua his successor “both to receive directions from God, as a Prophet” and to command the army. He then merges this chapter with ch. 36: the chief men of Manasseh ask whether Zelophehad's daughters may inherit, and Moses answers that they keep the estate only if they marry within their tribe.

Following the Midrash, Rashi says that when Moses heard daughters could inherit, he hoped his own sons would inherit his office, but God chose Joshua, who never left the tent (Exodus 33:11). “God of the spirits of all flesh” (v. 16) is Moses asking for a leader who can bear with each person's temper. And Moses is to put some of his honor on Joshua (v. 20), some but not all: Moses' face shone like the sun, Joshua's like the moon.

Moses' plea that the congregation not be “as sheep which have no shepherd” (v. 17) returns in the Gospels. Jesus sees the crowds and is moved with compassion because they are like sheep without a shepherd; in Mark he responds by teaching them, and then feeds them. Jesus bears the Greek form of Joshua's name, which made the echo easy for early readers to hear.

Justin sees Joshua as a figure of Christ. Moses renamed him, appointed him successor, and he, not Moses, led the people into the land and divided it by lot to those who entered with him. So Christ will gather the dispersed and give each an eternal possession, where Joshua's was temporary. Hebrews 4:8 makes a related point: if Joshua had given Israel rest, God would not have spoken of another day.

28.overview:
The LORD gives Moses the schedule of Israel's public offerings, starting with the most frequent. Two lambs are to be burned every day, one in the morning and one at evening, each with flour, oil, and wine. Each Sabbath adds two more lambs. Each new moon adds two bulls, a ram, seven lambs, and a goat for a sin offering. The same set is offered on each of the seven days of Unleavened Bread after Passover, and again on the day of firstfruits at the feast of weeks.

Notice how often the text says “beside the continual burnt offering” (vv. 10, 15, 24, 31; compare v. 23). No holy day replaces the daily lambs. Every Sabbath, month, and feast is stacked on top of them, so the whole calendar rests on an offering that never stops.

28.hermeneutics:
Temples in Israel's world fed their gods on a timetable. A ritual tablet from Uruk, copied in the Hellenistic period, lays out four meals a day for the god Anu, his consort Antu, and the other gods of the city: a main meal and a second meal in the morning, and the same pair in the evening, with set amounts of bread, beer, wine, sheep, and oxen. Afterward the food went to the king and the temple staff. Numbers 28 has the same frame: a fixed offering every morning and every evening (vv. 3–8), measured in tenths of an ephah and fractions of a hin, and the LORD calls it “my bread” (v. 2). A first hearer would recognize the language of a god's table. What is missing is the meal. The lambs are burned whole, the wine is poured out, and nothing is set before an image to eat.

The smell of sacrifice was old language too. In the flood story of the Gilgamesh epic (tablet XI), when the survivor offers sacrifice after the waters go down, the gods smell the sweet savor and crowd around him like flies, hungry after days without offerings. Numbers 28 repeats the phrase “a sweet savour unto me” (v. 2), as Genesis 8:21 does for Noah. Israel kept the wording while denying the hunger behind it: “If I were hungry, I would not tell thee” (Psalm 50:12). The point of the schedule is that it is kept, by the whole people, morning and evening, without a gap.

rows.text: First month: Passover and unleavened bread

notes: **Continual:** *tamid*, “continual” (once “daily,” 29:6), occurs 17 times from 28:3 to 29:38, mostly in the refrain “beside the continual burnt offering.”
**One set for every feast:** the new moon, each day of unleavened bread, and the day of firstfruits all receive two bulls, one ram, seven lambs, and a goat (vv. 11, 15, 19, 22, 27, 30).
**Sweet savour:** the phrase *reach nichoach* occurs 11 times in chs. 28–29, six of them in ch. 28 (vv. 2, 6, 8, 13, 24, 27).

Chapters 28–29 are one list, opened by “Command the children of Israel” (28:2) and closed when Moses tells Israel all that the LORD commanded (29:40). It stands between Joshua's commission (ch. 27) and the war with Midian (ch. 31), so the new generation receives the full calendar of public worship before it fights or settles. Leviticus 23 named the feasts and their days; these chapters add what the community offers on each.
**Forward:** the returned exiles restore “the continual burnt offering” of new moons and set feasts (Ezra 3:4–5).

traditions.text: When John the Baptist conferred the Aaronic Priesthood on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, he said it would not be taken from the earth until the sons of Levi “offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.” D&C 84 adds that the sons of Moses and of Aaron will offer an acceptable offering and sacrifice in the house of the Lord. Both look back to the Levitical service that Numbers 28 sets out.

After the destruction at Christ's death, his voice tells the Nephites to offer no more the shedding of blood; their sacrifices and burnt offerings are done away. In their place they are to offer “a broken heart and a contrite spirit.” The daily and festival burnt offerings of this chapter are the kind of offering the Lord says has come to an end.

The Mishnah reads “my offering… shall ye observe” (v. 2) as a duty of every Israelite. Since a man's offering cannot be made while he is absent, the prophets divided the people into standing groups (*ma'amadot*) matched to the priestly watches. Each week some went up to Jerusalem to stand by the daily offering, and the rest gathered in their towns and read the creation story.

Why does the calendar come right after Joshua's appointment? Following Sifre, Rashi says Moses had just asked God to appoint a leader over his children (27:16). God answered: instead of commanding me about my children, command my children about me. Rashi also reads “in its due season” as making every day an appointed season for the daily offering.

A whole tractate describes the daily offering as it was done in the Second Temple. It ends with the psalm the Levites sang for each day of the week, from Psalm 24 on the first day to Psalm 92 on the Sabbath, which it reads as a song for the age to come that will be all Sabbath.

Rabbi Joshua ben Levi teaches that the daily prayers were instituted to correspond to the daily offerings. A supporting teaching ties the hours to the lambs: the morning prayer may be said until noon because the morning lamb could be offered until then. Jewish prayer times still follow the morning and evening offering of vv. 3–8.

In a dialogue built on Genesis 15, Abraham asks how his descendants will find atonement once the temple is gone. God answers that he has already given them the order of the offerings: whenever they read these passages, he will count it as if they had offered them and will pardon their sins. Chapters like this one became texts to be recited.

Among the disasters remembered on the seventeenth of Tammuz, the Mishnah lists the day the daily offering ceased. Daniel had already made its removal the sign of desecration: five times it speaks simply of “the daily” (*ha-tamid*), which the KJV renders “the daily sacrifice,” taken away by a hostile king.

Philo calls the two lambs thank offerings, one at dawn for the kindnesses of the day and one at evening for “the mercies which have been vouchsafed in the night.” The Sabbath doubles them because it is the birthday of the world. He reads the ten animals of the new moon as a perfect number for a completed month: two bulls for the moon's waxing and waning, seven lambs for its seven-day phases.

Josephus says the daily lamb was offered at the beginning and the end of the day “out of the publick expences,” which matches the Mishnah's sense of it as the whole people's offering. His summary of the Sabbath and new moon follows Numbers closely, but his offering for Pentecost, three bullocks and two rams, is larger than the two bulls and one ram of v. 27.

The daily offering frames several scenes in Luke's writings. Zacharias is chosen by lot to burn incense while the people pray outside, and Peter and John go up to the temple “at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour,” the afternoon hour when the evening offering was made. The first Christians in Jerusalem still kept time by it.

Hebrews contrasts the priest who “standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices” with Christ, who offered himself once. The repetition that Numbers 28 requires is, for Hebrews, the sign that these sacrifices could not finish the work.

Barnabas quotes Isaiah 1 to show that God “wanteth neither sacrifices nor whole burnt offerings,” ending with Isaiah's complaint against new moons and Sabbaths. He concludes that these were annulled so that the new law of Christ might have an offering not made by human hands.

29.overview:
The festival list continues into the seventh month, which holds three occasions. The first day is a day of blowing the trumpets. The tenth is a day to afflict the soul and do no work. From the fifteenth comes a seven-day feast, followed by an eighth day of solemn assembly. Each occasion has its burnt offerings, grain and drink offerings, and a goat for a sin offering, all added to the daily and monthly offerings. Moses then tells Israel everything the LORD has commanded.

Watch the bulls during the seven-day feast. Thirteen are offered on the first day, then twelve, then eleven, down to seven on the seventh day, seventy in all, while the rams and lambs stay the same. No other occasion in the calendar comes near that scale, and the count ends with a single bull on the eighth day (v. 36).

29.hermeneutics:
The seventh month was a turning point across the region. In first-millennium Babylonia the great *akitu* festival was held twice a year: in the first month, Nisannu, and again in the seventh, Tashritu, near the autumn equinox. Texts from Ur centuries earlier already name an akitu of harvest and an akitu of sowing, set in the first and seventh months. Israel counted its months from spring (Exodus 12:2), yet Numbers 29 crowds its heaviest festivals into the seventh month: a trumpet day at the new moon, a fast on the tenth, and a week of feasting at the full moon. A first hearer would know this as the season when the year turns and the harvest has been gathered (Deuteronomy 16:13).

Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, has left a ritual for its own vintage month, preserved on two tablets of the 13th century BC (KTU 1.41 and 1.87). It is laid out day by day. At the new moon a cluster of grapes is cut and offered, and on the thirteenth the king bathes and is pure, with set animals owed to set gods on set days. Numbers 29 belongs to the same kind of text, a temple schedule of what is owed and when. Its distinctive feature is the arithmetic. One bull drops away each day of the feast, from thirteen to seven, and v. 39 marks the whole list as the community's fixed duty, apart from anything a person vows or gives freely.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the month moves in sequence, with a countdown of bulls inside the seven-day feast.

rows.text: Days 15–21: bulls from thirteen down to seven

notes: **Seventy bulls:** 13 + 12 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 8 + 7 = 70, with 14 rams and 98 lambs over the seven days. The seventh day has seven bulls.

**After the manner:** from day two on, the grain and drink offerings are no longer spelled out but given “after the manner” (*kammishpat*), a phrase that occurs seven times (vv. 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 37).

**Back to one:** the eighth day returns to the set of the first and tenth days, one bull, one ram, and seven lambs (vv. 2, 8, 36). A goat for a sin offering comes with every occasion, ten times in all.

Chapter 29 completes the list that began at 28:1, and v. 40 closes it: Moses tells Israel all that the LORD commanded. Verse 39 looks ahead. The set feasts come “beside your vows, and your freewill offerings,” and ch. 30 turns at once to the law of vows.
**Back and forward:** Leviticus 23:23–43 named these days; Zechariah 14:16 pictures the nations going up each year to keep the feast of tabernacles.

traditions.text: A thematic link. When King Benjamin gives his last address, the people come up to the temple with the firstlings of their flocks to offer “sacrifice and burnt offerings according to the law of Moses.” They pitch their tents around the temple, family by family, with the doors facing it. The text does not name the feast, but it shows a Nephite assembly built from the same parts as this chapter: burnt offerings, thanksgiving, and the people camped by the house of God.

Jubilees makes Abraham the first to keep the feast of tabernacles, at the Well of the Oath after the promise of Isaac. He builds booths and for seven days offers two oxen, two rams, seven sheep, and a goat for a sin offering, a fixed number each day instead of Numbers' falling count. He circles the altar with palm branches, and the book says the feast is ordained on the heavenly tablets for Israel forever.

Philo says the trumpet was played in the temple as the new moon offerings were made. He gives two reasons. For Israel it recalls the trumpet heard from heaven when the law was given at Sinai. For all people the trumpet is the instrument of war, so the feast thanks God as “the giver of peace,” who ends wars among nations and in nature.

traditions.source: Philo, on the fast and the feast
traditions.text: Philo says the tenth-day fast was kept seriously even by people who did nothing religious the rest of the year. He counts the feast's seventy bulls, fourteen rams, and ninety-eight lambs, all burned whole. Why a goat for sin every day of a joyful feast? Because festivals had often opened the way to drunkenness and excess, and good cheer needs a purified mind.

Josephus walks through the seventh month in order. He combines the offerings of v. 8 with those of Leviticus 16, so the tenth day has two goats, one sent into the wilderness. For the feast he describes booths built against the cold of the season and branches of myrtle, willow, and palm with a citron, and he notes the bulls abating by one each day “till they amounted to seven only.”

The Mishnah works out who offered what. All twenty-four priestly watches served at this feast, and the animals of each day were shared among them, the watches with fewer animals taking two lambs each. As the bulls fall by one a day, the shares shift, until on the seventh day the seven bulls, two rams, goat, and fourteen lambs make exactly twenty-four offerings, one for every watch. Watches also rotated so that no watch offered bulls two days running.

Rabbi Elazar says the seventy bulls correspond to the seventy nations of the world, offered for their atonement, and the single bull of the eighth day stands for the one nation, Israel. Rabbi Yohanan adds: woe to the nations, who lost something without knowing it, for while the temple stood these bulls atoned for them. Zechariah 14:16 imagines those nations coming to keep the feast themselves.

Rashi sets the lambs against the bulls. The bulls, for the nations, shrink each day; the lambs, for Israel, stay fixed, and their total of ninety-eight is to ward off the ninety-eight curses of Deuteronomy 28. He also notes small spelling changes on days two, six, and seven whose extra letters spell *mayim*, “water,” a hint the rabbis read as the source of the water libation poured at this feast.

The eighth day is an *atzeret*, from a root meaning to hold back. Rashi, following the Talmud, pictures a king who has given a week-long banquet for many guests and then says to his own children: your leaving is hard for me, stay one more day. The one bull of v. 36 is that small private meal, for Israel alone.

John sets one of Jesus' great sayings at this feast. On the last and great day he stands and cries that whoever thirsts should come to him and drink, and that rivers of living water will flow from the believer. John explains that he spoke of the Spirit. Read beside the rabbinic tradition of a water libation at the feast, the setting gives the invitation its force.

The offerings of the tenth day come every year. Hebrews takes that repetition as its argument: sacrifices offered “year by year continually” could not perfect the worshipers, and instead they bring a yearly remembrance of sins, since the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sins away.

30.overview:
Moses gives the heads of the tribes the LORD's law on vows. A man who vows to the LORD, or binds himself with an oath, must do everything he said. A woman's vow depends on her household. If she is a young woman in her father's house, or a wife, her father or husband may cancel it on the day he hears of it, and the LORD will forgive her; if he says nothing, it stands. A widow's or a divorced woman's vow stands on its own.

The hinge is the phrase “in the day that he heareth.” Silence confirms a vow, and a veto counts only if it comes at once (vv. 4–5, 7–8, 14). A husband who objects later cannot undo the vow. Instead he bears her iniquity (v. 15).

30.hermeneutics:
Vows in Israel's world were conditional promises: help me, and I will give you this. Thousands of votive stones from Phoenician and Punic sanctuaries, more than three thousand at Carthage alone, record the outcome in a fixed formula: this is what so-and-so vowed to the god, “for he heard his voice.” The gift was paid after the prayer was answered, so a vow was a debt that could fall due long after it was spoken. Hannah's vow works that way (1 Samuel 1:11), and it would cost her household a son. Her husband Elkanah's reply, “only the LORD establish his word” (1 Samuel 1:23), is the kind of consent Numbers 30 has in view. A woman's vow could commit the goods and labor of a house that legally belonged to her father or her husband, so the law gives him one chance, on the day he hears, to refuse.

Jeremiah 44 shows the same rule from the other side. Judean women in Egypt defend their vows to “the queen of heaven”: incense, drink offerings, and cakes baked for her. The Hebrew word for those cakes, *kawwanim*, is probably borrowed from Akkadian *kamanu*, a cake used in the worship of the goddess Ishtar. The women tell Jeremiah they did none of it “without our men” (44:19), and the prophet then charges husbands and wives together with having vowed and kept their vows (44:25). Under Numbers 30, a husband who heard and stayed silent owned the vow as well.

close.text: Statutes between a man and his wife, a father and his daughter

A woman marrying under a vow: her husband may cancel

A wife: her husband may cancel, but only at once

notes: **Hold his peace:** *charash* occurs six times (vv. 4, 7, 11, and three times in v. 14). Silence is the act that confirms a vow.
**Stand:** *qum*, “stand” or “establish,” occurs 12 times, the verb for a vow that holds. *Neder*, “vow,” occurs 13 times.
**Forgiven:** “the LORD shall forgive her” comes three times (vv. 5, 8, 12), once in each case where a father or husband cancels. The widow's case has no such line, since no one can cancel for her.

Chapter 30 closes the subsection on worship. The calendar ended by setting its fixed offerings “beside your vows, and your freewill offerings” (29:39), and this chapter takes up those voluntary promises. Leviticus 27 set the silver value of things vowed; this chapter settles who may let a vow stand. The war with Midian follows in ch. 31.
**Forward:** Jephthah cannot take back what he opened his mouth to say (Judges 11:30–31, 35), and Hannah's vow is confirmed by her husband (1 Samuel 1:11, 23).

traditions.text: A thematic link. When Nephi takes Laban's servant Zoram out of Jerusalem, he swears with an oath that Zoram will be a free man if he comes, and Zoram in turn makes an oath that he will stay with them. Nephi writes that once Zoram had sworn, “our fears did cease concerning him.” The story assumes what v. 2 requires: a sworn word binds the one who speaks it.

A thematic link. The converted Lamanites had sworn never again to shed blood, and when the Nephites defending them suffered, they wanted to take up arms. Helaman persuaded them not to, fearing that by breaking the oath they would lose their souls, and their sons, who had made no such oath, went instead. The episode treats a vow to God the way v. 2 does: it is kept even at great cost.

Philo explains the father's and husband's authority. Young women may not grasp the weight of an oath and need others to judge for them, while wives sometimes swear “out of easiness of disposition” against their husbands' interests. Widows, he warns, should not swear rashly, because no one is left to release them; their oaths stand by default. He then reads the whole law as an allegory of the soul, guarded by reason as a wife by her husband.

The Mishnah fills in what the chapter leaves open. A betrothed girl's vow needs both father and husband to cancel it; if only one does, it stands. “In the day that he heareth” means the rest of that calendar day: a vow heard on Friday evening can be cancelled until dark on the Sabbath, but one heard just before nightfall must be cancelled before dark.

traditions.source: Mishnah Nedarim, on what may be cancelled
traditions.text: Not every vow falls under the husband's power. The Mishnah names vows that “afflict the soul” (v. 13), such as a vow not to bathe or not to adorn herself, and vows that harm the relationship between husband and wife. A vow not to work for her own father or brother does not qualify. Rabbi Yosei objects that bathing and adornment are not affliction at all.

traditions.source: Rashi, on the heads of the tribes
traditions.text: Why does Moses speak to the heads of the tribes (v. 1)? Rashi says it shows that a vow can be released by a single expert sage, or by three ordinary men where no expert is found. He also distinguishes two acts: a sage “releases” a vow, while a husband or father “annuls” it, and using the wrong term has no effect.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 30:2 (Hebrew numbering = KJV 30:1); Nedarim 78a

traditions.text: The rabbis admitted how thin the written basis was for a sage's release of vows. The Mishnah says those laws “fly in the air” with nothing to support them, since the Torah only hints at them. This chapter gives fathers and husbands the power to cancel; the sage's power had to be built on tradition.

If the father cancelled the vow, why would she need forgiveness (v. 5)? Following Sifre, Rashi says the verse means a woman whose vow, say a Nazarite vow, was cancelled without her knowing, who then drank wine thinking she was breaking it. Even she needs pardon; how much more someone who breaks a vow that still stands.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 30:6 (Hebrew numbering = KJV 30:5); Sifre Numbers 153

traditions.text: Verse 15 says a husband who cancels a vow after he has already confirmed it “shall bear her iniquity.” Rashi draws a general rule from Sifre: whoever causes another person to stumble takes that person's place for every penalty the stumble would bring.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Numbers 30:16 (Hebrew numbering = KJV 30:15); Sifre Numbers 156

traditions.text: Jesus quotes the old teaching, “perform unto the Lord thine oaths,” the duty v. 2 lays down, and then says not to swear at all: let your yes be yes and your no be no. Elsewhere he attacks teachers who ruled that an oath by the temple binds nothing while an oath by its gold makes a man a debtor. James repeats the Sermon's teaching almost word for word. Where Numbers regulates oaths, these texts aim at speech that needs no oath.

Early Christians still made and kept vows. Paul cuts his hair at Cenchrea “for he had a vow,” and in Jerusalem the elders ask him to join four men under a vow, pay their costs, and purify himself with them so that they may shave their heads. The shaving matches the close of a Nazarite vow (Numbers 6:18), and the elders want it to show that Paul himself walks orderly and keeps the law.

31.overview:
The LORD tells Moses to avenge Israel on Midian before he dies. A thousand men from each tribe go out with Phinehas, the holy vessels, and the trumpets. They kill the men of Midian, its five kings, and Balaam, burn the settlements, and bring back the women, children, and herds. Moses is angry that the women were spared, because they led Israel into sin at Peor on Balaam's advice. He orders the boys killed, and every woman who has lain with a man; only the girls are kept alive. Then come seven days of purification, a count of the spoil, and an offering of gold.

The fighting takes two verses (vv. 7–8). The rest deals with the aftermath: the killing of captives, purification, Eleazar's ruling on metal and fire, and a ledger of spoil down to the last donkey. War here defiles even the winners, and it has to be cleansed and accounted for before the camp takes them back.

31.hermeneutics:
About 840 BC Mesha, king of Moab, set up a stone at Dibon boasting that he took Nebo from Israel and killed all seven thousand of its men, boys, women, and girls, because he had devoted the town to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. Killing a whole population as something owed to a god was a known practice just east of the Jordan, and this chapter belongs to that world. Its own details stand out against it. The chapter never uses the Hebrew word for that kind of devotion (*herem*, used at Hormah in 21:2–3), it frames the war as vengeance for Peor (vv. 2–3, 16), it spares the girls, and it sends every soldier who killed or touched the dead outside the camp for a week.

Letters from the kingdom of Mari on the Euphrates (18th century BC) use the term *asakkum* for spoil reserved to a god or the king, and a soldier who kept it was said to have “eaten” it. Numbers sets its reserved portion by arithmetic. The whole booty is split evenly between the 12,000 who fought and the congregation who stayed, then one in 500 of the soldiers' half goes to the priest and one in 50 of the people's half to the Levites (vv. 27–30). David later makes the even split a statute in Israel (1 Samuel 30:24–25).

Midian was a loose people rather than a single state. Genesis makes Midian a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), Midianite traders carry Joseph to Egypt (Genesis 37:28), and Moses marries into a Midianite priest's family (Exodus 2:16). The “goodly castles” burned in v. 10 translate a word used elsewhere for tent camps (Genesis 25:16, “castles” of Ishmael's tribes), which fits a herding people better than walled cities.

No man missing: the officers' gold brought as a memorial
