Division of the spoil and the LORD's tribute

notes: **Two vengeances:** in v. 2 the LORD calls the war Israel's vengeance on Midian; in v. 3 Moses calls it the LORD's vengeance.
**Refrain:** “as the LORD commanded Moses” marks the battle (v. 7) and each stage of the division (vv. 31, 41, 47). Eleazar is named 10 times, and in v. 21 he gives a ruling himself.

**Echoing figures:** the LORD's share from the soldiers' half is 675 sheep, 72 cattle, 61 asses, and 32 persons (vv. 37–40), the same digits as the totals in thousands (vv. 32–35), since one in 500 of half is one in 1,000 of the whole.

Chapters 31–32 settle unfinished business east of the Jordan before Moses dies. Verse 2 carries out the order of 25:16–18 and repeats the death notice of 27:12–13, “gathered unto thy people,” which is not fulfilled until Deuteronomy 34. Once Midian is beaten, Reuben and Gad ask to keep the conquered pastureland (ch. 32).
**Forward:** Midian is not finished. In Judges 6–8 it oppresses Israel for seven years until Gideon defeats it.

traditions.text: Philo retells the campaign as a war of piety and has Moses ask how Israel could punish its own sinners and spare those who taught them. His version differs from Numbers on the captives: the army itself kills the grown men and women, and spares the young boys along with the girls. He explains the week outside the camp this way: even lawful killing in war leaves a man “guilty of blood” because all people share “a common father.”

Josephus names Phinehas as commander of the twelve thousand and says the Midianites saw the attack coming and fortified the passes into their country. He identifies the fifth king, Rekem, with the city the Arabs called Arecem and the Greeks called Petra, the Nabataean capital of his own day. His spoil figures differ from the chapter's (52,000 cattle, 75,600 sheep, 60,000 asses, about 32,000 virgins), and he says the virgins were spared “as Moses had commanded Phineas.”

The rabbis asked why Phinehas went to war and his father Eleazar did not. One answer: he had begun the work by killing the Midianite Cozbi at Peor, so he should finish it. Another traces his mother's line to Joseph, whom Midianites sold into Egypt (Genesis 37:36), so he went to avenge his ancestor. The Talmud adds that he went as the priest anointed for war.
traditions.cite: Sifre Numbers 157; b. Sotah 43a; Rashi on 31:6

traditions.text: Why does Eleazar, not Moses, teach the purification law in v. 21? Because Moses had just been angry with the officers (v. 14), and anger made him forget the law. The midrash lists two other times anger led Moses into error: with Eleazar and Ithamar over the sin offering (Leviticus 10:16) and at the rock (Numbers 20:10). Rashi adds that Moses' anger at the officers shows a generation's failings are charged to the leaders who could have objected.

Rashi asks why Midian is punished and Moab is not, though Moab hired Balaam. His first answer is that Moab acted out of fear for its land, while Midian joined a quarrel that was not its own. His second, from the Talmud, is that God would spare Moab and Ammon for the sake of two women yet to come from them: Ruth the Moabitess and Naamah the Ammonitess, Solomon's wife.

The Talmud takes up Balaam's death in v. 8, which Joshua 13:22 repeats. A rabbi reasons from Psalm 55:23, that bloody and deceitful men do not live out half their days, that Balaam died at thirty-three or thirty-four. In the story a heretic agrees, claiming to have seen a chronicle that said Balaam “the lame” was thirty-three when “Pinehas the highwayman” killed him, so the talmudic story also makes Phinehas the one who struck him down.

The officers' gold “to make an atonement for our souls” (v. 50) puzzled the rabbis, since v. 49 says no man was lost and nothing suggests anyone had sinned. The Talmud has Moses ask the officers why they need atonement, and they answer that they had escaped sin in deed but not in thought toward the Midianite women. Rashi reads one of the ornaments in the list in the same light, and Moses and Eleazar lay the gold up in the tabernacle as a memorial (v. 54).

Verse 16 is the only place in the Torah that says Balaam advised the plan at Peor; chapters 22–24 show him only blessing Israel. The risen Christ's letter to the church at Pergamos assumes the reading of v. 16: Balaam “taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel,” to eat idol sacrifices and commit fornication. Josephus tells the same story at length, with Balaam advising the kings to send their daughters into the camp to draw the young men to their gods.

Eusebius's gazetteer of biblical places puts Midian beyond Arabia to the south, in the desert east of the Red Sea, and recalls that Moses' wife was the daughter of a priest of Midian. It adds a second Midian near the Arnon and Areopolis, east of the Dead Sea, whose ruins were still shown in his day. The two sites match the two faces of Midian in scripture, a people of the far desert and a neighbor of Moab.

32.overview:
Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, see that the conquered land of Jazer and Gilead is good pasture and ask Moses to let them settle there without crossing the Jordan. Moses hears Kadesh-barnea all over again, when the spies' report turned the people back and a generation died in the wilderness. The two tribes answer with an offer: they will build folds for the flocks and towns for their families, then march armed ahead of Israel and stay until every tribe has its land. Moses accepts on that condition, binds Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads to enforce it, and grants them the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Clans of Manasseh take northern Gilead.

The proverb “be sure your sin will find you out” (v. 23) comes from this chapter. Moses says it to two tribes who have not yet sinned, as a warning about a promise they might fail to keep.

32.hermeneutics:
The Mesha Stele, set up about 840 BC and found at Dibon in 1868, names many of this chapter's towns from the Moabite side: Ataroth, Dibon, Nebo, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim, Aroer, Jahaz. Mesha says the men of Gad had lived in “the country of Ataroth from ancient times,” and that the king of Israel fortified it before Mesha took it back. Gad's hold on the tableland was remembered even by its enemies, and the land Moses grants here was still contested centuries later. Dibon, which Gad builds in v. 34, became Mesha's own capital.

The tableland between the Arnon and Heshbon is open, rolling country with enough rain for grain and grass, and it was sheep country in antiquity. Second Kings 3:4 calls Mesha a “sheepmaster” who paid Israel a hundred thousand lambs a year. Reuben and Gad choose the land as herders choose (vv. 1, 4), and their first plan is stone folds for the flocks (v. 16). Excavation has complicated the picture at some sites: Tell Hesban (Heshbon) and Dhiban (Dibon) have yielded little or nothing from the Late Bronze Age, one reason scholars debate when the conquest stories took shape.

Renaming a captured town marked a change of owner. Shalmaneser III of Assyria took Til-Barsip on the Euphrates in 856 BC and renamed it Kar-Shalmaneser, “Fort Shalmaneser.” The chapter ends with the same move three times over: the Reubenites give their cities “other names” (v. 38), Jair calls his villages Havoth-jair, “the tent-villages of Jair” (v. 41), and Nobah renames Kenath after himself (v. 42).

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. It is a negotiation, and the terms are restated until both sides have said them in public.

rows.text: Moses repeats them to the leaders

notes: **“Before the LORD”:** the Hebrew phrase comes 7 times in vv. 20–32 (vv. 20, 21, 22 twice, 27, 29, 32). The tribes first offer to march “before the children of Israel” (v. 17); in the terms the army marches before the LORD. KJV has an eighth in v. 22, where the Hebrew says “from the LORD.”

**Kadesh retold:** Moses' speech (vv. 8–13) compresses chs. 13–14. The verb “discourage” frames it (vv. 7, 9), and those who “have not wholly followed” are set against Caleb and Joshua, who have (vv. 11–12).

The request follows the defeat of Midian and the earlier conquest of Sihon and Og (21:21–35). The land is already taken; the question is who will live in it. This is the first tribal settlement in the book, and it lies outside the borders of Canaan as ch. 34 draws them (34:13–15).

**Forward:** Joshua sends the eastern tribes home with praise for keeping this promise (Joshua 22:1–4), and their altar by the Jordan nearly starts a war over whether they still belong to Israel (Joshua 22:10–34).

traditions.text: Philo notes that the two tribes were a sixth of the whole army and that they were already living in the well-watered land they asked for. He gives Moses a long speech asking whether they will sit at ease while their kinsmen fight: “ye are one race, ye have the same fathers.” The tribes answer that they fear no hard service and ask only to leave families and herds behind walls, and Philo says they then marched out more eagerly than anyone, as men repaying a gift already received.

Josephus includes the half tribe of Manasseh in the original request. He has Moses call them cowards who had invented the cattle as a decent excuse for avoiding the war while others labored for the land. The tribes reply that they want their prey and families in safe places so that they can fight unencumbered. Moses then grants the land of the Amorites before Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal chiefs on that condition, and they build strong cities for their wives, children, and goods.

Moses states the deal both ways: if the tribes cross, they get Gilead; if not, they take land in Canaan (vv. 29–30). Rabbi Meir made this the model for conditional agreements such as betrothals: a condition that does not spell out both outcomes, as Moses did with Gad and Reuben, is no condition at all. Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel disagreed, arguing that the negative half was needed here only so that no one would think the tribes would lose their share in Canaan too.

The phrase “guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel” (v. 22) became a rule for Temple officials. The man who drew coins from the treasury chamber could not wear a hemmed garment, shoes, sandals, phylacteries, or an amulet, anything that might hide a coin. If he later grew poor, people might call it punishment for theft, and if he grew rich, they might say he had stolen. A person must appear innocent to people as well as to God, and the Mishnah cites this verse as its proof.

The midrash notices that the tribes offer folds for cattle before cities for children (v. 16), and that Moses hands the plan back the other way round (v. 24): put first things first. It sets wealth beside wisdom and strength as gifts that last only when they come from God. Because Reuben and Gad loved their possessions and separated from their brothers to keep them, it says, they were the first tribes taken into exile, citing 1 Chronicles 5:26.
traditions.cite: Numbers Rabbah 22:7, 9; Tanhuma Mattot 7; Rashi on 32:16

traditions.text: Rashi reads “do that which hath proceeded out of your mouth” (v. 24) as treating the tribes' words as a vow, like the vows of ch. 30, and as holding them to more than Moses asked. Moses required them to stay only until the land was subdued (v. 22), but they had promised to stay until every Israelite had his inheritance (v. 18). Rashi counts that as seven more years west of the Jordan while the land was divided.

Explaining “their names being changed” (v. 38), Rashi says Nebo and Baal-meon were names of idols, since the people of the land named their cities after their gods, so the Reubenites gave them new names. He identifies Shibmah in v. 38 with Shebam in v. 3. On Nobah's naming of Kenath (v. 42), he reports an earlier teacher's view that an unusual spelling hints the name did not last, and then questions that argument himself.

This Aramaic paraphrase replaces the town names with ones its readers knew and fills them with history. In v. 3 and v. 38 it renders Nebo as the place of Moses' grave, looking ahead to Deuteronomy 34. It turns Baal-meon into the city of Balak, rebuilt after the idol of Peor was torn out of it, and says the builders then named the towns after themselves.

Eusebius locates several of the chapter's towns in the Roman province of Arabia. Heshbon is “now called Esbus,” a well-known city; Elealeh belongs to Reuben; Baal-meon is the town “which the sons of Ruben built”; Jazer marks the border of Ammon near Philadelphia (modern Amman); Mount Nebo is pointed out about six miles west of Heshbon. His entries show the names of Numbers 32 still in use some fifteen centuries later.

33.overview:
Moses writes down Israel's journeys at the LORD's command, and the chapter lists them in order: out of Rameses the day after Passover, through the sea, to Sinai, on through a long run of camps to Ezion-gaber and Kadesh, then to Mount Hor, where Aaron dies at 123 in the fortieth year, and finally to the plains of Moab opposite Jericho. Then the LORD gives orders for Canaan. Israel is to drive out the inhabitants, destroy their images and high places, and divide the land by lot. Any people left behind will be thorns in Israel's sides.

Watch the middle of the list. Between Hazeroth (v. 17) and Kadesh (v. 36) come eighteen camps, most named nowhere else in scripture, with nothing said about any of them. For the long wilderness years the rest of Numbers passes over, this list is nearly all the record there is.

historicalContext.text: Verse 2 says Moses wrote down the stages at the LORD's command. Tradition credits Moses with Numbers; many scholars see the list as compiled later from older itineraries.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: From the fifteenth day of the first month (v. 3) to the fortieth year (v. 38). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The eastern Nile Delta, the Sinai peninsula, the Negev and the Arabah, the border of Edom, and the plains of Moab; many stations cannot now be located.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 12:37–19:2 and Numbers 10–21 tell the journey as story; Numbers 21:10–20 and Deuteronomy 10:6–7 give shorter itineraries that differ in places.

33.hermeneutics:
Assyrian royal annals of the 9th century BC record marches in a fixed formula. Texts of Tukulti-Ninurta II (890–884 BC) and Ashurnasirpal II repeat “From city A I departed, in city B I spent the night,” and stop now and then to note a river crossing, a shortage of water, a battle, or tribute received. Numbers 33 uses the same two-part formula, they departed from one place and pitched in the next, with the same kind of notes: twelve springs and seventy palms at Elim (v. 9), no water at Rephidim (v. 14), Aaron's death on Mount Hor (vv. 38–39). G. I. Davies, who set these texts side by side, noted that none of them gives distances. The genre is a record of a real expedition, kept to show what the journey meant.

Dibon (v. 45) shows both the difficulty and the help that outside evidence brings. Excavations at Dhiban found no Late Bronze Age town there, yet the list of places in Canaan and beyond carved for Thutmose III at Karnak in the 15th century BC includes Dibon. Charles Krahmalkov argued that Egyptian route lists match the last stages of this itinerary in the Transjordan; others read the Egyptian lists differently.

Only a handful of the stations can be placed with confidence. Rameses is the Delta capital Pi-Ramesses, excavated at Qantir. Ezion-gaber lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, “beside Eloth” (1 Kings 9:26). Kadesh is usually placed at the springs of Ein el-Qudeirat in northeastern Sinai, Punon at Feinan in the Arabah, and Dibon at Dhiban. Most camps between Hazeroth and Ezion-gaber (vv. 18–34) have never been identified, and the places of the sea crossing and of Mount Sinai itself are still debated. Names attached to wells and campsites rather than towns rarely leave remains.

King Arad hears of Israel's coming

notes: **The formula:** the Hebrew verb for setting out occurs 42 times (vv. 3–48) and the verb for camping 42 times (vv. 5–49). After Rameses, 41 different places are named.
**Other lists:** Deuteronomy 10:6–7 runs from Bene-jaakan to Mosera, the reverse of vv. 30–31, and has Aaron die at Mosera rather than Mount Hor.
**Kadesh:** the spies return to Kadesh in the second year (13:26), but this list reaches Kadesh only in v. 36, shortly before the fortieth year.

Chapters 33–35 stand on the plains of Moab and look both ways: back over the road from Egypt (33:1–49), then ahead to the land, its conquest and division (33:50–56), its borders (ch. 34), and its cities (ch. 35). The list closes the wilderness story that began at the Exodus.

**Forward:** the warning of vv. 55–56 returns when Joshua, old and near death, says the nations left behind will be “scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes” (Joshua 23:13), and again in Judges 2:3.

traditions.text: A thematic link. Nephi's account of his family's journey through the Arabian wilderness is itself partly an itinerary: they travel so many days, pitch their tents, and name the place, Shazer, then Nahom, then Bountiful by the sea, eight years in all (17:4). When his brothers refuse to help build a ship, Nephi recites Israel's own journey, the sea divided, manna, water from the rock, the LORD leading by day and by night, as proof that God guides those who listen to his word.

Why list the stations at all? Rashi, following an earlier teacher, Moses the Preacher, says they show God's kindness: though Israel was sentenced to wander, it did not move constantly and without rest. Of the 42 stages, fourteen came in the first year, from Rameses to Rithmah, where Rashi places the sending of the spies, and eight came after Aaron's death, from Mount Hor to the plains of Moab. That leaves only twenty moves in the thirty-eight years between, long stays rather than endless marching.

The midrash compares the list to a king who took his sick son far away to be healed and on the way home pointed out each stop: here we slept, here we caught cold, here your head ached. So God tells Moses to recount the places where Israel provoked him. A second reading says each desert place is named because it gave Israel shelter, and its reward is Isaiah's promise that the wilderness will blossom and grow cedars and a highway will run through it (Isaiah 35:1, 8; 41:19).

The midrash opens with a legal question, whether a person fleeing for his life may break the Sabbath. It tells of leaders in Sepphoris who asked Rabbi Elazar ben Perata whether to flee an imperial decree, and he, afraid to say “flee” outright, pointed them to Jacob, Moses, and David, who all fled. God, by contrast, never let Israel flee in forty years in the wilderness, and he told Moses to write the journeys down so that later generations would know the miracles done for them.

The Aramaic paraphrase fills in the bare list with places and stories its readers knew. Rameses becomes Pelusium, the fortress town on Egypt's eastern edge. At Succoth Israel is sheltered by “seven glorious clouds.” Punon (v. 42) becomes the place where the LORD sent the burning serpents and the people's cry went up to heaven, which ties this list to the story told in Numbers 21:4–9.

Josephus sets Aaron's death near Petra, the city the Arabs regarded as their capital and which he says was formerly called Arce. Aaron climbs one of the high mountains that ring it, in sight of the whole army, after Moses has told him he is to die. Local tradition still marks Jebel Harun, the mountain of Aaron, above Petra, a different peak from the northern Mount Hor of 34:7.

Origen opens his homily on this chapter by admitting that hearers who enjoy the Gospels want to spit out Numbers as food too heavy for a weak stomach, yet nothing the Spirit wrote is useless. He notes that Israel made forty-two stages coming out of Egypt, and that Matthew traces Christ's coming through forty-two generations (Matthew 1:17). Christ descended by forty-two steps to the “Egypt” of this world, and the believer climbs back by forty-two stages with him. He then takes the station names one at a time as steps in the soul's progress toward God.

Jerome wrote a whole treatise on the forty-two “mansions,” or halting places, of Numbers 33. He had promised it to his friend Fabiola and finished it only after her death, sending it on to their friend Oceanus. Following Origen's lead, he treats each station as a stage in the Christian's pilgrimage from earth to heaven, the true Hebrew hurrying to pass from one to the next.

Eusebius tried to fix many of the stations on the map of Roman Palestine and Arabia, entry by entry. He calls Succoth the first station after Egypt, before the crossing of the sea, and lists Oboth and Dibon simply as stations in the desert, with nothing more to say about them. Punon he identifies with Phainon, where copper was mined in his day between Petra and Zoar.

34.overview:
The LORD gives Moses the borders of the land Israel will inherit. The south line runs from the wilderness of Zin along Edom and the end of the Salt Sea, past the ascent of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea, to the river of Egypt and the sea. The Great Sea is the west border. The north line runs from the sea to a Mount Hor and the entrance of Hamath and out to Hazar-enan, and the east line comes down by the Sea of Chinnereth and the Jordan to the Salt Sea. The LORD then names the men who will divide it: Eleazar, Joshua, and a prince from each of ten tribes.

The map leaves out land Israel already holds. Canaan, as drawn here, ends at the Jordan (v. 12), so the pastures just given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh lie outside it (vv. 13–15). The land is for nine and a half tribes.

34.hermeneutics:
From the 15th to the 12th century BC Egypt ruled a province in the Levant that its records call Canaan, reaching from the edge of Sinai north into the Lebanon valley. Benjamin Mazar identified “the entrance of Hamath” (v. 8) as a town, Lebo-hamath, modern Lebweh in the Beqaa, named in Egyptian sources, and Yohanan Aharoni argued that vv. 3–12 trace the borders of that province. Others, among them Yigal Levin, tie the map instead to the late 7th century BC, when Pharaoh Necho briefly held the same region. Either way the line describes a real political unit of the region, and it reaches farther north than Israel usually did. Israel's usual extent was “from Dan even to Beer-sheba” (Judges 20:1); only Solomon's assembly is said to come “from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt” (1 Kings 8:65).

Lots were an ordinary way to make a fair division. A small clay cube from Assur, inscribed for Yahalu, an official of Shalmaneser III (9th century BC), calls itself his lot, Akkadian *puru*, and asks that it fall to choose the year named after him. The same word stands behind Purim in Esther 3:7, “they cast Pur, that is, the lot.” Hebrew uses the same image of falling: this is the land that “shall fall unto you for an inheritance” (v. 2). A lot took the choice out of human hands, and v. 13 says the land is to be inherited by lot as the LORD commanded.

open.text: The land of Canaan with the coasts thereof

close.text: This shall be your land with the coasts thereof round about

notes: **Border:** the Hebrew word for border occurs 14 times in vv. 3–12, and a related word for the land's bounds opens and closes the frame (vv. 2, 12). The west and north sides each end with a refrain, “this shall be your … border” (vv. 6, 9).

**The princes:** the ten tribes come in pairs of later neighbors, Judah and Simeon first, Asher and Naphtali last, roughly south to north. Caleb (v. 19) is the only prince who also appears among the twelve spies of 13:4–15.

After the road behind (ch. 33) comes the land ahead. Chapter 34 draws its outer line and names who will divide it; ch. 35 sets aside cities within it. By placing the eastern tribes outside Canaan proper (vv. 13–15), the map confirms the grant of ch. 32 without changing the borders.
**Forward:** Joshua 14:1–2 opens the division with this same team, Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes, dividing by lot, and Joshua 19:51 closes it with the same names.

traditions.text: Why spell out the borders so carefully? Rashi answers that many commandments apply only inside the land, so Scripture marks exactly where they begin to bind, and he counts islands off the coast as part of the western border (v. 6). He also notes that the land “falls” to Israel because it will be divided by lot. A midrash he cites reads the word more boldly: God cast down from heaven the guardian angels of the seven nations of Canaan and showed them bound before Moses.
traditions.cite: Rashi on 34:2, 6; b. Gittin 8a; Tanhuma Masei 4

traditions.text: The midrash reads the command to describe the land (v. 2) together with the view from Pisgah in Deuteronomy 34:4, where God shows Moses the land he will not enter. It says God showed Moses not only the land but everything that would happen in it: Samson coming from Dan, Barak from Naphtali, and every generation's judges, leaders, and teachers, its righteous and its sinners. The border list becomes a preview of Israel's whole history in the land.

The Aramaic paraphrase translates the old border points into places its readers knew from the Roman and Byzantine map. The northern Mount Hor becomes Mount Umanis, the Amanus range in the far north of Syria; the east border runs past Apamea, the cave of Panias at the Jordan's source, and the snowy mountain; the river of Egypt becomes the Nile itself. The effect is a much larger land than most modern maps draw from these verses, and an ancient sign of how uncertain the border points already were.

Josephus describes how the division ordered here was carried out. Joshua sent ten men with surveyors to measure the land and to estimate how fertile each part was, because a single acre near Jericho or Jerusalem could be worth a thousand acres elsewhere. Then Joshua, with Eleazar, the elders, and the heads of the tribes, cast lots and gave each tribe a share sized to its numbers. The Talmud's account of the same division, below, also adjusts for unequal value.

The rabbis treated the land's outer border as a matter of law. For the sabbatical year the Mishnah divides the land into three zones: the land resettled by those who returned from Babylon, the wider land held by those who came up from Egypt, reaching north to the Amanah, and land beyond. The rules relax as one moves outward. The Amanah is the same Amanus range the Targum puts on the north border.

Was the land divided by lot or by the high priest's oracle? A baraita answers both. Eleazar stood wearing the Urim and Thummim, with Joshua and all Israel before him and the urns of lots beside him; he announced by the Spirit which tribe would draw which region, and then the lot came up to match. The same passage adds that shares of unequal value were evened out with money, since a measure of land in Judea was worth five in Galilee.

One prince from each tribe takes possession of the land for his tribe (v. 18), and Rashi explains that each acted as his tribe's representative. The Talmud cites a teacher, Rav Giddel, who found in this verse the principle that a person's agent stands in for him. The discussion then questions whether the verse proves it, since many of those represented were children, who cannot appoint agents.

Eusebius places Kadesh-barnea, a fixed point on the south border (v. 4), “on the desert which extends up to the city of Petra.” His gazetteer, written for Christian readers of the Bible, treats these border names as places a traveler in Roman Palestine could still locate, much as the Targum does for the north. For Eusebius, as for the rabbis, the borders were a matter of present geography, not only of history.

A thematic link. Joshua is named in v. 17 as one of the two men who will divide the land. Hebrews, reading Psalm 95, argues that Joshua (“Jesus” in the KJV, from the Greek form of the name) did not give Israel final rest by bringing them into Canaan, or God would not later have spoken of another day. A rest still remains for the people of God, beyond any border drawn on a map.

35.overview:
The LORD tells Moses that the tribes must give the Levites forty-eight towns, with pastureland measured out around each, more from large tribes and fewer from small ones. Six of these towns are to be cities of refuge, three east of the Jordan and three in Canaan, where anyone who kills a person by accident can flee from the avenger of blood. The chapter then sets out how to tell murder from accident: the weapon, the hatred, the lying in wait. The congregation judges the case. A murderer dies on the word of more than one witness, and an accidental killer must stay in his city of refuge until the high priest dies.

The last two verses give the reason behind the whole system. Shed blood pollutes the land, and nothing cleanses it except the blood of the one who shed it (v. 33). The land must stay clean because the LORD lives in it among his people (v. 34).

35.hermeneutics:
Across the ancient Near East a killing was usually settled by payment between families. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) let a man who struck another in a quarrel swear “I did not injure him wittingly” and pay; if the man died and was free-born, the price was half a mina of silver (laws 206–207). The Hittite Laws set compensation in persons: four for a killing in a quarrel, two for an accidental death (laws 1 and 3). Numbers shares the concern with intent, and the tests of vv. 16–23 sort the deliberate from the accidental much as those laws do. It refuses the payment. No “satisfaction,” Hebrew *kofer* or ransom, may be taken for a murderer, nor even for a manslayer who wants to go home early (vv. 31–32).

The Greek world knew sanctuaries where anyone in danger could take refuge. Strabo, writing about the time of Augustus, says the temple of Artemis at Ephesus was still a refuge in his day and that its bounds had been moved several times; when Mark Antony doubled them to take in part of the city, the town fell into the power of criminals, and Augustus cancelled the extension. Israel also knew asylum at the altar (Exodus 21:14; 1 Kings 2:28). Numbers moves refuge from the altar to six towns with measured bounds (vv. 26–27), and the refuge holds only for one the congregation finds did not kill on purpose (vv. 24–25). A murderer who runs there is given back to the avenger.

notes: **One word for both:** the Hebrew *rotseach* occurs 20 times. KJV renders it “slayer” or “manslayer” for the accidental killer and “murderer” for the guilty one; the tests of vv. 16–23 decide which he is.

**Counted words:** the avenger of blood (*go'el*) appears 7 times and “refuge” (*miqlat*) 11 times. “The death of the high priest” sounds three times (vv. 25, 28 twice), and once more as “the death of the priest” (v. 32).

Chapter 35 completes the arrangements for the land. After the outer borders (ch. 34) come towns inside them that belong to no tribe. The Levites, who receive no territory of their own (18:20–24), are spread among all the tribes instead. The closing line, “I the LORD dwell among the children of Israel” (v. 34), echoes the camp law of 5:3.
**Forward:** Joshua 20 names the six cities, and Joshua 21 lists the Levites' towns tribe by tribe, forty-eight in all (21:41).

traditions.text: Philo asks four questions of the refuge law: why the refuges are Levite towns, why there are six, why three lie beyond the Jordan, and why the high priest's death sets the term. The Levites, he says, are themselves fugitives who left family for God. He admits the literal law seems unfair, since one exile lasts weeks and another decades depending on when the high priest dies, and resolves it by allegory: the high priest “is not a man, but is the word of God.”

Josephus says Moses himself built the first ten of the forty-eight Levite towns before his death and set apart three of them as refuges east of the Jordan: Bezer on the border of Arabia, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan. The other three were to wait until Israel held Canaan. He ties the length of exile to the high priest under whom the killing happened, and notes that only the dead man's relatives could kill the slayer outside the city's bounds; no one else had that right.

The Mishnah worked out the details. Whether a killing was deliberate or not, the killer ran to a city of refuge, and the court of his own town brought him back for trial, then returned him to the city if he was found to be an accidental killer. Any high priest's death set him free, whether anointed with oil or installed by vestments. The mothers of high priests, the Mishnah says, sent food and clothing to the exiles so that they would not pray for their sons to die.

Signs reading “Refuge, refuge” stood at every crossroads so that a fleeing killer would not lose his way, a rule the Talmud draws from Deuteronomy 19:3, “prepare thee a way.” One teacher opened his lectures on these laws with Psalm 25:8: if God guides sinners by putting up signposts, how much more will he guide the righteous.

Why must the exile last until the high priest dies? The high priest brings God's presence to dwell in Israel and so lengthens life, while a killer drives it away and shortens life; such a man is unfit to stand in the high priest's presence. A second answer from the Talmud holds the high priest partly responsible: he should have prayed that no such accident would happen in his days.

traditions.text: Why do two and a half tribes east of the Jordan get three cities, as many as the nine and a half tribes in Canaan (v. 14)? The Talmud answers that killers were more common in Gilead, and quotes Hosea: “Gilead is a city of them that work iniquity.” Rashi repeats the answer in his comment on the verse.

The 2,000 cubits measured around each Levite town (v. 5) became a basis for the Sabbath limit, the distance a person may walk beyond his town on the Sabbath. Rabbi Akiva reconciled the 1,000 cubits of v. 4 with the 2,000 of v. 5 this way: the first is the Levites' open land, and the second marks the Sabbath boundary. Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean, disagreed, giving the Levites 1,000 cubits of open land plus 2,000 more for fields and vineyards. Another passage reaches the 2,000-cubit limit by a chain of word links from “place” in Exodus 16:29 to the refuge laws of vv. 26–27.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On Flight from the World
traditions.text: Ambrose takes up Philo's four questions almost point for point, but reads them as a call to flee the world. The Levites, who left parents and kin to cling to God alone, are the model, and Ambrose applies Christ's call to deny oneself and follow him to them. The six cities are stages of refuge, the first being knowledge of the Word and life after his pattern, the others contemplation of creation, of God's majesty, and of his mercy, then keeping what the law commands and avoiding what it forbids. Like Philo, he reads the high priest's death as more than a date.

A thematic link. Hebrews describes believers as those who “have fled for refuge” to the hope set before them, anchored by an oath God cannot break. Two verses on, it names Jesus as high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Christian readers have long set that passage beside the refuge in this law, which lasts until the high priest's death, though Hebrews itself does not mention the cities.

36.overview:
The heads of the clan of Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh, come to Moses with a problem left by the ruling for Zelophehad's daughters (27:1–11). If the daughters marry men of other tribes, their father's land will pass to those tribes for good, and even the jubilee will not bring it back. Moses answers by the word of the LORD that the clan is right. The daughters may marry whom they think best, so long as the husband is from their father's tribe, and every heiress after them is bound by the same rule. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah marry their cousins, and the land stays in Manasseh.

The book ends on a property case. Numbers opened by counting the tribes family by family (1:2), and it closes by making sure each tribe keeps the share it was counted for, so that no inheritance will “remove from one tribe to another” (v. 9).

36.hermeneutics:
Daughters inheriting was rare in the ancient Near East but not unheard of. Gudea, ruler of Lagash about 2100 BC, records that during his reign, in a house with no son, the daughter could stand as its heir (Statue B vii 44–46). Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian records show a few fathers naming a daughter heir, often with conditions attached. Numbers follows the same pattern across two chapters: the daughters win the right to inherit in ch. 27, and here a condition is attached to protect the estate.

The condition answers a fear found wherever land was tied to families. At Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (15th–14th centuries BC) family land was not supposed to be sold outside the family, so buyers had themselves formally “adopted” as sons, and one wealthy man, Tehip-tilla, was adopted by family after family to collect their fields. The law of Israel says the land is the LORD's and may not be sold for ever (Leviticus 25:23), and the clan of Gilead sees that marriage could do what sale could not. An heiress who married out would carry her father's fields into another tribe, and no rule of redemption would apply. Requiring heiresses to marry within the tribe closes that gap without taking back the daughters' right.

notes: **Key words:** “inheritance” (*nachalah*) comes 17 times in thirteen verses and “tribe” 14 times. The ruling twice forbids land to “remove” from tribe to tribe (vv. 7, 9).

**Two closings:** v. 13, “These are the commandments and the judgments,” echoes the last verse of Leviticus (27:34). Leviticus ends with the laws given at Sinai; Numbers ends with those given on the plains of Moab.

Chapter 36 is a sequel to 27:1–11, held back to the end of the book so that the last case in Numbers concerns keeping the land in the tribes. Verse 13 closes the whole block of law given on the plains of Moab, where Israel has been camped since 22:1.

**Forward:** the daughters receive their land among Manasseh's ten portions (Joshua 17:3–6), and Deuteronomy opens with Moses speaking in the same place, “on this side Jordan, in the land of Moab” (Deuteronomy 1:5).

traditions.text: Tobit, a story set among the exiles of the northern tribes, warns its hero's son to take a wife from his father's tribe and not a stranger. Later the angel tells young Tobias that Sara, Raguel's only daughter and heir, belongs to him because he alone is her kinsman, and that Raguel cannot give her to another “according to the law of Moses” without incurring guilt. When Raguel gives her, he tells Tobias to take her after that law. The book treats the heiress rule of Numbers 36 as binding long after the conquest and far from the land.

Josephus tells the whole Zelophehad story in a few lines, as a question the chief men of Manasseh brought to Moses about an eminent man of their tribe who left daughters and no sons. In his version Moses answers that daughters who marry within their tribe take the estate with them, while those who marry into another tribe leave it in their father's tribe. He ends with the general law that every inheritance stays in its own tribe.

The rabbis praised Zelophehad's daughters as wise, as skilled interpreters of scripture, and as righteous. Their wisdom showed in how they framed their claim in ch. 27: had their father left a son, they said, they would not have spoken. As proof of their righteousness the Talmud notes that they did not hurry to marry but waited for husbands fit for them, and one teacher says even the youngest was at least forty when she married.

The daughters are named in a different order in v. 11 (Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, Noah) than in 27:1 and Joshua 17:3 (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah). The Talmud explains that here they are listed by age, the order in which they married, and elsewhere by wisdom. Rashi takes the shifting order to mean they were all of equal worth. A rabbinic rule follows from the two orders: at study and in court, seat people by wisdom; at a meal, by age.

Was the rule meant for every generation? Shmuel taught that the daughters were free to marry anyone, and that the words about their father's tribe were good advice to marry someone suited to them. A baraita in the same passage limits the rule to the generation that received the land. The Targum writes the limit into v. 6 itself: the command is “not for the generations” that come after the division of the land, but for the daughters of Zelophehad.

traditions.text: The Mishnah calls the fifteenth of Av one of the two happiest days in Israel's year, when the daughters of Jerusalem went out in borrowed white clothes to dance in the vineyards, so that no girl who lacked fine clothes would be shamed. The Talmud asks why the day was so joyful. One answer is that on that day the tribes were first permitted to marry into one another, the ban that grew out of the clan of Gilead's complaint having been lifted. Another answer links it to the day Benjamin was readmitted after the war of Judges 21.

Rashi explains the clan's worry about the jubilee (v. 4). A field that is sold goes back to its owner in the jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10), but an inheritance is not a sale, so it never goes back. Marriage into another tribe would make the loss permanent, and the jubilee would only confirm it. He also records a reading from the Sifra: since the Hebrew of v. 4 can be read as a condition, if there is a jubilee, it hints that the jubilee would one day cease to be kept.

Eusebius quotes Julius Africanus' long letter explaining the different genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke through a levirate marriage, then adds a point of his own. Once Joseph's line is traced, he says, Mary's is shown too, because she must have been of the same tribe: the law of Moses did not allow marriage between tribes, and the command is to marry within one's own family and lineage “so that the inheritance may not pass from tribe to tribe.” Eusebius reads Numbers 36 as a permanent rule, where the Talmud and Targum limited it to one generation.
